title: Shell scripting I – variables and arguments
text:
1 Introduction

1.1 Learning goals
This week, you will learn how to write shell scripts to run programs with command-line interfaces (CLIs), like various bioinformatics tools. In this session, we will talk about:

What shell scripts are
Writing a shell script that runs FastQC
Boilerplate shell script header lines: shebang and safe settings
Shell variables
Command-line arguments to scripts
“Logging” statements that report what a script is doing



1.2 Getting ready

At https://ondemand.osc.edu, start a VS Code session in /fs/ess/PAS3493/people/$USER.
Open a terminal and create and then navigate to a week07 dir.
Within the week07 dir, create a dir scripts (but don’t navigate there).

title: Shell scripting I – variables and arguments
text:
2 Introduction to shell scripts

Running command-line programs
Last week, we saw a first example of running a bioinformatics tool (FastQC) from the command line. This was quite similar to how we ran basic shell commands in the previous weeks, both in terms of the structure of the commands (commands, options, and arguments), and how we ran them interactively in the terminal.
And while many bioinformatics tools are run with similarly structured commands, it’s best not to run them interactively in the terminal for real analyses. Instead, it’s better to run them via shell scripts: plain-text files that contain shell code and can be executed as a single command, and be submitted as batch jobs that will run even if you log out of the system.


Why use shell scripts
Some general reasons why it can be beneficial to use shell scripts instead of running code interactively line-by-line:

It is a good way to save and organize your code.
You can easily rerun scripts and re-use them in similar contexts.

And importantly for our purposes at OSC, we can submit scripts as “batch jobs”, which allows us to:

Easily perform long-running analyses (taking many hours or even multiple days)
Run analyses many times simultaneously, such as for different files/samples
Run analyses while being able to disconnect from the system. We can submit a script, log out from OSC and shut down our computer, and it will still run.

Most of these reasons don’t apply (as much) to quick shell commands, but they are very important when running bioinformatics tools. We’ll talk about batch jobs in two weeks, and will start learning about shell scripts today.






TipRecap: Bash vs. shell (Click to expand)





So far, we’ve mostly talked about the Unix shell and shell scripts. From today onwards, we’ll also see the term “Bash” more.
Recall the difference we talked about in the Unix shell intro session: there are multiple Unix shell language variants and the specific one we’ve been using is Bash (which is by far the most common).
Our shell scripts are therefore in the Bash language, can be specifically called Bash scripts, and can be run with the bash command.

title: Shell scripting I – variables and arguments
text:
3 Your first shell scripts
Let’s start with the simplest possible kind of script: one that contains a single command. Create a script hello.sh (shell scripts usually have the extension .sh) as follows:
# Create an empty file
touch scripts/hello.sh
Open the file in your VS Code editor pane, and type or paste the following line inside the script, and save it:


scripts/hello.sh

echo "Hello world"

That’s it — this one-line file is a functional shell script! One way of running a script is by typing bash followed by the path to the script:
bash scripts/hello.sh
Hello world
Running the script has the exact same effect as typing echo "Hello world" directly in the terminal.
Let’s make one more very basic script and run it:
touch scripts/info.sh


scripts/info.sh

date
pwd

bash scripts/info.sh
Mon Oct  5 14:13:31 EDT 2026
/fs/ess/PAS3493/people/jelmer/week07
This shows the basic idea of a shell script: when you run it, its commands are executed one by one, from top to bottom, just as if you had typed them in the terminal. (Also note that pwd printed week07, not week07/scripts: commands in a script run in your working dir, not in the dir where the script is stored.)
In practice, you wouldn’t bother writing a script for simple commands like these. Scripts pay off for commands that you want to save and rerun, and/or that take a long time to run, such as those that run bioinformatics tools. So let’s move on to a more useful example.

title: Shell scripting I – variables and arguments
text:
4 A script to run FastQC

4.1 The initial script
In the previous lecture, you ran FastQC for a FASTQ file by executing the following commands directly in the terminal:
mkdir -p results/fastqc
apptainer exec oras://community.wave.seqera.io/library/fastqc:0.12.1--104d26ddd9519960 \
    fastqc --outdir results/fastqc ../garrigos/fastq/S63_R1.fastq.gz
Let’s put these commands in a shell script instead. Create a script fastqc.sh:
touch scripts/fastqc.sh
Open the file and type or paste the following inside the script:


scripts/fastqc.sh

# Create the output dir if needed
mkdir -p results/fastqc

# Run FastQC with its container
apptainer exec oras://community.wave.seqera.io/library/fastqc:0.12.1--104d26ddd9519960 \
    fastqc --outdir results/fastqc ../garrigos/fastq/S63_R1.fastq.gz


Like your first two scripts, this script simply contains shell commands — a couple of notes:

The output dir is created with mkdir -p
Recall that FastQC won’t create the output dir for you. Using mkdir -p inside the script ensures that the output dir exists, whether or not it existed before running the script — see the box below for details.






TipMore about the -p option to mkdir (Click to expand)





Using mkdir’s -p option does two things at once, both of which are very useful when including this command in a script:

It will enable mkdir to create multiple levels of directories at once (i.e., to act recursively): by default, mkdir errors out if the parent directory/ies of the specified directory don’t yet exist.
mkdir newdir1/newdir2
mkdir: cannot create directory ‘newdir1/newdir2’: No such file or directory
# This successfully creates both directories:
mkdir -p newdir1/newdir2
If the directory already exists, with -p, mkdir won’t do anything and won’t return an error. Without this option, mkdir would return an error, which would in turn make the script stop (given the settings you’ll learn about below):
mkdir newdir1/newdir2
mkdir: cannot create directory ‘newdir1/newdir2’: File exists
# This does nothing since the dirs already exist
mkdir -p newdir1/newdir2




The file paths are relative to your working dir, not to the script
As you saw with info.sh, relative paths in a script, like results/fastqc, are interpreted relative to your working dir at the time you run the script, not relative to where the script itself is stored. This means that this script only works as intended if you run it from your week07 dir: from any other dir, ../garrigos/fastq/S63_R1.fastq.gz would point to a non-existent file.

Let’s run the script:
bash scripts/fastqc.sh
INFO:    Using cached SIF image
INFO:    gocryptfs not found, will not be able to use gocryptfs
application/gzip
Started analysis of S63_R1.fastq.gz
Approx 5% complete for S63_R1.fastq.gz
Approx 10% complete for S63_R1.fastq.gz
Approx 15% complete for S63_R1.fastq.gz
# [...output truncated...]
Analysis complete for S63_R1.fastq.gz
Nice! Next, you’ll learn about two header lines that are good practice to add to every shell script. But first, let’s install a VS Code extension that will alert you to the first of these.




4.2 Install the Shellcheck extension
Shellcheck is a really useful VS Code extension that checks your shell scripts for errors and bad practices. Let’s install it:

In the narrow side bar, click on the Extensions icon.
In the wide side bar, search for shellcheck (by timonwong) and install it.












4.3 Shebang line
If Shellcheck is working, you should now see a red squiggly line on the first line of your fastqc.sh script:





Hover over it to see the warning: Shellcheck wants you to add a “shebang” line. (More generally, keep an eye out for these squiggly lines — Shellcheck will also flag things like typos in variable names.)





A so-called “shebang” line is used as the very first line of a script to indicate which computer language the script uses. Add it to the top of your fastqc.sh script:


scripts/fastqc.sh (excerpt)

#!/bin/bash

It starts with #! (hash-bang), followed by the path to the program that should run the script: here, Bash, whose executable is located at /bin/bash. Adding a shebang line to every shell script is good practice, especially when you submit your script to OSC’s Slurm queue, as we’ll do later.


4.4 Safe shell settings
Some default settings of the Bash shell are bad ideas inside scripts:

A script keeps running after a command fails, executing all remaining lines anyway. At best, this wastes time, but it can also produce results downstream of the error that are wrong — and if your script prints a lot of output, you may not even notice the error message.
When you reference a non-existent (“unset”) variable, the shell silently replaces it with nothing (you’ll learn more about variables below).

To make shell scripts safer and error out when such things happen, we can apply a few “safe” settings by adding a single line of code to the script.
Add this line to the top of your fastqc.sh script, right after the shebang line:


scripts/fastqc.sh (excerpt)

#!/bin/bash
set -euo pipefail








TipWhy place the set command near the top of the script?



The safe shell settings will apply to the lines of code in the script that come after the set command, which is why it’s important to place the set command near the top of the script. This way, the settings will be in effect for the entire script.








NoteWhat does each of these options do? (Click to expand)





With these settings, the script stops with an error message if:

-e — a command fails.
-u — a non-existent variable is referenced.
-o pipefail — any command in a shell “pipeline” (e.g., sort | uniq) fails. (Without this option, -e only notices failures of the last command in a pipeline.)






4.5 Rerunning the script with the new header lines
Your fastqc.sh script should now contain the following:


scripts/fastqc.sh

#!/bin/bash
set -euo pipefail

# Create the output dir if needed
mkdir -p results/fastqc

# Run FastQC with its container
apptainer exec oras://community.wave.seqera.io/library/fastqc:0.12.1--104d26ddd9519960 \
    fastqc --outdir results/fastqc ../garrigos/fastq/S63_R1.fastq.gz

Run the script again (this will overwrite the output files from the previous run, which is fine):
bash scripts/fastqc.sh
INFO:    Using cached SIF image
INFO:    gocryptfs not found, will not be able to use gocryptfs
application/gzip
Started analysis of S63_R1.fastq.gz
Approx 5% complete for S63_R1.fastq.gz
# [...output truncated...]
Analysis complete for S63_R1.fastq.gz
That didn’t change the output, but we confirmed that the script still works.






NoteCan I run scripts without the bash command? (Click to expand)





By default, you need to run a script with the bash command, like bash scripts/fastqc.sh. When doing so, you are telling the computer to run the script with Bash (and the shebang line is actually ignored; Bash will be used to run the script regardless of what the shebang line says).
It’s possible to execute scripts by only typing their path, using syntax like:
# If the script is in a different dir:
scripts/fastqc.sh

# If the script is in your working dir:
./fastqc.sh
To be able to do this, the script:

Must have a shebang line so the computer knows which language to execute the script with
Must be “executable”. You can make it executable by running:
# Add 'execute permissions' for fastqc.sh:
chmod +x scripts/fastqc.sh


Finally, why do you need ./ in the second example above (./fastqc.sh), where the script is in your working dir? The ./ is necessary to make explicit that you’re referring to a file name and not a command. With yet another step, it is possible to add your script to the computer’s registry of commands/programs, but we won’t cover that here (see this optional self-study page if you’re curious).





4.6 The problem with “hard-coded” file paths
Your script works, but it can only do one thing: run FastQC for the file S63_R1.fastq.gz, with output going to results/fastqc. These file paths are “hard-coded” in the script: to run FastQC for the R2 file of the same sample, or for any other sample, you would have to create a new script or edit the script every time.
It would be better to make the script flexible so that it can run FastQC for any FASTQ file, with output going to any output dir. We’ll do this in two steps:

Using shell variables to define the file paths only once, at the top of the script
Using command-line arguments to pass the file paths to the script when you run it, so you won’t have to edit the script at all

title: Shell scripting I – variables and arguments
text:
5 Shell variables

5.1 Variables
In week 3, you learned about environment variables like $USER and $HOME, which are pre-set by the system. But you can also define your own variables in the shell and in scripts, which is especially useful for items that:

Are referred to repeatedly and/or
Are subject to change

For example, variables may be useful for settings like the paths to input and output files and parameter values for programs. When using variables, these can be changed in one place (the variable definition) instead of having to change them in multiple places throughout your code.

Assigning and referencing variables
To assign a value to a variable in the shell, use the syntax variable_name=value:
# Assign a FASTQ file path to a variable with the name "fastq":
fastq=../garrigos/fastq/S63_R1.fastq.gz

# Assign an output dir path to a variable with the name "outdir":
outdir=results/fastqc
A variable can contain any value: besides file paths, it could for example be any word (e.g., treatment=inoculated) or number (e.g., nr_samples=200).






No spaces are allowed around the equals sign: outdir = results/fastqc fails, because the shell would try to run a command called outdir.



To reference a variable (i.e., to access its value) by its name:

Always put a dollar sign $ in front of it: outdir becomes $outdir.
To be safe, also double-quote it: $outdir becomes "$outdir".

As before with the environment variables $USER and $HOME, use echo to see what values your variables contain:
echo "$fastq"
../garrigos/fastq/S63_R1.fastq.gz
echo "$outdir"
results/fastqc
More usefully, you can use a variable anywhere you would otherwise type its value. For example:
ls -lh "$fastq"
-rw-rw----+ 1 jelmer PAS0471 21M Sep  9 13:46 ../garrigos/fastq/S63_R1.fastq.gz
mkdir "$outdir"
mkdir: cannot create directory ‘results/fastqc’: File exists
(We get an error here because the dir already exists, and we didn’t use the -p option, but that proves that the command was executed as intended.)







NoteHow to name variables



Some rules for variable names in the shell — they:

Can contain letters, numbers, and underscores
Cannot contain spaces, periods (.), dashes (-), or other special symbols1
Cannot start with a number

Ideally, variable names are descriptive, like $fastq and $outdir above and not cryptic like $x.
Like with file names, you can distinguish words using capitalization (“camelCase”, $inputFile) or underscores (“snake case”, $input_file). In this course, we’ll mostly use lowercase variable names, except for “constants” in scripts, which we’ll write in uppercase — see the box at the end of the arguments section.





5.2 Quoting variables
I have mentioned that it is good practice to quote variables (i.e. to use "$outdir" instead of $outdir). One reason is that quoting variables prevents “word splitting”, which is when the shell interprets spaces in a variable’s value as separators between multiple words. Let’s look at an example:

Say that you have a variable today, and its value contains spaces:
today="Mon, Oct 5"
Printing the value of the variable with or without quotes doesn’t seem to make a difference:
echo "$today"
Mon, Oct 5
echo $today
Mon, Oct 5
Next, you try to create a file with a name that includes this variable, and you don’t quote it:
touch README_$today.txt
ls
5.txt  Oct  README_Mon,  results  scripts
Oops! The shell performed “word splitting” to split the value into three separate units. As a result, three files were created: 5.txt, Oct, and README_Mon,.
This can be avoided by quoting the variable:
touch README_"$today".txt

# The 4th file listed below is the one we intended to create all along:
ls
5.txt   Oct   README_Mon,  'README_Mon, Oct 5.txt'   results   scripts








TipWord splitting is like unescaped spaces in file names



This is the same behavior you saw with spaces in file names in week 4, where rm -r extra data removed the data dir instead of the extra data dir: the shell treats spaces as separators between arguments.
The difference is that with a variable, the space is hidden inside its value, so you can’t see it when you look at the command — which is why it’s a good habit to always quote variables. And just like "$today" above, quoting a file name (rm -r "extra data") is one way to prevent the problem.


Not quoting a variable can also cause confusion about where the variable name ends (see the exercise below).

 Self-study exercise 1: Where does a variable name end?
First, assign a sample ID to a variable:
sample_id="A1"
For each command below, first predict what it will print, and then run it to check your prediction.

echo $sample_id.fastq.gz


 Click for the solution

This works as intended, because a period can’t be part of a variable name, so the shell knows that the variable name is sample_id:
A1.fastq.gz

echo $sample_id_R1.fastq.gz (the intent is to print A1_R1.fastq.gz)


 Click for the solution

This prints only .fastq.gz!
Underscores and letters can be part of a variable name, so the shell looked for a variable called sample_id_R1. That variable doesn’t exist, and the shell silently replaced it with nothing (!):
.fastq.gz

echo "Processing sample: $sample_ID"


 Click for the solution

Variable names are case-sensitive, so $sample_ID is a different, non-existent variable. Again, the shell doesn’t complain, it just replaces it with nothing:
Processing sample:
This is why the set -u setting you added to your script is so useful: it makes a script fail with an error message instead.


Finally:

Fix the command from item 2 so that it prints A1_R1.fastq.gz.


 Click for the solution

Quote the variable, so that the shell knows where the variable name ends:
echo "$sample_id"_R1.fastq.gz
A1_R1.fastq.gz











NoteQuoting as “escaping” special characters, and double vs. single quotes (Click to expand)





By double-quoting a variable, you essentially escape (“turn off”) the default special meaning of the space as a word separator, asking the shell to interpret it instead as a literal space.
Similarly, double quotes will escape other special characters in the shell, like shell wildcards. Compare:

Due to shell expansion, this will show all files in the current working dir:
echo *
5.txt Oct README_Mon, README_Mon, Oct 5.txt results scripts
But with the * enclosed in double quotes, it will simply print the literal “*” character:
echo "*"
*

However, double quotes do not turn off the special meaning of $ (which is to denote a string as a variable):

With double quotes, the shell will still interpret $today as a variable:
echo "$today"
Mon, Oct 5
With single quotes, the shell will interpret $today literally as a string, and not as a variable:
echo '$today'
$today











TipCurly braces notation for variables: ${myvar} (Click to expand)





The $var notation to refer to a variable in the shell is actually an abbreviation of the full notation, which includes curly braces:
echo ${today}
Mon, Oct 5
Putting variable names between curly braces will also make it clear where the variable name begins and ends (so echo ${sample_id}_R1.fastq.gz would also have solved item 4 of the exercise above), although it does not prevent word splitting:
touch README_${today}_final.txt

ls -1 *final*
5_final.txt
But you can combine curly braces and quoting:
touch README_"${today}"_final.txt

ls -1 *final*
 5_final.txt
'README_Mon, Oct 5_final.txt'






5.3 Using variables in your FastQC script
Now, let’s change the FastQC script to use variables for the container URI, the input file, and the output dir:


scripts/fastqc.sh

#!/bin/bash
set -euo pipefail

# FastQC container
CONTAINER=oras://community.wave.seqera.io/library/fastqc:0.12.1--104d26ddd9519960

# Define in- and outputs
fastq=../garrigos/fastq/S63_R1.fastq.gz
outdir=results/fastqc

# Create the output dir if needed
mkdir -p "$outdir"

# Run FastQC with its container
apptainer exec "$CONTAINER" fastqc --outdir "$outdir" "$fastq"

This is an improvement: the container URI and file paths are now clearly defined in one place at the top of the script, and the output dir, which is used twice, would only need to be changed once.
(Also, the apptainer exec command has become short enough to fit on a single line. But why is CONTAINER in uppercase? See the box on “constants” below.)
However, you’d still need to edit the script to run it for a different FASTQ file. Let’s see how we can make this more flexible using command-line arguments.






TipShellcheck warns you about unused variables



While editing the script, you may have noticed orange squiggly lines under variable names, for example:





Above, it’s warning that the script has defined variables that are not used (yet). That’s a good thing to know about, because it may indicate a typo in the variable name, or that you forgot to use the variable in your code.
Conversely, Shellcheck also warns you when you reference a variable that hasn’t been assigned.
If you finished the script as shown above, the squiggly lines should disappear.

title: Shell scripting I – variables and arguments
text:
6 Command-line arguments for scripts
When you run a script, you can pass arguments to it, such as an input file and an output dir. That way, one script can process any file without being edited. And you can run the same script for many files at once (in parallel), which can dramatically speed up your analysis. All shell scripts we’ll write in this course will accept arguments.

6.1 Executing a script with arguments
Executing a script with arguments is just like providing a command like ls with arguments:

Pass two file names as arguments to ls:
ls data/sampleA.fastq.gz data/sampleB.fastq.gz
Pass two arguments, an input file and an output dir, to a script:
bash scripts/fastqc.sh data/sampleA.fastq.gz results/fastqc



6.2 Accessing arguments inside the script
Inside the script, any arguments you pass are automatically assigned to variables named after their position:

Any first argument will be assigned to the variable $1 (above: data/sampleA.fastq.gz).
Any second argument will be assigned to $2 (above: results/fastqc).
Any third argument will be assigned to $3 — and so on.

However, the script won’t use these “placeholder” variables unless you reference them in your code. Let’s see how to do that.






NoteOther variables that are automatically available inside scripts




$# contains the number of command-line arguments passed to the script (this can be useful for validation — see this section of the optional self-study page).
$0 contains the script’s path (as typed when running it, e.g. scripts/fastqc.sh)2.





6.3 Using arguments in your FastQC script
In your FastQC script, let’s replace the hard-coded file paths with $1 and $2:


scripts/fastqc.sh

#!/bin/bash
set -euo pipefail

# FastQC container
CONTAINER=oras://community.wave.seqera.io/library/fastqc:0.12.1--104d26ddd9519960

# Copy the placeholder variables
fastq="$1"
outdir="$2"

# Create the output dir if needed
mkdir -p "$outdir"

# Run FastQC with its container
apptainer exec "$CONTAINER" fastqc --outdir "$outdir" "$fastq"

Only the two lines that define $fastq and $outdir changed: their values now come from the command line instead of being hard-coded.
You could use the $1-style variables throughout your script, like so:


fastqc.sh (alternative - don't use)

apptainer exec "$CONTAINER" fastqc --outdir "$2" "$1"

But I recommend always copying them to descriptively named variables like we did here. This is better because:

It will make your script easier to understand for others and for your future self
It will make it less likely that you accidentally mix up the variables

Now, you can run the script for any FASTQ file without editing it — for example, for both FASTQ files of sample S63:
bash scripts/fastqc.sh ../garrigos/fastq/S63_R1.fastq.gz results/fastqc
Started analysis of S63_R1.fastq.gz
Approx 5% complete for S63_R1.fastq.gz
# [...output truncated...]
Analysis complete for S63_R1.fastq.gz
bash scripts/fastqc.sh ../garrigos/fastq/S63_R2.fastq.gz results/fastqc
Started analysis of S63_R2.fastq.gz
Approx 5% complete for S63_R2.fastq.gz
# [...output truncated...]
Analysis complete for S63_R2.fastq.gz


6.4 Safe settings in action
Our script currently requires two arguments: the input FASTQ file and the output dir. No default values are set for these variables, so if you forget to pass them to the script, it won’t be able to run successfully. Let’s see what happens exactly if you don’t pass arguments to the script:
bash scripts/fastqc.sh
scripts/fastqc.sh: line 8: $1: unbound variable
Thanks to our safe settings with set, the script stops right away, with an error message that tells you exactly what went wrong: the variable $1 doesn’t exist (“is unbound”).
Without this setting, the script would have continued with empty values for $fastq and $outdir, leading to much more confusing error messages downstream.

 In-class exercise 1: A script with two arguments

Create a script scripts/printname.sh with the following contents:


scripts/printname.sh

#!/bin/bash
set -euo pipefail

first_name="$1"
last_name="$2"

echo "This script will print a first and a last name"
echo "First name: $first_name"
echo "Last name: $last_name"

What do you think the script’s output will be when you run it with the arguments John and Doe like so:
bash scripts/printname.sh John Doe


Next, in each of the three scenarios described below, think about what might happen. After you have thought about it, run the script as instructed in the scenario to test your prediction.

Double-quoting the entire name, e.g. bash scripts/printname.sh "John Doe".

Passing three names, e.g. bash scripts/printname.sh John Michael Doe.

After “commenting out” the line with set settings, running the script without passing arguments to it.


 Click here to learn what “commenting out” means

You can deactivate a line of code without removing it by inserting a # as the first character of that line. This is often referred to as “commenting out” code. For example, below I’ve commented out the ls command, and nothing will happen if I run this line:
#ls


Back to your FastQC script: what do you think will happen if you accidentally swap the two arguments? Think about it first, then try it:
bash scripts/fastqc.sh results/fastqc ../garrigos/fastq/S63_R1.fastq.gz




 Self-study exercise 2: Quoting arguments
What do you expect the output to be when you run your printname.sh script from In-class exercise 1 as follows? Make a prediction, then run it to check.
bash scripts/printname.sh "$USER" '$USER'
Hint: see the box on double vs. single quotes above.


 Click for the solution

The shell expands variables before passing arguments to the script, so the first argument is your username. The single quotes prevent that expansion, so the second argument is the literal string $USER:
This script will print a first and a last name
First name: jelmer
Last name: $USER









WarningWhy ignoring non-existent variables can be dangerous (Click to expand)





The shell’s default behavior of ignoring the referencing of unset variables can lead to accidental file removal in a couple of ways. Here are two examples:

Using a variable, you try to remove temporary files whose names start with temp_:
temp_prefix="temp_"
rm "$tmp_prefix"*
Using a variable, you try to remove a temporary directory:
tempdir=output/tmp
rm -rf $tmpdir/*

In both examples, there is a similar typo: temp vs. tmp, which means that we are referencing a (likely) non-existent variable.

In the first example, rm "$tmp_prefix"* would have been interpreted as rm *, because the non-existent variable is simply ignored. Therefore, we would have removed all files in the current working directory.
In the second example, along similar lines, rm -rf $tmpdir/* would have been interpreted as rm -rf /*. This would attempt to remove the computer’s entire filesystem: recall that a leading / in a path is a computer’s root directory (-r makes the removal recursive and -f forces removal).

These kinds of accidents are especially likely to happen inside scripts, where it is common to use variables and to work non-interactively.
Luckily, you can’t remove system files this way, neither at OSC nor (without “admin” rights) on your own computer. But rm -rf /* would still remove every file that you do have permission to remove. At OSC, that includes your Home dir and project dirs — and since project files are often group-writable (see the rw-rw---- in ls -l output), possibly also your labmates’ files! This is one more reason to always use set -u in your scripts.










TipHard-coded settings as “constants” (Click to expand)





Our FastQC script gets the input file and output dir from arguments, but the container URI is still hard-coded in the script. That’s fine: you could also use arguments for settings like the container or program options (e.g., a quality threshold), but a long list of arguments makes a script confusing to use.
When you do hard-code settings that may change, store them in variables that you clearly define at the top of your script, like we did with CONTAINER. Such variables are often called “constants”: they make the script easier to maintain, but unlike variables that get their values from arguments, they can’t be changed from outside the script.
In this course, we’ll name constants in uppercase (e.g., CONTAINER) and most other variables in lowercase, so the two are easy to tell apart. (Conventions vary, though: some people use uppercase for all shell variables, and environment variables like $USER and $HOME are always uppercase.)

title: Shell scripting I – variables and arguments
text:
7 “Logging” statements

7.1 Add logging statements to your script
It is often useful to have your shell script report or “log” what it is doing. For instance:

The date and time at which the script was run
The arguments that were passed to the script
The designated output dirs/files
Perhaps even summaries of the output (we won’t do this here)

This information can help with troubleshooting and record-keeping.
Let’s add some code to the FastQC script to make it produce logging information:


scripts/fastqc.sh

#!/bin/bash
set -euo pipefail

# FastQC container
CONTAINER=oras://community.wave.seqera.io/library/fastqc:0.12.1--104d26ddd9519960

# Copy the placeholder variables
fastq="$1"
outdir="$2"

# Initial logging
echo "Starting script fastqc.sh"
date
echo "Input FASTQ file:   $fastq"
echo "Output dir:         $outdir"
echo

# Create the output dir if needed
mkdir -p "$outdir"

# Run FastQC with its container
apptainer exec "$CONTAINER" fastqc --outdir "$outdir" "$fastq"

# Final logging
echo
echo "Used FastQC version:"
apptainer exec "$CONTAINER" fastqc --version
echo
echo "Successfully finished script fastqc.sh"
date

A couple of notes about the lines that were added to the script above:

A “marker line” Successfully finished script indicates that the end of the script was reached. This is useful because of your set settings: seeing this line printed means that no errors were encountered.
Running date at the beginning and end of the script is one way to be able to see how long the script took to run, and to keep a record of when it was run.
Printing the input file names can be particularly useful for troubleshooting.
The lines that only have echo will simply print a blank line, basically as a separator between sections.
For scripts that run bioinformatics tools, it’s a good idea to include a line that prints the program version.



7.2 Run your final FastQC script
Make sure you’ve updated your scripts/fastqc.sh script with the code from the box above, and then run your final FastQC script again for one FASTQ file:
bash scripts/fastqc.sh ../garrigos/fastq/S63_R1.fastq.gz results/fastqc
Starting script fastqc.sh
Mon Oct  5 14:23:13 EDT 2026
Input FASTQ file:   ../garrigos/fastq/S63_R1.fastq.gz
Output dir:         results/fastqc

INFO:    Using cached SIF image
INFO:    gocryptfs not found, will not be able to use gocryptfs
application/gzip
Started analysis of S63_R1.fastq.gz
Approx 5% complete for S63_R1.fastq.gz
# [...output truncated...]
Analysis complete for S63_R1.fastq.gz

Used FastQC version:
INFO:    Using cached SIF image
INFO:    gocryptfs not found, will not be able to use gocryptfs
FastQC v0.12.1

Successfully finished script fastqc.sh
Mon Oct  5 14:23:19 EDT 2026
Great! This logging information is useful as a record of what was done, and for example allows you to see that the script took only 6 seconds to run for this small FASTQ file. Though currently, the logging information is only printed to the screen, which is not ideal for record-keeping. In two weeks, we’ll run scripts as batch jobs, and the logging information will be printed to a text file that you can keep along with the output files.

title: Shell scripting I – variables and arguments
text:
8 Recap and next steps
In this session, you’ve learned the basics of shell scripts, using a script that runs FastQC as an example. As you’ve seen, shell scripts mostly consist of “regular” Unix shell code, but with some added bells and whistles like:

Boilerplate shell script header lines: shebang and safe settings
Variables, to clearly define settings like file paths in one place
Command-line arguments, which are available in variables in the script and make the script flexible
Logging statements, which report what the script is doing

In the next class, you will learn how to write loops to easily run a script many times, such as for every FASTQ file or every sample in a dataset.

title: Using software at OSC: modules and containers
text:
1 Introduction

1.1 Learning goals
As we discussed in the previous lecture, you can use software at OSC by loading “modules” with system-wide installations, or by using containers or Conda. In this session, you will learn to use modules and containers, while an optional self-study page covers Conda.
We’ll use the program FastQC to illustrate how to use modules and containers, so along the way, you’ll also learn what FastQC does and how to run it.


1.2 Setting up



The usual

At https://ondemand.osc.edu, start a VS Code session in /fs/ess/PAS3493/people/$USER.
Open a terminal. In it, create and then navigate to a week06 dir.
Optional: Create a new Markdown file for class notes and save it in your week06 dir.



Install a VS Code extension
VS Code extensions are small programs that add extra functionality to the IDE. We’ll install several of these during the course, starting now with a VS Code extension for viewing HTML files, since we’ll need to look at an HTML file later in this lecture (without this extension, HTML files would only open as plain-text source documents).

In the Activity Bar, click the Extensions icon at the bottom (see screenshot on the right).
The wide side bar now shows the Extensions view. In the search box at the top, type “HTML preview”.
The first result should be the extension called “HTML Preview” by Thomas Haakon Townsend. Click the blue “Install” button to install it.
When asked if you “trust the publisher”, click the blue “Trust Publisher & Install” button.














Activity Bar, with the Extensions icon (bottom) highlighted.

title: Using software at OSC: modules and containers
text:
2 Intermezzo: The FastQC software
As an example piece of bioinformatics software, we will use FastQC (Andrews 2010) in this session. FastQC is a ubiquitous tool for quality control of FASTQ files. Running FastQC (or a similar program) is the first step in nearly any high-throughput sequencing project, and it is a good introductory example of a CLI program.
For each FASTQ file that it analyzes, FastQC outputs an HTML file with about a dozen graphs showing different QC (Quality Control) metrics. Typically, the most important one is this per-base quality score graph:







A FastQC per-base quality score graph for files with reasonably good quality reads.The y-axis shows Phred quality scores (higher is better, see also the color-coding),and the x-axis shows the position along the read.

title: Using software at OSC: modules and containers
section: 3 Loading software at OSC using modules
text:
3 Loading software at OSC using modules
As discussed in the previous lecture, a lot of software installed at OSC can only be used after its module is loaded. You can find and load them using the module command and its various subcommands.






The three OSC clusters mostly have the same software available through modules, but there are some differences. In this course, our VS Code sessions run on the Pitzer cluster.




3.1 Searching for available modules
While OSC OnDemand has a Module Browser to search for available software modules, you can also do so directly in the shell using two subtly different module commands:

module spider lists all modules.
module avail lists modules that can be loaded directly given your current shell environment1.

Simply running module spider or module avail spits out complete lists of available programs, so it’s typically useful to add a search term as an argument. For example, try to use module spider to search for fastqc:
module spider fastqc
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  fastqc: fastqc/0.12.1
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

    This module can be loaded directly: module load fastqc/0.12.1

    Help:
      A quality control tool for high throughput sequence data.
We can see that fastqc is available, namely version 0.12.1 (the module is printed as <software>/<version>).






NoteCase-sensitivity



These two search commands are not case-sensitive: for example, module spider FastQC would also find the fastqc module.




3.2 Loading modules
To make a program available to you, use the module load command. But first, let’s confirm that the fastqc command, which is used to run FastQC, is not already available before doing so:
fastqc -v
bash: fastqc: command not found...
Failed to search for file: GDBus.Error:org.freedesktop.DBus.Error.NameHasNoOwner: Could not activate remote peer.
These error messages tell us that the fastqc command is not currently available. If it were available, this command would have printed the FastQC version instead, since many programs print their version with -v and/or --version2.
Now, load the module by specifying the module name and its version exactly as module spider printed it:
module load fastqc/0.12.1
And then check once again whether you can use FastQC:
fastqc -v
FastQC v0.12.1
Success! 🥳


3.3 Final notes on modules
Module loading does not persist across shell sessions. Whenever you are in a fresh shell session (including but not limited to after you log into OSC for the day), you’ll have to reload any modules you want to use.
Modules are convenient, but not all software is available as a module. Containers are a more universal approach, with the added benefit of improved reproducibility and portability3 — as you’ll see below.
Here, we only covered the very basics of using module — see the boxes below for some more information.






NoteOther module commands (Click to expand)






To check which modules are loaded, use module list. Its output also includes modules that OSC loads by default in every shell — for example, after loading fastqc/0.12.1, it may show something like the below, where only the last one was loaded by you:
module list
Currently Loaded Modules:
  1) intel-oneapi-mkl/2023.2.0   2) intel/2021.10.0   3) mvapich/4.1   4) modules/sp2024   5) fastqc/0.12.1
Occasionally, when you run into conflicting (mutually incompatible) modules, it can be useful to unload modules, which you can do with module unload or module purge:
# Unload a specific module with 'module unload':
module unload fastqc/0.12.1

# Unload all loaded modules with 'module purge':
module purge
If you ran these commands to try them out, reload FastQC with module load fastqc/0.12.1 before continuing.










NoteAnother module load example: R (Click to expand)





If you’re familiar with R, you may only have used it within RStudio, but R can also be started from the command line. First, test if R is available without loading anything:
R
bash: R: command not found...
Nope. Is it available as a module?
module spider R
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  R:
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
     Versions:
        R/4.4.0
        R/4.5.2
     Other possible modules matches:
        amber  app_code_server  app_jupyter  app_marimo  benchmark  blender  connectome-workbench  cryosparc-worker  darshan-runtime  darshan-util  deepemhancer  fmriprep  freesurfer  gromacs  gurobi  ibamr  ior  libjpeg-turbo  linaro-forge  mricrogl  mriqc  ...

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  To find other possible module matches execute:

      $ module -r spider '.*R.*'

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  For detailed information about a specific "R" package (including how to load the modules) use the module's full name.
  Note that names that have a trailing (E) are extensions provided by other modules.
  For example:

     $ module spider R/4.5.2
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Let’s try to load the most recent version, currently 4.5.2:
module load R/4.5.2
Lmod has detected the following error:  These module(s) or extension(s) exist but cannot be loaded as requested: "R/4.5.2"
   You encountered this error for one of the following reasons:
   1. Missing version specification: On Pitzer, you must specify an available version.
   2. Missing required modules: Ensure you have loaded the appropriate compiler and MPI modules.
   Try: "module spider R/4.5.2" to view available versions or required modules.
   If you need further assistance, please contact oschelp@osc.edu with the subject line "lmod error: R/4.5.2"
Didn’t work! As the error message suggests, let’s use module spider specifically on this version:
module spider R/4.5.2
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  R: R/4.5.2
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    You will need to load all module(s) on any one of the lines below before the "R/4.5.2" module is available to load.
      gcc/12.3.0

    Help:
      R is 'GNU S', a freely available language and environment for
      statistical computing and graphics which provides a wide variety of
      statistical and graphical techniques: linear and nonlinear modelling,
      statistical tests, time series analysis, classification, clustering,
      etc. Please consult the R project homepage for further information.
So, it appears you first need to load the module gcc/12.3.0 before you can load R/4.5.2.
Therefore, let’s try to load gcc along with R — you can use the command below to load both at the same time:
module load gcc/12.3.0 R/4.5.2
Lmod is automatically replacing "intel/2021.10.0" with "gcc/12.3.0".
Due to MODULEPATH changes, the following have been reloaded:
  1) mvapich/4.1
(gcc and intel are two different compilers — programs that translate code into a runnable program. OSC loads the intel compiler by default, but each program is built with (and needs) one specific compiler. Since we explicitly loaded gcc above, the module system swapped out the default intel compiler for it.)
Finally, let’s check that R now indeed is available:
R
R version 4.5.2 (2025-10-31) -- "[Not] Part in a Rumble"
Copyright (C) 2025 The R Foundation for Statistical Computing
Platform: x86_64-pc-linux-gnu

R is free software and comes with ABSOLUTELY NO WARRANTY.
You are welcome to redistribute it under certain conditions.
Type 'license()' or 'licence()' for distribution details.

R is a collaborative project with many contributors.
Type 'contributors()' for more information and
'citation()' on how to cite R or R packages in publications.

Type 'demo()' for some demos, 'help()' for on-line help, or
'help.start()' for an HTML browser interface to help.
Type 'q()' to quit R.

>
Now you’re in the R console — type q() or use the general keyboard shortcut for exiting, Ctrl+D, to exit R. (If R asks whether to “Save workspace image”, type n and press Enter.)




 Self-study exercise: Modules

Check whether there is a module for the program STAR, an aligner for RNA-seq data that we’ll later use to align the reads from Garrigós et al. (2025) to a reference genome.


 Click for the solution.

Yes, it’s available, but be careful: two modules with similar names are shown: star and starccm. The one we want is the first one, star, which is the actual RNA-seq aligner.
module spider star
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
star: star/2.7.10b
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  Other possible modules matches:
     starccm
 This module can be loaded directly: module load star/2.7.10b
 Help:
   STAR is an ultrafast universal RNA-seq aligner.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
starccm:
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  Versions:
     starccm/19.06.009-mixed
     starccm/19.06.009

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
For detailed information about a specific "starccm" package (including how to load the modules) use the module's full name.
Note that names that have a trailing (E) are extensions provided by other modules.
For example:

$ module spider starccm/19.06.009

Load the module. Then, test whether you can use the program by running the command STAR (in uppercase, and without adding any options).


 Click for the solution.

Make sure to load the module with the correct case, as printed by module spider:
module load star/2.7.10b
For example, this fails, because module load is case-sensitive and the module name is lowercase star, even though the command is uppercase STAR:
module load STAR/2.7.10b
Lmod has detected the following error:  The following module(s) are unknown: "STAR/2.7.10b"
Then, to see if the program is available, run the command STAR:
STAR
Usage: STAR  [options]... --genomeDir /path/to/genome/index/   --readFilesIn R1.fq R2.fq
Spliced Transcripts Alignment to a Reference (c) Alexander Dobin, 2009-2022
STAR version=2.7.10b
STAR compilation time,server,dir=2026-06-11T15:35:30-04:00 pitzer-rw02.ten.osc.edu:/tmp/kkoepcke/spack/stage/spack-stage-star-2.7.10b-itj64jf32ufsx7x6kbmlpcprqq5xo5
in/spack-src/source
For more details see:
<https://github.com/alexdobin/STAR>
<https://github.com/alexdobin/STAR/blob/master/doc/STARmanual.pdf>
To list all parameters, run STAR --help

Use module spider to see if the program Salmon4 is available. Then, look for Salmon in the OnDemand Module Browser. Why did the former say it is not available, while the latter says it is?


 Click for the solution.

No, it isn’t available as a module!
module spider salmon
Lmod has detected the following error:  Unable to find: "salmon".
It’s listed in the OnDemand Module Browser, but if you click on it, you will see that it is only available on the Cardinal cluster, which is not the cluster we are using.

title: Using software at OSC: modules and containers
text:
4 Running a FastQC analysis
Now that we’ve loaded the FastQC module, let’s try to put it to use with one of the FASTQ files from Garrigós et al. (2025).
Recall that your copy of the data is in /fs/ess/PAS3493/people/$USER/garrigos, so from your working dir /fs/ess/PAS3493/people/$USER/week06, you can most easily reach it with ../garrigos. List the FASTQ files for sample S63 to check that the path works:
ls -lh ../garrigos/fastq/S63*
-rw-rw----+ 1 jelmer PAS0471 21M Sep  9 13:46 ../garrigos/fastq/S63_R1.fastq.gz
-rw-rw----+ 1 jelmer PAS0471 22M Sep  9 13:46 ../garrigos/fastq/S63_R2.fastq.gz
To analyze a FASTQ file with default settings, the most basic command is simply fastqc followed by the file path:
fastqc ../garrigos/fastq/S63_R1.fastq.gz
However, an annoying default behavior of FastQC is that it writes its output files in the same dir that contains the input FASTQ files — this means mixing your raw data with your results, which, as we discussed in week 2, we don’t want!
To figure out how to change that behavior, consider that (as you already know from standard shell commands!) most bioinformatics tools also have a -h and/or --help option that prints usage information to the screen.


 Exercise 1: FastQC help and output dir

Run FastQC with the -h option to see its help info, and use it to find the option for specifying a custom output directory.


 Click for the solution.

The option to do this is -o/--outdir:
fastqc -h
           FastQC - A high throughput sequence QC analysis tool

SYNOPSIS

       fastqc seqfile1 seqfile2 .. seqfileN

   fastqc [-o output dir] [--(no)extract] [-f fastq|bam|sam]
         [-c contaminant file] seqfile1 .. seqfileN

 # [...output truncated...]

  -o --outdir     Create all output files in the specified output directory.
                    Please note that this directory must exist as the program
                    will not create it.  If this option is not set then the
                    output file for each sequence file is created in the same
                    directory as the sequence file which was processed.

Use the output dir option you found in the previous step to type out the complete command for a FastQC run on S63_R1.fastq.gz that writes its output to results/fastqc/.


 Click for the solution.

The option is --outdir, and it takes the path to the output dir as an argument (in the same way that head -n takes a number as an argument):
fastqc --outdir results/fastqc/ ../garrigos/fastq/S63_R1.fastq.gz

You could equivalently use the short -o option instead of --outdir.
You don’t need the trailing / in the output dir path, but it doesn’t hurt either.


Run the command you wrote in the previous step. Even if you got the command correct, this should result in an error. Try to understand the error message and fix the underlying issue, then rerun FastQC.


 Click for the solution.

The problem is that the output dir results/fastqc does not exist yet, and FastQC does not create it automatically (this is unusual: most bioinformatics programs would do this for you):
fastqc --outdir results/fastqc/ ../garrigos/fastq/S63_R1.fastq.gz
Specified output directory 'results/fastqc/' does not exist
So, let’s create the output dir first, and then rerun the command:
mkdir -p results/fastqc
fastqc --outdir results/fastqc ../garrigos/fastq/S63_R1.fastq.gz
Started analysis of S63_R1.fastq.gz
Approx 5% complete for S63_R1.fastq.gz
Approx 10% complete for S63_R1.fastq.gz
Approx 15% complete for S63_R1.fastq.gz
[...truncated...]
Analysis complete for S63_R1.fastq.gz
Success! Above, FastQC printed some “logging” information to screen, telling us about its progress. The main output, however, is in the output dir we specified:

A .zip file, which contains tables with FastQC’s data summaries.
An .html (HTML) file, which contains the graphs we’d like to see.

ls -lh results/fastqc
total 512K
-rw-rw----+ 1 jelmer PAS0471 241K Sep 30 09:53 S63_R1_fastqc.html
-rw-rw----+ 1 jelmer PAS0471 256K Sep 30 09:53 S63_R1_fastqc.zip

Once your run for the R1 file has successfully completed, run FastQC for the R2 FASTQ file of the same sample. Do you use the same output dir or a different one?


 Click for the solution.

It makes sense to use the same output dir. This is because, as you could see above, the output file names have the input file identifiers in them. As such, because we don’t need to worry about overwriting files, it will be more convenient to have all results in a single dir.
To run FastQC for the R2 (reverse-read) file:
fastqc --outdir results/fastqc ../garrigos/fastq/S63_R2.fastq.gz
Started analysis of S63_R2.fastq.gz
Approx 5% complete for S63_R2.fastq.gz
Approx 10% complete for S63_R2.fastq.gz
Approx 15% complete for S63_R2.fastq.gz
[...truncated...]
Analysis complete for S63_R2.fastq.gz
ls -lh results/fastqc
total 1008K
-rw-rw----+ 1 jelmer PAS0471 241K Sep 30 09:53 S63_R1_fastqc.html
-rw-rw----+ 1 jelmer PAS0471 256K Sep 30 09:53 S63_R1_fastqc.zip
-rw-rw----+ 1 jelmer PAS0471 234K Sep 30 09:55 S63_R2_fastqc.html
-rw-rw----+ 1 jelmer PAS0471 244K Sep 30 09:55 S63_R2_fastqc.zip
Now, we have four files: two for each of our preceding successful FastQC runs.

In the VS Code file explorer, find the two FastQC output HTML files. Right-click on the first one (for the R1 file) and click “Open Preview”, which should open the HTML file in a new tab in VS Code5.
Explore the file. The “Summary” on the left gives each graph a green check (pass), orange exclamation mark (warning), or red cross (fail). Take a look at one or more graphs that got a warning or fail, and try to figure out from the graph what FastQC is flagging (I’d recommend skipping the “Per Base Sequence Content” graph, which is more complicated to interpret — see also the box below this exercise).


 Click here for a hint.

Other than the “Per Base Sequence Content” graph, the other warnings and fails mostly relate to an issue with these sequences that we had already identified a few weeks ago.

Open the second HTML file (for the R2 file) in a new tab, and compare it to the first one. What are the main differences you observe?


 Click for the solution.

One key difference is that the R2 reads have somewhat lower quality scores, especially toward the end of the reads: in Illumina paired-end sequencing, the reverse reads are sequenced after the forward reads, and quality degrades as the sequencing run goes on.









TipDon’t take FastQC’s flags at face value (Click to expand)





FastQC’s pass/warn/fail thresholds assume a diverse library of random DNA fragments. For other data types, some “failures” are expected. For RNA-seq data, for example:

Sequence Duplication Levels typically gets a warning or fail, since highly expressed genes produce many identical reads.
Per Base Sequence Content typically fails, because library preparation makes the first ~10 bases of reads non-random.




Finally, a few notes on the behavior of bioinformatics programs like FastQC:

Specifying an output dir vs. output file(s)
FastQC allows us to specify the output directory, but not the output file names: these will be automatically determined based on the input file name(s). This kind of behavior is fairly common for bioinformatics programs that produce multiple output files in a single run, like FastQC does.
Logging output is printed to screen, but its main output is stored in files.
So far with shell commands, we’ve seen that output is printed to screen, and we can redirect it to a file if we want. With bioinformatics programs, however, the main output is often written to files, while the output printed to screen is just logging information about the program’s progress.

title: Using software at OSC: modules and containers
text:
5 Using Apptainer containers
As discussed in the previous lecture, containers are a great way to use programs that aren’t available as OSC modules. You can think of a container as a small, separate computer system that contains only the program(s) it was built with, plus everything those programs need to run (so-called “dependencies”). Because dependencies are included in a container, it works the same way on any computer that can run containers.
We’ll use pre-built containers from the Seqera Containers webpage, which provides a wide range of bioinformatics tools in containerized form. It even allows you to easily build custom containers with multiple programs installed.
The containers can be downloaded as .sif files, which are so-called container “images” in the Apptainer format (Apptainer is the container platform that can be used at OSC). Using a program from Seqera Containers is a two-step process:

Get a link to the container image from the Seqera Containers webpage.
Use that link to run the program inside the container image.

We’ll go over these steps below.






NoteA bit more background on containers (Click to expand)






Container platforms: Docker and Apptainer (formerly, and sometimes still, called Singularity) are the most widely used container platforms. Docker can’t be used at OSC (or at most other supercomputers), because it requires administrator privileges. But luckily, Apptainer can convert container images made for Docker on the fly.
Terminology:

Container image — a binary file that contains the container application (.sif extension).
Container (strictly speaking) — a running container image.
Definition file — a plain-text file with the recipe to build a container image. We won’t see these in the course, since Seqera Containers builds the images for us.











NoteWhat is Seqera Containers, and which software can it provide? (Click to expand)






Who runs it
Seqera Containers is a free service by Seqera, the company behind the pipeline tool Nextflow (which we’ll use later in the course).
It doesn’t package software itself
Seqera doesn’t develop or package the programs you find there. Instead, it takes existing software packages from other repositories, builds container images with them on request, and hosts those images so you can download them.
What is available?
All packages from two community-maintained sources, which together contain the vast majority of bioinformatics software:

The Conda channels Bioconda (bioinformatics software) and conda-forge (general software).
PyPI, the main repository for Python packages.






5.1 Obtaining a container image
Let’s see how we can obtain a link to a container image from Seqera Containers. Again, we’ll use FastQC as the example, but it works the same for any other program that is available at this site:

Go to https://seqera.io/containers.
In the search box below “Containers”, type fastqc.
After waiting for the list to populate, the top hit should be bioconda::fastqc, with version 0.12.1 selected (the most recent version is always selected by default).







A screenshot of the Seqera containers website, showing the search result for FastQC.


Add FastQC to your container request by clicking the blue + Add button. You could now add more programs, but for this example, we are happy with a container that only has FastQC.
In “Container settings” below the search box, change from Docker to Singularity, Apptainer’s former name (and leave the other dropdown as is — linux/amd64 should be selected).







When a program is added to the container request, it appears in the search box as shown in this screenshot.


Get a link to the container image by clicking the blue Get Container button.
Copy the link to the container image that should appear immediately — this type of link is called a URI (Uniform Resource Identifier). The link should be: oras://community.wave.seqera.io/library/fastqc:0.12.1--104d26ddd9519960. We’ll use this link below to run the container.







After clicking “Get Container”, the link to the container image appears in the popup window.


A few more tips on selecting programs for your container on Seqera Containers:

To select a different version of a program, you can use the dropdown menu next to the search box:







You should generally pick Conda-based search hits, since that is how nearly all bioinformatics programs are distributed. You can recognize them in two ways:

The program name will be prefixed by bioconda:: (most commonly) or conda-forge::.
The Conda logo, the green open circle (snake) shown in the screenshot above.

(The other hits are typically Python packages, which can be recognized by the yellow-and-blue logo — see the second hit in the screenshot above.)







WarningYou can’t use a container image before it’s ready (Click to expand)





In this case, after we clicked Get Container, the pop-up box should have immediately said “Container is ready”. That means the container image was already available in the repository.
In other cases, however, the container may still need to be built, and the box should say “Fetching container” for a while. This could take one or a few minutes, and even though the URI is made available immediately and won’t change, you can only download/use the container once the box says “Container is ready”.
If you use a URI before the container is ready, you get this type of error:
apptainer exec oras://community.wave.seqera.io/library/multiqc_trim-galore:15a1e9f26daf266f \
    multiqc -v
FATAL:   Unable to handle oras://community.wave.seqera.io/library/multiqc_trim-galore:15a1e9f26daf266f uri: failed to get checksum for oras://community.wave.seqera.io/library/multiqc_trim-galore:15a1e9f26daf266f: GET https://community.wave.seqera.io/v2/library/multiqc_trim-galore/manifests/15a1e9f26daf266f: MANIFEST_UNKNOWN: manifest unknown; map[Tag:15a1e9f26daf266f]






5.2 Running a container image
To run a command in a container, the general syntax is:
apptainer exec <container-URI> <command>
For example, if the command (<command> above) you want to run is fastqc -v:
apptainer exec <container-URI> fastqc -v
Put another way, you need to preface your “regular” command to run a program with apptainer exec <container-URI>. All in all, here is the full command to run fastqc -v with the FastQC container URI we obtained above:
apptainer exec oras://community.wave.seqera.io/library/fastqc:0.12.1--104d26ddd9519960 \
    fastqc -v
INFO:    Downloading oras image
384.0MiB / 384.0MiB [======================================================================================================================] 100 % 51.8 MiB/s 0s
INFO:    gocryptfs not found, will not be able to use gocryptfs
FastQC v0.12.1
The first time you run this command, the container image will be downloaded to a default location (see box below), as you can see in the output above — this will take a minute or so.






TipLong commands




Above, I broke the command up across two lines, which can be done by ending the first line with a \. With a \, the shell understands that the command is still incomplete despite the newline. Using this technique to break up your commands across multiple lines helps with readability for long commands like this one. (Just make sure that the \ is the very last character on the line: even a space after it will break the command.)
Also, this long command prefix to use containers may seem like a big pain. Keep in mind, though, that you’ll rarely type such commands directly in the terminal. Instead, you’ll put them in a script that you can reuse (you’ll learn to write scripts next week), so you only type the prefix once.





5.3 The container image cache (storage)
The easiest way to run a container image you already downloaded is to simply reuse the exact same command with the URI to the container (!). Apptainer will realize that the image has already been downloaded, and will automatically use the downloaded version. Let’s try it:
apptainer exec oras://community.wave.seqera.io/library/fastqc:0.12.1--104d26ddd9519960 \
    fastqc -v
INFO:    Using cached SIF image
INFO:    gocryptfs not found, will not be able to use gocryptfs
FastQC v0.12.1

The Using cached SIF image line tells you that a previously downloaded SIF file is being used — “cache” means that the file is stored locally for reuse.
You will keep seeing the gocryptfs not found message, but this is nothing to worry about.







NoteMore about the container image cache (Click to expand)





By default, containers are downloaded to a hidden directory in your Home dir, ~/.apptainer/cache. That is generally fine, though if you download hundreds of containers, your Home dir can get quite full.

To change the cache location for your current shell session, set the $APPTAINER_CACHEDIR environment variable using export, e.g.:
export APPTAINER_CACHEDIR=/fs/scratch/PAS3493/$USER/containers
To permanently change this location, you would need to add this line to your ~/.bashrc shell configuration file. (We won’t cover this file in class, but it is explained in this optional self-study page.)
You can check what’s in your cache as follows — though this is only informative in terms of how many containers there are and how much space they take up, because the container names are very cryptic:
apptainer cache list -v
NAME                     DATE CREATED           SIZE             TYPE
sha256:e0c976cb2eca5fe   2026-09-30 10:02:18    383.99 MiB       oras

There are 1 container file(s) using 383.99 MiB and 0 oci blob file(s) using 0.00 KiB of space
Total space used: 383.99 MiB
To clear your cache, i.e. remove all cached containers (e.g., to free up space in your Home dir), run:
apptainer cache clean
This is harmless in the sense that any container you run again will simply be re-downloaded.
You can also run a container by referring to the downloaded image file (i.e., apptainer exec <path-to-sif-file> <command>) rather than the URI. But there is little benefit to doing so, since Apptainer already uses the cached image when you give it the URI. And it reduces portability: a URI works for anyone on any computer, whereas a path to a local file will only work for you on this computer.







5.4 Using a container instead of a module
In the example above, we ran FastQC on a FASTQ file using its OSC module. To run the same analysis with the container instead, you would simply preface the exact same fastqc command with apptainer exec <container-URI>.
For example, let’s try running the container-based equivalent of our final FastQC command above:
# (This will overwrite the previous FastQC results, which is fine)
apptainer exec oras://community.wave.seqera.io/library/fastqc:0.12.1--104d26ddd9519960 \
    fastqc --outdir results/fastqc ../garrigos/fastq/S63_R1.fastq.gz
Started analysis of S63_R1.fastq.gz
Approx 5% complete for S63_R1.fastq.gz
Approx 10% complete for S63_R1.fastq.gz
Approx 15% complete for S63_R1.fastq.gz
[...truncated...]
Analysis complete for S63_R1.fastq.gz


5.5 What happens when you run apptainer exec?
Recall that a container is like a small, separate computer system. When you run apptainer exec <container-URI> <command>, the command is executed inside the container:

Therefore, it can only use software installed in the container — which modules you have loaded doesn’t matter.
However, you can access files that are outside of the container: at OSC, your Home dir and the /fs/ess and /fs/scratch dirs are automatically made available inside containers. That’s why FastQC could read the FASTQ file and write to results/fastqc above.







WarningWhat if a program isn’t available as a module or container? (Click to expand)





As mentioned above, nearly all bioinformatics programs are available through Seqera Containers.
If you do run into a program that isn’t, first consider whether you really need to use it. As a rule of thumb, if a program isn’t available, it is likely to either not be open-source software or be poorly maintained (exceptions do exist). Therefore, unless you have a good reason to use a program you can’t find, you should first consider finding an alternative that is available.
If you’re sure you need a program that isn’t available as a module or container, you have two options:

Contact OSC Help
They may be able to help you install the program yourself, or, for commonly used software, may be willing to do a system-wide installation (i.e., make it available as a module). See the previous lecture for how to contact them.
Install the software “manually”
In the best case, you can download a directly functioning executable, but more commonly you need to “compile” (build) the program. This can get very tricky at OSC, because you don’t have administrator privileges and will often run into issues with dependencies (other software that the program depends on).






Can you think of any reasons why containers improve reproducibility and portability compared to modules?

The answer will be added after class.

title: Using software at OSC: modules and containers
text:
6 In closing
In research with full-size datasets, you typically don’t want to run bioinformatics programs like FastQC “interactively” like we just did, i.e. by executing the command directly in the terminal.
Instead, it is better to write small shell scripts to run such programs, and then submit those scripts as so-called “batch jobs” at OSC. In the coming weeks, you will learn the why and how:

Next week: writing shell scripts.
Week 9: running shell scripts as batch jobs.
