title: Week 4 exercises: Files in the Unix shell
section: Exercise 4: Exploring the GTF annotation file
text:
Exercise 4: Exploring the GTF annotation file

GTF file info
This exercise will work with the GTF file in the example dataset, so we’ll start with some more info about GTF files. As mentioned in the genomics file types lecture, GTF files typically start with header lines that contain metadata. Then, the main part of a GTF file is essentially a table, with:

One row for each annotated “genomic feature” (gene, exon, transcript, etc.)
Columns with information like the genomic coordinates of the features

Here is a snippet of our Culex pipiens GTF table, again with column names added for clarity (they aren’t in the file!):
seqname       source  feature     start   end     score   strand  frame   attributes
NC_068937.1   Gnomon  gene        2046    110808  .       +       .       gene_id "LOC120427725"; transcript_id ""; db_xref "GeneID:120427725"; description "homeotic protein deformed"; gbkey "Gene"; gene "LOC120427725"; gene_biotype "protein_coding";
NC_068937.1   Gnomon  transcript  2046    110808  .       +       .       gene_id "LOC120427725"; transcript_id "XM_052707445.1"; db_xref "GeneID:120427725"; gbkey "mRNA"; gene "LOC120427725"; model_evidence "Supporting evidence includes similarity to: 25 Proteins"; product "homeotic protein deformed, transcript variant X3"; transcript_biotype "mRNA";
NC_068937.1   Gnomon  exon        2046    2531    .       +       .       gene_id "LOC120427725"; transcript_id "XM_052707445.1"; db_xref "GeneID:120427725"; gene "LOC120427725"; model_evidence "Supporting evidence includes similarity to: 25 Proteins"; product "homeotic protein deformed, transcript variant X3"; transcript_biotype "mRNA"; exon_number "1";
NC_068937.1   Gnomon  exon        52113   52136   .       +       .       gene_id "LOC120427725"; transcript_id "XM_052707445.1"; db_xref "GeneID:120427725"; gene "LOC120427725"; model_evidence "Supporting evidence includes similarity to: 25 Proteins"; product "homeotic protein deformed, transcript variant X3"; transcript_biotype "mRNA"; exon_number "2";
Some details on what’s in each column:








Column #
Column ID
Explanation




1
seqname
Name of the chromosome, scaffold, or contig.


2
source
Name of the program that generated this feature, or the data source (e.g. database).


3
feature
Name of the genomic feature type, e.g. “gene”, “transcript”, “exon”, “CDS”.


4
start
Start position of the feature.


5
end
End position of the feature.


6
score
A confidence score for the feature, often absent (in which case it is .).


7
strand
Whether the feature is on the + (forward) or - (reverse) strand1.


8
frame
The “frame” for coding features, either 0, 1, or 2 (or . for no frame). E.g. 0 means the first base of the feature is the first base of a codon.


9
attributes
A semicolon-separated list of key-value pairs with additional information. Can be very wide!





Your turn
You should still be in your ex3 dir with the GTF file and can stay there.

Explore annot.gtf.gz with less, using its -S option to prevent line wrapping (see the box just above this point). Just look around a bit and try to navigate with the keybindings shown in the lecture, then consider the following questions:

How many header lines does the file have?
How can you tell where the header ends and the table part begins?
Is the -S option useful here? If you’re not sure, you can compare the output with and without it to see why.

Recall that zcat is the counterpart of cat for gzip-compressed files: it prints their contents in human-readable form. Pipe the output of zcat to another command to print only the first 15 lines of annot.gtf.gz.
Count the number of lines in the GTF file both in compressed and uncompressed form. Are the counts the same?


 Click to show a hint.

Use the zcat-then-pipe trick from the previous question to get the “uncompressed count”. The “compressed count”, on the other hand, is simply the number of lines in annot.gtf.gz.

Count the number of lines in the GTF file that contain the text “carbonic anhydrase”. Based on this count, what can you conclude about the number of carbonic anhydrase genes in the genome?

Exactly as many as the line count, because each line in a GTF file is one gene.
Fewer than the line count, because each gene is described by multiple lines.
More than the line count, because grep -c counts at most one match per line.
You can’t tell, because line counts of compressed files are meaningless.

Build on your command from the previous question to create a frequency table of feature types among the “carbonic anhydrase” lines. Then answer these questions:

How many carbonic anhydrase genes are there?
Why do you think there are more transcripts than genes?



 Click to show a hint.

The feature type is in column 3 of the GTF file. To create the frequency table, use the cut-sort-uniq combination from the lecture.

Exercise 1


1. Create a new dir and navigate there.

Or, with absolute paths:

2. Create a new file called newfile.txt in your working dir.

3. What do you think the command would do or attempt to do?

Because we added a trailing forward slash to more_data/, we are making clear that we are referring to a directory. So the command will attempt to copy the file into a dir more_data, with the file keeping the same name.



4. Do you think the command will succeed?

The more_data/ dir does not exist, and cp will not create a dir on the fly — so it will fail:
cp newfile.txt more_data/
cp: cannot create regular file 'more_data/': Not a directory



5. What would the command have done if you had omitted the trailing slash?

If you had omitted the trailing forward slash, it would have created a copy of the file with file name more_data (if that seems confusing: note that in Unix, files don’t need to have a file extension).
P.S.: To copy the file according to the original intention, first create the destination dir and then copy:
mkdir more_data
cp newfile.txt more_data/
Note also that once the more_data dir exists, it does not make a difference whether or not you use a trailing slash.

3. Run the rmdir command.

3. Count the number of lines in the GTF file both in compressed and uncompressed form.


Uncompressed count:
zcat annot.gtf.gz | wc -l
408402
Compressed count:
wc -l annot.gtf.gz
22934 annot.gtf.gz

So: no, the counts are not the same! The lesson: line counts of compressed files are meaningless — to count lines in a compressed file, count the lines of its decompressed output, e.g. with zcat <file> | wc -l.



4. What can you conclude about the number of carbonic anhydrase genes?


Count the lines that contain “carbonic anhydrase”:
zcat annot.gtf.gz | grep -c "carbonic anhydrase"
243
The correct answer is b): fewer genes than lines. Recall from the GTF snippet at the top of this exercise that a single gene is described by multiple lines: one gene line, but also transcript, exon, and (for protein-coding genes) CDS lines.
Regarding answer d): because we used zcat, grep operated on the decompressed contents, so this count is meaningful.




5. Create a frequency table of feature types among the “carbonic anhydrase” lines.


Select column 3 with cut, then sort and count with uniq -c. Unlike in the lecture, you don’t need something along the lines of tail -n +2 here: the header lines don’t contain “carbonic anhydrase”, so grep has already removed them.
zcat annot.gtf.gz | grep "carbonic anhydrase" | cut -f 3 | sort | uniq -c
     81 CDS
     89 exon
     16 gene
     19 start_codon
     19 stop_codon
     19 transcript
So, there are 16 carbonic anhydrase genes.
Besides the feature types we’ve discussed, you also see start_codon and stop_codon lines, which give the positions of the first and last codon of each coding sequence.
There are more transcripts (19) than genes (16) because some genes have multiple transcripts — different versions of the gene’s mRNA, mostly due to alternative splicing. In the GTF snippet at the top of this exercise, you can see a hint of this in the product attribute: transcript variant X3.

title: An introduction to the VS Code editor
text:
1 What is VS Code?
As a brief intermezzo, let’s take a look at VS Code, the fancy text editor you’ll use throughout the course to write code and documentation. Its full name is Visual Studio Code, while the version you can use in your browser at OSC is called “Code Server”.
To emphasize the additional functionality relative to basic text editors like Notepad and TextEdit, editors like VS Code are also referred to as IDEs: Integrated Development Environments. The RStudio program is another good example of an IDE. Just like RStudio is an IDE for R, VS Code will be our IDE for the Unix shell and Markdown1.

title: An introduction to the VS Code editor
text:
2 Starting VS Code at OSC

Log in to OSC’s OnDemand portal at https://ondemand.osc.edu. Already done during the OSC intro.
In the blue top bar, select Interactive Apps and near the bottom of the dropdown menu, click Code Server. Already done during the OSC intro.
Fill out the form to start a VS Code session. This is needed because Interactive Apps like VS Code run on compute nodes rather than login nodes, and compute nodes always need to be “reserved”.

The Cluster we want to use: pitzer
The Account, the OSC Project to be billed for the compute node usage: PAS3493
The Number of hours we want to make a reservation for: 2
The Working Directory (starting location — replace <user> with your OSC username): /fs/ess/PAS3493/people/<user>
The App Code Server version: 4.8.3 (this should be the only available option) Edit 2026-09-04: A newer version, 4.129.0, is now available: select this version instead.







When selecting the Working Directory, ignore the “Select Path” button in this case. This is an alternative to typing the path in the text box, not a way to confirm the path you already typed.











Here’s what the filled-out form should look like, except that you want to point it to your personal folder.



Click Launch and you’ll be sent to the My Interactive Sessions page with a card for your job at the top.
Your job may initially be Queued for some seconds (i.e., waiting for computing resources to be assigned to it), but it should soon switch to Starting and then be ready to use (Running) in another couple of seconds:







Once the blue Connect to VS Code button appears, click it to open VS Code in a new browser tab.
When VS Code opens, you may get a pop-up similar to this — check the box and click “Yes”:

title: An introduction to the VS Code editor
text:
3 The VS Code user interface



3.1 The Primary Side Bar (wide)
The Primary Side Bar (wide side bar) shows a file explorer by default, where you can see files, create new folders and files, and so on.
If you’re in the correct location, you should see just two entries in the file explorer: the week02 and week03 folders you created in the previous session. If that’s not what you see, the box below will tell you how you can switch to your personal folder.
(Your OSC username should be printed above that, not because it knows who you are, but because that’s the name of the folder you are in.)


3.2 The Activity Bar (narrow)
The Activity Bar (narrow side bar) on the far left has, from top to bottom:

A  (“hamburger menu”), with menu items like File — the kind you often find in a program’s top bar.
Icons such as  to switch what the wide Side Bar shows: we’ll talk about those in a later session.
A circled user icon  that we’ll also ignore for now.
A  (cog wheel icon) at the bottom, with access to:

Settings, where you can configure VS Code.
“Command Palette”, a search bar to find and run all VS Code functionality.



 Your Turn
The screenshots on the right show the VS Code interface with the “Light (Visual Studio)” color theme, but the default is a dark theme. Themes are a matter of personal preference, so feel free to pick one you like.
In the cog wheel  menu, click Themes > Color Theme to explore the options and optionally change your theme.









The narrow black bar is the Activity Bar, and the rest of the screenshot shows the Primary Side Bar.







The menu that pops up when you click the cog wheel  in the bottom of the Activity Bar.









TipA folder as a starting point



VS Code takes a specific folder as a starting point in all parts of the program, including its file explorer and the Unix shell in its terminal. You selected this folder when you started your VS Code session at OSC.
Generally speaking, if you’re not in the folder you want to work in, you should switch to the correct folder before continuing. For information on how to switch to a different folder, see the box below.








NoteSwitching folders (Click to expand)





If there was a problem with the Working Directory you selected when starting your VS Code session, you may have ended up in your Home dir instead (recall that this is /users/<project>/<user>). You can confirm this by looking at your browser’s address bar, which has the folder path at the end:





If you instead see a path that starts with /users/, then you can switch to your personal folder from within VS Code:

Click  > File > Open Folder.
Enter the correct path /fs/ess/PAS3493/people/<user>, replacing <user> with your OSC username.
This will cause the program to reload.





3.3 Terminal (with a Unix shell)
Open a terminal by clicking  > Terminal > New Terminal. A whole new panel will appear at the bottom of the window, with a Terminal tab. We’ll start using this in the next lecture.






The VS Code window with a terminal open at the bottom. The editor pane above shows the Get Started document.







TipResizing panes



You can resize panes by hovering your cursor over the borders between them and then dragging. Try doing this with the border between the Primary Side Bar and the editor pane, and that between the panel with the terminal and the editor pane.




3.4 Editor pane and “Get Started” document
The main part of VS Code is the editor pane. Here, you can open scripts and other types of text files, images, and so on. Like in a web browser and other modern editors, you can have multiple tabs open.
Whenever you open VS Code, an editor tab with a “Get Started” document is automatically opened. This provides some help and shortcuts to recently opened files and folders.
 Let’s create a new file and save it as a Markdown file, for the next lecture:

Open a new file by clicking  > File > New Text File2.
The file will be called “Untitled-1” and will contain some “ghost text” you can ignore:







Before typing anything, save the file: press Ctrl/⌘+S (i.e., the common “Save” shortcut you are likely familiar with) and save it within your week02 dir as 2d_markdown.md.







Because you saved it with the .md extension, VS Code will recognize it as a Markdown file, hence the Markdown icon (downward arrow) in the tab.

title: Project file organizationand documentationfor reproducible research
text:
Learning goals
Learn best practices for:

Organization and management of your research project files
Documentation of your research project









Two guiding principles (Noble 2009):




Someone unfamiliar with your project should be able to look at your computer files and understand in detail what you did and why.
Everything you do, you will probably have to do over again.


Keep these principles in mind while we discuss the recommendations below!

title: Project file organizationand documentationfor reproducible research
text:
Why does this matter?
Thoughtful and systematic project documentation and organization:

Improve the reproducibility of your research



Facilitate collaboration with others and “your future self”




Enable automation and effective use of version control (week 5) and agentic AI (week 8)

title: Project file organizationand documentationfor reproducible research
text:
Why does this matter?
In turn, why does reproducibility matter?
You’ll learn more about this in “Five selfish reasons to work reproducibly” (Markowetz 2015), this week’s reading.

title: Project file organizationand documentationfor reproducible research
text:
Recommended practices

Use one folder for one project, with a systematic subfolder structure.



Never edit your raw data, and avoid editing your results manually.




Follow file and folder naming practices that favor machine- and human-readability.




Prefer plain-text file formats.




Document your project extensively with Markdown files.


We’ll now get into these one by one.

title: Project file organizationand documentationfor reproducible research
section: 1a. Use one folder for one project
text:
1a. Use one folder for one project


Use a separate folder for each project, which should contain:

All files related to that project,
and only those files
Subfolders to cleanly organize your files



This strategy makes it easier to:

Find files
Share or back up your entire project
Avoid deleting files by accident









Two project folder hierarchies. Each box is a folder.

title: Project file organizationand documentationfor reproducible research
section: 1b. Separate files using a systematic structure
text:
1b. Separate files using a systematic structure


Use subfolders to keep different kinds of files separate, such as:

Code
Data
Results









Multiple reasonable ways exist to organize and name your project folders.
Use what works for you while keeping in mind these principles, and apply it consistently.








    For example:

title: Project file organizationand documentationfor reproducible research
section: 1b. Separate files using a systematic structure
text:
1b. Separate files using a systematic structure









Where would you put each file?



The FASTQ files you got back from the sequencing facility.
A figure you made for a paper.
The code you wrote to make that figure.
A spreadsheet listing your sample IDs and collection dates.




     Click for the answers


data (e.g., data/seqs)
data (e.g., data/meta)
results
scripts

title: Project file organizationand documentationfor reproducible research
text:
2a. Avoid editing original data
Raw data files should not be edited once produced.
Any processing or correction of the data should be done on separate copies.








What if you need to add data to a file that is being updated over time?


If you are entering data piecemeal e.g. during a longer experiment, consider using separate files for each batch of data. At the very least, don’t combine directly entered data with data analysis or visualization in a single spreadsheet — the less you touch the raw data files, the better.

title: Project file organizationand documentationfor reproducible research
text:
2b. Avoid manually editing results
Avoid manually editing files with (intermediate) results — do this with code instead.

As Abdill et al. (2024) explain:

For example, if script A processes raw data into a table of gene expression levels, and script B summarizes this table by pathway, we should be concerned if there is a step after script A that requires a user to open the table and edit fields by hand to prepare the data for script B. Such quick fixes can be tempting, but they also add risk: A researcher could easily add a typo, corrupt a file in unexpected ways, or forget the step altogether.



Doing this with code has several advantages:

Can be easily included as part of your project workflow, and is therefore reproducible.
Can be easily repeated if needed. Recall Noble (2009): “Everything you do, you will probably have to do over again.”

title: Project file organizationand documentationfor reproducible research
text:
2c. Treatment of data versus results


Raw data

Read-only — never edit the originals.
Highly valuable — make backups.






Results

Generally disposable, since you should be able to regenerate them.








There is some nuance here, as some results may take many hours to regenerate.

title: Project file organizationand documentationfor reproducible research
section: 3. Use best practices for file naming
text:
3. Use best practices for file naming
Three key principles (from Jenny Bryan ) — file names should:

Be machine-readable
Be human-readable
Enable correct default alphanumeric sorting

title: Project file organizationand documentationfor reproducible research
text:
3a. Use machine-readable names

Don’t use spaces in file names.
Limit special characters to underscores (_), hyphens (-), and periods (.).




Where appropriate, include metadata like sample ID, date, and treatment:

sample032_2016-05-03_low.txt
samples_soil_treatment-a_2019-01.txt

title: Project file organizationand documentationfor reproducible research
text:
3b. Use human-readable names

“Name all files to reflect their content or function. For example, use names such as bird_count_table.csv, manuscript.md, or sightings_analysis.py.” (Wilson et al. 2017)




One good scheme:

Use underscores (_) to delimit units like sample ID, batch, treatment, date.
Use hyphens (-) to delimit words within a unit: grass-and-soil.
Limit periods (.) to file extensions.
Generally avoid capital letters (though standard conventions such as R1/R2 are fine).





For example:
s01_grass-and-soil_R1.fastq
s01_grass-and-soil_R2.fastq
s02_grass-and-soil_R1.fastq
s02_grass-and-soil_R2.fastq

title: Project file organizationand documentationfor reproducible research
text:
3c. Use names that sort correctly
Write dates in the format YYYY-MM-DD (e.g., 2026-08-31).



Sorting with the M/D/YY format:
12/31/20
8/12/20
8/13/19



Can you see two ordering problems with this format?


Sorting happens by month first, so years are never sorted correctly.
Within years, months and days are not sorted correctly (though they would be when using leading zeros: 08/12/20 and 12/31/20).





Sorting with the YYYY-MM-DD format:
2019-08-13
2020-08-12
2020-12-31



Can you think of two benefits of using four digits for the year?


Ensures correct sorting across centuries.
Eliminates ambiguity about which set of digits represents the year.

title: Project file organizationand documentationfor reproducible research
text:
3c. Use names that sort correctly
Use leading zeros in file names — for example, sample05 instead of sample5.


Without leading zeros:
sample1
sample10
sample11
sample2
sample3

With leading zeros:
sample01
sample02
sample03
sample10
sample11









How many digits?


Choose the number of digits based on how many samples (or other items) you expect to have. For example, if you may get 100 or more samples, use three digits: sample001, sample002, …, sample999.

title: Project file organizationand documentationfor reproducible research
text:
3c. Use names that sort correctly
Optional, and when it makes sense: group similar files by prefix, and/or number files in order.

A numbering example:
|-- results/
|   |-- 01_reference-seqs/
|   |-- 02_fastqc/
|   |-- 03_multiqc/
|   |-- 04_trimgalore/
|   |-- 05_star/
|   |-- 06_salmon/
|-- scripts/
|   |-- 01_download-reference.sh
|   |-- 02_fastqc.sh

title: Project file organizationand documentationfor reproducible research
text:
3. Your turn


What 2–4 problems does this file name have? Final Results May 3 2016 (2).xlsx

The main ones are:

Spaces and parentheses — not machine-readable
May 3 2016 — doesn’t sort correctly; use 2016-05-03

Additionally:

“Final” and especially “(2)” say nothing about the content, and keeping versions this way is what version control is for (week 5)
Use of capital letters

title: Project file organizationand documentationfor reproducible research
text:
4. Use plain-text files







Which of these are plain-text formats, and which are not?



.xlsx
.txt
.csv
.pdf
.R




   Click for hints about .csv and .R files


.csv stands for “comma-separated values”, a tabular format with columns separated by commas.
.R files are “R scripts”: files containing code written in the R programming language.





   Click for the answer


.txt, .csv, and .R are plain-text files; .xlsx and .pdf are not.

title: Project file organizationand documentationfor reproducible research
text:
4. Use plain-text files


What are plain-text files?
Plain-text files:

Contain only readable characters with no hidden formatting or binary encoding
Can be opened and edited with any basic text editor, including in a terminal









In this course, you’ll use Markdown (.md) files — a nice balance between ease of writing/reading and formatting options. More on Markdown later this week!









Why use plain-text files?
Plain-text files are preferable for reproducible science because they:

Can be accessed on any computer, including remotely, without needing any special or proprietary software
Can be operated on by Unix shell commands and any programming language



Are future-proof
Can be tracked line-by-line with version control (week 5)

title: Project file organizationand documentationfor reproducible research
text:
Discussion







Do you have a note-keeping/documentation system?



What kinds of files do you use?
How do you organize these files?
Do you use any specialized electronic lab notebook systems?

title: Project file organizationand documentationfor reproducible research
text:
5. Document your research project


Rationale

Documenting isn’t easy: it can feel like a waste of time when things are obvious then and there.



But you won’t have a clear picture a month later, and a collaborator won’t either.
Make a conscious effort to take a step back, slow down, and write down what you did and why.









Code is partially self-documenting, but that shouldn’t make you complacent about further documenting your work!









What to document
Documentation should contain all information needed to reproduce your research, e.g.:

Where/when/how each data and metadata file originated
Versions of software, databases, reference genomes

title: Project file organizationand documentationfor reproducible research
text:
Three types of documentation files


README
(README.md in the top-level folder, and optionally in subfolders such as data/)

Project overview
Folder structure & file naming
Data details
Contact info




Lab notebook
(e.g., doc/diary.md)



What you did and why
Organize by date with most recent first
Not “clean” — keep failed attempts too




Workflow/protocol
(e.g., doc/workflow.md)



Code to rerun final analyses
Should be “clean”
Organize by analysis step, not date

title: Project file organizationand documentationfor reproducible research
section: Documentation files in your project folder
text: Documentation files in your project folder

title: Project file organizationand documentationfor reproducible research
text:
Recap

File organization — Use one folder per project; separate file kinds into subfolders.
Edit habits — Never manually edit data/results: use code.
File names — Use machine- and human-readable file names, sorted correctly by default.
Plain-text files — Use plain-text formats wherever possible.
Documentation — Maintain README, lab notebook, and workflow/protocol files, in Markdown.









Another take-home message: find your style and be consistent


File structures, file naming conventions, and documentation styles are not one-size-fits-all. Find a good approach that works for you, and then consistently apply that.

title: Project file organizationand documentationfor reproducible research
text:
Bonus slide: Alternative organization
When it comes down to the details, multiple reasonable ways exist to organize your project folder. Some examples of possible alternatives to consider:


Folder structure

Noble (2009): Organize subfolders in results by date and then by topic/software (e.g., results/2026-08-30/multiqc).
Buffalo (2015): Processed data in data/processed rather than in results.






Folder naming

analysis instead of results
src (“source”) instead of scripts

title: Project file organizationand documentationfor reproducible research
text:
References




Abdill, Richard J., Emma Talarico, and Laura Grieneisen. 2024. “A How-to Guide for Code Sharing in Biology.” PLOS Biology 22 (9): e3002815. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pbio.3002815.


Buffalo, Vince. 2015. Bioinformatics Data Skills [Reproducible and Robust Research With Open Source Tools]. First edition. O’Reilly.


Markowetz, Florian. 2015. “Five Selfish Reasons to Work Reproducibly.” Genome Biology 16 (1): 1–4. https://doi.org/10.1186/s13059-015-0850-7.


Noble, William Stafford. 2009. “A Quick Guide to Organizing Computational Biology Projects.” PLOS Computational Biology 5 (7): e1000424. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1000424.


Wilson, Greg, Jennifer Bryan, Karen Cranston, Justin Kitzes, Lex Nederbragt, and Tracy K. Teal. 2017. “Good Enough Practices in Scientific Computing.” PLOS Computational Biology 13 (6): e1005510. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1005510.

section: Exercise 1: Fixing a broken Markdown file
text:

title: Week 2 exercises:Markdown and project organization
text:
Exercise 2: Writing a Markdown document
In this exercise, you’ll build a Markdown document from scratch. The idea is to practice the syntax, so don’t spend a lot of time thinking about the content.

Create a file 2_writing-markdown.md in your week02/exercises folder.
Open a preview of the Markdown document to the side. Keep an eye on the preview after every step below.
On the first line, add a level-1 header with the document’s title: Markdown practice.
Add a level-2 header Course tools, and below it a paragraph of two sentences about the tools you’ve used so far in this course.
Below that paragraph, add a bulleted list with three tools. For each item, put the name of the tool in bold, followed by a dash and a few words about what it’s used for.
Add a level-2 header Starting a VS Code session at OSC, and below it a numbered list of steps to start a VS Code session.
Add a level-2 header Useful links with a bulleted list of three links to the OSC websites we discussed (links can show or hide the URL — as you wish).
Add a level-2 header A quote, and below it a blockquote with one sentence that you found interesting from this week’s reading (Markowetz 2015). Below the blockquote, in a regular paragraph, say where the quote is from.
Add a level-2 header Code, and below it:

A sentence that mentions the file name README.md, formatted as inline code.
A code block with bash syntax highlighting containing these two lines:
# Print the current date and time
date

Add a horizontal rule, followed by a level-2 header To do and a bulleted list of two things you want to practice more.
In the OnDemand file browser, use the Upload button to upload an image from your own computer into your week02/exercises folder. Then embed it in 2_writing-markdown.md, and check that it shows up in the preview.
Browse the Markdown Guide’s cheat sheet, find one syntax element that we didn’t cover in class, and try it out in your document.

title: Week 2 exercises:Markdown and project organization

title: Week 2 exercises:Markdown and project organization
text:
Exercise 4: A project folder
In this exercise, you’ll build the skeleton of a research project folder, with placeholder files and a README.md. Start by picking one of the two project options below.

Option A: Your own projectOption B: A fictional RNA-seq project


Use a research project of your own; either one you are working on now, or one you expect to start soon.
Only pick this option if you can name about ten files that the project has or will have, and can say several things about its data: where it came from, when, and from whom.
Since this is just for practice, it’s fine if you make up some placeholder/dummy file names and details, but if you feel like you’d have to make up too much, use Option B instead.


You are studying how drought stress affects gene expression in maize (Zea mays).
You grew 24 plants (12 well-watered “control” plants and 12 drought-treated plants) and harvested leaf tissue from each plant. The CFAES Molecular Biology and Genomics Core prepared and sequenced the RNA-seq libraries, and you downloaded the raw sequence data from them on May 1, 2026. The next day, you downloaded the maize reference genome (assembly GCF_902167145.1) from NCBI.
These are the files you have so far:

SampleSheet Final.xlsx — the spreadsheet from the sequencing facility with sample IDs, treatments, and harvest dates
ctrl01_R1.fastq.gz and ctrl01_R2.fastq.gz — raw reads for control plant 1
drought10_R1.fastq.gz and drought10_R2.fastq.gz — raw reads for drought-treated plant 10
GCF_902167145.1_genomic.fna — the reference genome you downloaded
01_align-reads.sh — a script that aligns the reads to the reference genome
counts.csv — the gene count table produced by that script
02_plot-counts.R — a script that makes figures from the count table
Fig 1 FINAL v3.png — a PCA plot of all samples, made by that script
diary.md — your lab notebook, with an entry for each day you worked on the project

Final notes:

You also have the reads for the other 22 plants, but there is no need to list all of those.
_Most of these names are already fine: only two of them need to be changed.





Now, whichever project you picked:

Within your week02/exercises folder, create a folder for the project.
Inside it, create the top-level subfolders you would use. For example, data, scripts, results, and doc, but you’re free to use a different (consistent!) set of names.
Add any subfolders you need, such as data/raw and data/meta.
Create an empty placeholder file for each of the project’s files, in the folder where it belongs and with a name that follows the file naming rules:

Option A — use about ten files that your project has or will have.
Option B — use the file list above, fixing the two file names that don’t follow the rules.

In the top level of your project folder, create a README.md with:

A level-1 header with the project name
A paragraph describing what the project is about
A level-2 section Folder structure with a list of your folders, each with a few words about what goes in it. Format the folder names as inline code.
A level-2 section Data describing where the data came from, when, and from whom
A level-2 section Contact with your name and your email address as a clickable link

In your doc folder, open (or create) the lab notebook file diary.md, and add one entry: a level-2 header with a date, followed by a couple of sentences about what you did that day.

Option A — use today’s date and describe this exercise.
Option B — use 2026-05-03, the day you ran the alignment script.

Check both Markdown files in the preview and fix any formatting problems.

title: Week 2 exercises:Markdown and project organization
text:
Solutions

Exercise 1


The ten problems, and the fixed file.


The problems were:

No space after the # of the title, so it isn’t a header.
No blank line between the paragraph and the list below it. VS Code’s preview is forgiving and still shows a list here, but stricter renderers (including Quarto’s, in week 14) will not — so always leave the blank line.
No space after the - of the second list item, so it isn’t a list item and is added to the previous one instead, one the same line.
The link has its two parts reversed: the [link text] comes first, and then the (URL).
The inline code for notes.md has an opening backtick but no closing one, so it doesn’t show up as inline code in the preview.
**really* has two asterisks on one side and only one on the other. Only one asterisk on each side is used, so you get italic instead of bold, with a leftover (literal) * in the output.
No blank line before the ## Things to try next week header. Again, VS Code’s preview accepts this, but not every renderer will.
The bash/date code block lost its triple backticks, so it shows up as regular text and as a single line. Note: Within a code block, you do not need blank lines to avoid merging lines together! Since there are no “paragraphs” in a code block, the renderer will not merge lines together.
The table is missing the row of dashes below the header row, so it isn’t rendered as a table, and once again is collapsed into a single line.

Finally, the two sentences “I started a VS Code session at OSC.” and “Then I opened a Markdown file.” are on separate lines in the source but end up in one line in the output: a single line break is ignored. While notable, this isn’t necessarily a problem, and you may in fact deliberately write Markdown with short lines like this, so that the source is easier to read. But in the solution below, we assumed that the two sentences were meant to be two paragraphs, and we added a blank line between them.

And here is the fixed file:

I indented the second item by two spaces,
and it became a nested (indented) sub-item of the first one.

Two things to note:

Step 12 (embedding an uploaded image) is not shown here, since the image file itself isn’t something we can include in this solution — but the syntax is ![](image-file-name.png), assuming the image file is in the same folder as your Markdown file.
In the numbered list, every item is 1. in the source, but the preview numbers them 1, 2, 3, 4.




Exercise 3


Better file names.


Several other answers are possible — what matters is that your names are machine-readable, human-readable, and sort correctly.

sample2_R1.fastq → sample02_R1.fastq
Without a leading zero, sample10 sorts before sample2. With 40 samples, two digits are enough.
RNAseq counts FINAL.csv → rnaseq-counts.csv
The spaces are not machine-readable, and capitals are best avoided too. While there is some nuance here, you should generally also avoid qualifiers like “FINAL” (would the next version be “FINAL2”?). Instead, be more specific and/or use version control (week 5 of this course).
plot1.png → pca_all-samples.png
The original is machine-readable but not human-readable: it says nothing about what the figure shows.
2019_3_7_field_notes.txt → field-notes_2019-03-07.txt
The date needs leading zeros and hyphens to sort correctly, and underscores are better reserved for separating units (here: the date from the description).




Exercise 4
These solutions use the fictional project of Option B — but the same reasoning applies to your own project.


A) The project folder, with all files in place.


maize-drought/
|-- README.md
|-- data/
|   |-- meta/
|   |   |-- samples.tsv
|   |-- raw/
|   |   |-- ctrl01_R1.fastq.gz
|   |   |-- ctrl01_R2.fastq.gz
|   |   |-- drought10_R1.fastq.gz
|   |   |-- drought10_R2.fastq.gz
|   |-- ref/
|   |   |-- GCF_902167145.1_genomic.fna
|-- doc/
|   |-- diary.md
|-- results/
|   |-- counts/
|   |   |-- counts.csv
|   |-- figures/
|   |   |-- pca_all-samples.png
|-- scripts/
|   |-- 01_align-reads.sh
|   |-- 02_plot-counts.R

Some things to note about where the files go:

The sample sheet is a form of data so it belongs in data rather than in doc. In omics projects where the omics data is the main source of data, we often consider such sample information “metadata”, so it can go in data/meta.
counts.csv is produced by one of your scripts, which makes it a result, even though the next script uses it as input.
The reference genome is data that you downloaded rather than generated, so it goes in data too. But in its own subfolder, since it is not data about your samples.
The lab notebook is documentation, so diary.md goes in doc.


And about the two files that had to be renamed:

SampleSheet Final.xlsx → samples.tsv
The spaces and capitals make it hard to work with, “Final” says nothing about the content, and the file should be converted from Excel to a plain-text format.
Fig 1 FINAL v3.png → pca_all-samples.png
Again spaces and capitals, and the name says nothing about what the figure shows. Keeping track of versions in the file name is what version control is for (week 5).


The other names were already fine. Note that the scripts are numbered, which shows the order in which they should be run, and that the sample numbers have a leading zero (ctrl01 rather than ctrl1) so that they will sort correctly.



B) An example README.md file.


# Maize drought RNA-seq

An RNA-seq experiment to test how drought stress affects gene expression in
maize (_Zea mays_).
Leaf tissue was harvested from 24 plants:
12 well-watered controls and 12 drought-treated plants.

## Folder structure

- `data/raw` - raw FASTQ files as received from the sequencing facility
- `data/meta` - metadata about the samples
- `data/ref` - the maize reference genome
- `scripts` - all scripts, numbered in the order in which they are run
- `results` - output of the scripts: count tables and figures
- `doc` - project documentation, including the lab notebook `diary.md`

## Data

- The raw RNA-seq reads were produced by the CFAES Molecular Biology and
  Genomics Core and downloaded on 2026-05-01.
  Their sample sheet is in `data/meta/samples.tsv`,
  converted from the original Excel file.
- The maize reference genome (assembly `GCF_902167145.1`)
  was downloaded from NCBI on 2026-05-02.

## Contact

Jane Doe - [doe.1234@osu.edu](mailto:doe.1234@osu.edu)



C) An example diary.md entry.


# Lab notebook

## 2026-05-03

Aligned the reads of all 24 samples to the maize reference genome with
`scripts/01_align-reads.sh`, and made a gene count table.
Two of the control samples had a much lower alignment rate than the rest --
check the FastQC reports for those next.

section: Goals and focus of this course
text:
Goals and focus of this course


Main focus
General, foundational “computing skills”.
For example, you will learn to:

Code in the Unix shell and in R
Organize, document, manage, and share your research data, code, and results
Work with a remote supercomputer






Why learn all this?
To enable you to:

Work with large-scale “omics” datasets
Do your research more reproducibly and efficiently

title: Introduction to the course
text:
Working with omics data

Omics data analyses commonly require these computing skills. For example:

Many omics data analysis programs are command-line tools.
Datasets are often so large that a remote supercomputer is needed.





The next lecture will give an introduction to omics data itself.

but will not comprehensively cover specific omics analyses.

title: Introduction to the course
text:
Reproducibility
Reproducibility and replicability are two related but distinct ideas:

Research is replicable when independent experiments produce the same results.
Research is reproducible when re-analyzing the same data produces the same results.



Our focus is on reproducibility, because we have control over that.

title: Introduction to the course
text:
Reproducibility


In general terms,
your research is reproducible when:

You share your data
You share your methods — in sufficient detail for anyone to redo what you did
All reported data, methods, and results are congruent










From https://karlastarr.substack.com

title: Introduction to the course
text:
Reproducibility
The course will cover various practices that help you work reproducibly. For example:

Project organization and documentation (next week).



Using code (throughout the course):


“The most basic principle for reproducible research is: Do everything via code.”
—Karl Broman, University of Wisconsin–Madison (source )






Can you think of any reasons why this might be true?




Code is self-documenting
Code is easier to rerun



Code reduces the risk of human error
And more. We’ll get back to this!

title: Introduction to the course
text:
Efficiency & automation
When you use code instead of relying on point-and-click interfaces,
you can also improve automation and work more efficiently.


This can especially make a difference when you have to, for example:

Do repetitive tasks
Recreate a figure or redo an analysis after adding a sample
Redo most or all of an analysis after finding an early mistake

title: About this website and course
text:
Overview
This is the GitHub website for the course Practical Computing Skills for Omics Data (PLNTPTH 5006), a 3-credit course taught at Ohio State University during the Fall semester of 2026.
The course is taught by Jelmer Poelstra from the CFAES Bioinformatics Core  and Department of Plant Pathology , with TA Kelsey Starr from the Department of Plant Pathology.


Course description
Omics data is everywhere, but can you actually analyze it? This course will teach you the skills to do so: using the Unix shell, writing shell and R scripts, and running jobs on the Ohio Supercomputer Center. You will also learn how to improve the reproducibility of your research using best-practice project organization, documentation, and version control. No prior coding experience required.


Main topics taught

Reproducibility — project documentation with Markdown, file organization, data and management and sharing
Unix shell — basics, scripting, running command-line programs
HPC / Supercomputer usage — basics, software, and running Slurm batch jobs at OSC 
Version control — with Git and GitHub
Running pipelines — using Nextflow/nf-core pipelines
R — Basics, data wrangling & visualization, Quarto, and specifics to omics data
Omics data and analysis basics — with a focus on high-throughput sequencing data
AI — Using generative and agentic AI to help with coding

title: VS Code tips and tricks
text:
1 Introduction
This page collects tips and tricks that will make you more efficient in VS Code. None of this is required for the course, but the time you invest in learning your editor will pay off quickly, since you’ll spend many hours in it.
Nearly everything here applies both to VS Code at OSC, which runs in your browser, and to a VS Code installation on your own computer.






TipWhen a keyboard shortcut doesn’t work



Because VS Code at OSC runs inside your browser, a few keyboard shortcuts are “captured” by the browser instead of by VS Code. For example, Ctrl/⌘+W may close your browser tab rather than the file you have open in the editor.
Whenever a shortcut doesn’t do what you expect, you can find the same functionality through the menus or the Command Palette (see below).



1.1 Setting up
To try things out as you read, start a VS Code session at https://ondemand.osc.edu (or open your local VS Code installation) and open a file or two, such as one of the scripts you wrote in week 7.

title: VS Code tips and tricks
text:
2 Finding functionality

2.1 The Command Palette
To find and apply any menu option that is available in VS Code, the so-called “Command Palette” is handy. To access it, click  and then Command Palette (or press F1 or Ctrl/⌘+Shift+P). To use it, start typing something to search for an option.
The Command Palette also shows the keyboard shortcut for each option, if there is one, so it is a good way to discover shortcuts for things you do often.


2.2 Keyboard shortcuts overview
For a single-page PDF overview of keyboard shortcuts for your operating system:  > Help > Keyboard Shortcut Reference. (Or for direct links to these PDFs on the web: Windows / Mac / Linux.)
To see, change, or add keyboard shortcuts, click  > Keyboard Shortcuts, like you did in class to add the Ctrl+Enter shortcut to send code to the terminal.

title: VS Code tips and tricks
text:
3 Working in the editor

3.1 Line actions

Automatic whole-line selection
In VS Code’s editor pane, the entire line that your cursor is on is selected by default. As such, you don’t need to manually select the entire line when wanting to send it to the terminal — or when cutting/copying lines! The standard copy and cut shortcuts (Ctrl/⌘+C / X) will cut/copy the entire line that the cursor is on.
Move a line up or down: Alt/Option+⬆/⬇
Delete a line: Ctrl/⌘+Shift+K
Comment or uncomment a line: Ctrl/⌘+/
This inserts or removes the comment character for the current language, e.g. # in a shell script. This is handy to temporarily deactivate (“comment out”) code.

All of the above also work for multiple selected lines at once.


3.2 Go to a specific line
Error messages often mention a line number, as in:
scripts/fastqc.sh: line 8: $1: unbound variable
To jump to a line, press Ctrl+G (on a Mac too) and type the line number. Alternatively, click on the Ln <number>, Col <number> indicator in the Status Bar at the bottom of the window.


3.3 Find and replace

Find in the current file: Ctrl/⌘+F.
Find and replace in the current file: Ctrl+H (Windows/Linux) or Option+⌘+F (Mac).
Search across all files in the folder you opened in VS Code: click the magnifying glass icon in the Activity Bar, or press Ctrl/⌘+Shift+F. You can also replace across files from there.

The search box has buttons to make your search case-sensitive (Aa), match whole words only (ab), or use a regular expression (.*).


3.4 Multiple cursors
VS Code lets you type in multiple places at once, which is great for making the same edit on several lines:

Add a cursor where you click: hold Alt/Option while clicking.
Select the next occurrence of the currently selected text: Ctrl/⌘+D (press repeatedly to add more occurrences).
Column (“box”) selection: hold Shift+Alt/Option while dragging your mouse.

Press Esc to go back to a single cursor.

title: VS Code tips and tricks
text:
4 Navigating files and panes

4.1 Quick Open
To open a file without clicking through the Explorer, press Ctrl/⌘+P and start typing (part of) its name.


4.2 The Explorer

Copying a file’s path
Right-click on a file in the Explorer and select Copy Path (absolute path) or Copy Relative Path (relative to the folder you opened in VS Code). This is handy for pasting file paths into the terminal or into a script.
Moving files
You can drag and drop files and folders in the Explorer to move them.
Downloading files
Right-click on any file, and among the options shown, you should see “Download…”. Click on that to download the file to your computer! There is no way to upload, though — this should be done through the OnDemand file browser (or using a terminal on your own computer; you’ll learn more about that later).



4.3 Arranging your screen

Toggling (hiding/showing) the side bars
If you want to save some screen space while coding along in class, you may want to occasionally hide the side bars:

In  > View > Appearance, you can toggle both the Activity Bar and the Primary Side Bar.
For the primary/wide side bar, you can also drag it away, or use the keyboard shortcut Ctrl/⌘+B.

Splitting the editor
To see two files side by side (e.g., a script and your README.md), drag an editor tab to the right side of the editor pane, or right-click on a tab and select Split Right.
Switching between the terminal and the editor

Open a terminal, or move from the editor to the terminal: Ctrl+` (backtick)
Move from the terminal to the editor: Ctrl+1




4.4 Multiple terminals
You can have multiple terminals open at once — for example, to run a long command in one while you keep working in another. In the Terminal pane:

Click the + icon to open a new terminal.
Switch between terminals in the list on the right side of the pane.
Click the trash can icon to close (“kill”) a terminal.

Keep in mind that each terminal is a separate shell session: variables you assign and modules you load in one terminal are not available in the other.

title: VS Code tips and tricks
text:
5 Settings
You can open the Settings via  > Settings, and then search for the setting you want to change.






NoteUser settings vs. workspace settings (Click to expand)





The Settings editor has two tabs at the top: User and Workspace.

User settings apply everywhere you use VS Code.
Workspace settings only apply to the folder you currently have open, and are saved in a file .vscode/settings.json inside that folder.

Change your User settings unless you have a specific reason to do otherwise.



Some settings you may want to change:

Auto Save
Auto-saving is turned on by default using the “afterDelay” option. You can:

Quickly turn it off by clicking  > File > Auto Save (shows a checkmark when activated).
Search for “Auto Save” in the Settings, where you can pick from several options.

Word wrap
By default, long lines run off the right side of the editor. To wrap them instead, click  > View > Word Wrap (or press Alt/Option+Z). To make this permanent, search for “Word Wrap” in the Settings.
Minimap
The “minimap” is the zoomed-out view of your file on the right side of the editor. If you find it distracting, you can hide it via  > View > Appearance > Minimap.
Font size
Search for “Font Size” in the Settings to change the font size of the editor (“Editor: Font Size”) and, separately, of the terminal (“Terminal › Integrated: Font Size”).
A vertical line to mark line length
To keep your lines of code and Markdown text from getting too long, you can show one or more vertical lines (“rulers”) at a specific width: search for “Rulers” in the Settings, click Edit in settings.json, and add e.g. 80 between the square brackets: "editor.rulers": [80].
Tidying up whitespace
Search for and turn on “Trim Trailing Whitespace” (removes spaces at the ends of lines when you save a file) and “Insert Final Newline” (makes sure a file ends with a newline, which some command-line tools expect).

title: VS Code tips and tricks
text:
6 Extensions
VS Code extensions are small programs that add functionality to VS Code. To install one, click the Extensions icon in the Activity Bar (see screenshot below), search for the extension, and click Install.






Activity Bar, with the Extensions icon (bottom) highlighted.


6.1 Extensions used in the course

HTML Preview (by Thomas Haakon Townsend) — view HTML files, like FastQC output, inside VS Code (week 6).
ShellCheck (by timonwong) — check your shell scripts for errors and bad practices (week 7). At OSC, this needs a work-around to function — see the first shell scripting lecture.



6.2 Other useful extensions

Rainbow CSV (by mechatroner) — makes CSV/TSV files easier to view in the editor pane, with column-based colors.
Code Spell Checker (by Street Side Software) — flags spelling mistakes in your Markdown files and code comments.
markdownlint (by David Anson) — checks your Markdown files for formatting issues and inconsistencies.
Markdown All in One (by Yu Zhang) — adds keyboard shortcuts for Markdown formatting, automatic list continuation, and table of contents generation.

title: Connecting to OSC with SSH in a terminal
text:
1 Introduction
This page shows you how to connect to OSC with the ssh command in a terminal on your own computer, rather than through the OnDemand web portal.

1.1 Setting up
You’ll need a terminal application on your own computer (see step 1 below). To avoid having to type your OSC password every time you connect, first do the no-password setup on the local VS Code page.

title: Connecting to OSC with SSH in a terminal
section: 2 Basic SSH connection in a terminal
text:
2 Basic SSH connection in a terminal
To connect to OSC or other remote computers without using a web portal like OnDemand, you can use SSH. You can do so via the ssh command, which works in Windows and Unix-based (Max/Linux) terminals alike.

On your own computer, open a terminal application.

On a Mac, you should have an app called “Terminal” and potentially other options like “iTerm”: any of these fill work
On Windows 11+, this should be called the “Windows Terminal”

Type the command ssh <user>@<host>, replacing:

<user> with your OSC username
<host> with the name of the computer/cluster you want to connect to:

pitzer.osc.edu to connect to the Pitzer cluster
cardinal.osc.edu to connect to the Cardinal cluster


For example, if I (username jelmer) wanted to log in to the Pitzer cluster, I would use:
ssh jelmer@pitzer.osc.edu
The authenticity of host 'pitzer.osc.edu' can't be established.
RSA key fingerprint is 2a:b6:f6:8d:9d:c2:f8:2b:8c:c5:03:06:a0:f8:59:12.
Are you sure you want to continue connecting (yes/no)?
If this is the first time you are connecting to Pitzer via SSH, you’ll encounter a message similar to the one above. While the phrase “The authenticity of host ‘pitzer.osc.edu’ can’t be established.” sounds ominous, you will always get this warning when you attempt to connect to a remote computer for the first time, and you should type yes to proceed (you then won’t see this message again).
Assuming that you did the no-password setup on the local VS Code page, you should not be prompted for your password. (If you are asked for your password, then type it followed by Enter, and keep in mind that when you do so, no characters or even *s will appear on the screen!)
Your shell will now connect to OSC, and you should see some welcome messages and the familiar file quota listing – and your prompt should indicate that you’re at OSC, e.g.:
[jelmer@pitzer-login04 ~]$

title: Connecting to OSC with SSH in a terminal
section: 3 Custom names for your SSH connections
text:
3 Custom names for your SSH connections

3.1 Set up custom names
You can set up alternative names (“aliases”) for your SSH connections, such as shortening jelmer@pitzer.osc.edu to jp. This can be convenient when you use SSH a lot, especially when transferring files to and from OSC with SSH-based commands like scp and rsync (see this optional self-study page).
These two steps should both be done on your local machine:

Create a file called ~/.ssh/config:
touch ~/.ssh/config
Open the file in a text editor and add your alias(es) in the following format:
Host <arbitrary-alias-name>
   HostName <remote-address>
   User <user>
For instance, my file contains the following so as to connect to Pizer with jp and to Cardinal with jc:
Host jp
   HostName pitzer.osc.edu
   User jelmer

Host jc
   HostName cardinal.osc.edu
   User jelmer



3.2 Connecting from now on
From now on, you just need to use your alias to log in:
ssh jp
And these shortcuts also work with remote transfer commands like scp and rsync! For example:
rsync ~/scripts op:/fs/scratch/PAS3493

title: More Unix shell:wildcards, brace expansion, find & xargs
text:
1 Introduction
This page contains optional self-study material that builds on this week’s shell lectures (w4b and w4c):

Other shell wildcards
Brace expansion
The find command to find files
xargs to repeat commands


1.1 Setting up

At https://ondemand.osc.edu, start a VS Code session in /fs/ess/PAS3493/people/$USER.
In the terminal, navigate to your week04/sandbox dir, where you will create dummy files to practice on.

title: More Unix shell:wildcards, brace expansion, find & xargs
text:
2 Other shell wildcards
In w4b, you learned about globbing (selecting files) with the * wildcard. While not as frequently used as *, a few other shell wildcards exist. Here is a complete overview of shell wildcards:







Wildcard
Matches




*
Any number of any characters, including none


?
Exactly one of any character


[...]
Exactly one of the characters listed in the brackets


[^...]
Exactly one character that is not listed in the brackets




To get set up, create some dummy FASTQ files to practice with:
# (You should be in /fs/ess/PAS3493/people/$USER/week04/sandbox)
# (If you did the w4b globbing section, these files already exist)
touch sample1_R1.fastq sample1_R2.fastq
touch sample2_R1.fastq sample2_R2.fastq
touch sample3_R1.fastq sample3_R2.fastq
Using the more restrictive wildcard ? can be useful to prevent accidental matches. Here is an example of using the ? wildcard to match both R1 and R2:
ls sample1_R?.fastq
sample1_R1.fastq  sample1_R2.fastq
The character class wildcard [] can be useful when you want to include or exclude multiple files among a set of files with rather similar names. For example, to match files for sample1 and sample2 using only a character class with []:

Method 1 – List all possible characters (1 and 2 in this case):
# This is saying: after 'sample', there should be a 1 OR a 2 ('[12]'),
# followed by any character (*):
ls sample[12]*
sample1_R1.fastq  sample1_R2.fastq  sample2_R1.fastq  sample2_R2.fastq
Method 2 – Use a range like [0-9], [A-Z], [a-z]:
ls sample[1-2]*
sample1_R1.fastq  sample1_R2.fastq  sample2_R1.fastq  sample2_R2.fastq
Method 3 – Exclude the unwanted sample ID by prefacing the character class with a ^, which results in inverted behaviour:
# This is saying: after 'sample', there should be anything EXCEPT a '3':
ls sample[^3]*
sample1_R1.fastq  sample1_R2.fastq  sample2_R1.fastq  sample2_R2.fastq

These examples may seem trivial, but you can use these techniques to easily operate on selections among 100s or 1000s of files.







WarningA character class always matches a single character



So [10-13] does not mean “10 through 13”: it is read as “one character that is 1, 0-1, or 3”. To match multi-digit numbers, use separate patterns (e.g. sample1[0-3]*) or brace expansion (next section).

title: More Unix shell:wildcards, brace expansion, find & xargs
text:
3 Brace expansion
Brace expansion with {} is another type of shell expansion, but it works very differently from wildcards: a wildcard expands only to names of files that already exist, whereas brace expansion expands to whatever you tell it to, whether or not such files exist. That makes brace expansion the tool for creating many files or dirs with mkdir and touch, and wildcards the tool for selecting existing ones.
For example, use .. within {} to indicate ranges of numbers or letters:

Create 30 directories, one for each day in September:
# Writing '01' keeps the leading zero, so that alphabetical order = date order:
mkdir -p 2026-09-{01..30}

ls 2026-09*
2026-09-01  2026-09-04  2026-09-07  2026-09-10  2026-09-13  2026-09-16  2026-09-19  2026-09-22  2026-09-25  2026-09-28
2026-09-02  2026-09-05  2026-09-08  2026-09-11  2026-09-14  2026-09-17  2026-09-20  2026-09-23  2026-09-26  2026-09-29
2026-09-03  2026-09-06  2026-09-09  2026-09-12  2026-09-15  2026-09-18  2026-09-21  2026-09-24  2026-09-27  2026-09-30
Create 6 empty files:
touch fig-1{A..F}.png

ls fig-*
fig-1A.png  fig-1B.png  fig-1C.png  fig-1D.png  fig-1E.png  fig-1F.png


As the example below shows, you can also:

Use a comma-separated list, and
Combine multiple brace expansions to get all combinations among values in the expansions

mkdir -p treatment-{Kr,Df,Tr}_temp-{lo,med,hi}

ls treatment-*
treatment-Df_temp-hi   treatment-Kr_temp-hi   treatment-Tr_temp-hi
treatment-Df_temp-lo   treatment-Kr_temp-lo   treatment-Tr_temp-lo
treatment-Df_temp-med  treatment-Kr_temp-med  treatment-Tr_temp-med


 Exercise 1: Brace expansion and wildcards

Your sandbox still contains the sample1–sample3 FASTQ files. Predict the output of each of these commands, then run them to check:
ls sample{1..4}_R1.fastq
ls sample[1-4]_R1.fastq


   Click to see the answer

ls: cannot access 'sample4_R1.fastq': No such file or directory
sample1_R1.fastq  sample2_R1.fastq  sample3_R1.fastq
sample1_R1.fastq  sample2_R1.fastq  sample3_R1.fastq
Brace expansion doesn’t check which files exist, so ls received four file names, including sample4_R1.fastq, which it couldn’t find. The character class is a wildcard and therefore only expands to existing files.

Using brace expansion and the touch command, create empty R1 and R2 FASTQ files for 100 samples with IDs from 001 to 100: sample<ID>_R1.fastq and sample<ID>_R2.fastq.


   Click to see the answer

touch sample{001..100}_R{1,2}.fastq

ls sample???_R?.fastq
sample001_R1.fastq  sample026_R1.fastq  sample051_R1.fastq  sample076_R1.fastq
sample001_R2.fastq  sample026_R2.fastq  sample051_R2.fastq  sample076_R2.fastq
sample002_R1.fastq  sample027_R1.fastq  sample052_R1.fastq  sample077_R1.fastq
sample002_R2.fastq  sample027_R2.fastq  sample052_R2.fastq  sample077_R2.fastq
# [...output truncated...]

Now remove the six original FASTQ files (sample1–sample3) with a single rm command that leaves all 200 new files alone. Why would rm sample1* be a bad idea here?


   Click to see the answer

ls sample?_R?.fastq    # Always check first!
rm sample?_R?.fastq
Because ? matches exactly one character, sample?_ matches sample1_ but not sample001_. (rm sample[1-3]_* would also work.)
rm sample1* would remove sample1_R1.fastq and sample1_R2.fastq, but also sample100_R1.fastq and sample100_R2.fastq, as well as sample1.txt if you still have it from the w4b exercise.

Bonus: Count the number of R1 files by first using ls with a globbing pattern that only selects R1 files, and then piping the ls output into wc -l.


   Click to see the answer

ls *R1*fastq | wc -l
100
You may wonder how this works, since ls puts several files on each line. It only does that when it prints to your screen: when its output goes into a pipe, ls prints one file per line.

Bonus: Copy all FASTQ files except the two for sample100 into a new dir called selection, using a single cp command with a wildcard. (You will first need to create the new dir separately.)


   Click to see the answer

First create the selection dir:
mkdir selection
Method 1 — Exclude sample numbers starting with a 1:
cp sample[^1]* selection/
Method 2 — Other way around; include sample numbers starting with a 0:
cp sample0* selection/

title: More Unix shell:wildcards, brace expansion, find & xargs
section: 4 The find command to find files
text:
4 The find command to find files

4.1 Two problems you may run into
Consider the following two problems you may run into, adapted from Buffalo (2015). Say that you try to pipe ls output into the imaginary program process_fastq, which can operate on multiple FASTQ files at once, taking each as an argument:
ls *.fastq | process_fastq
Any spaces in the listed file names would lead to trouble here, since those file names would be erroneously split into separate arguments. A solution would be to use direct globbing:
process_fastq *.fastq
However, a different problem could occur here: if the number of globbed files is very high, you may get an error that the “argument list is too long”.
The find and xargs commands can deal with both of these problems. More generally, they are useful for:

find: file searching and processing beyond ls’s capabilities.
xargs: multi-file and parallel processing without loops.

Let’s create a small dummy project to try these commands, modeled on the maize SNP project from Buffalo (2015):
mkdir -p zmays-snps/{data/seqs,scripts,analysis}
touch zmays-snps/data/seqs/zmays{A,B,C}_R{1,2}.fastq


4.2 find basics
The basic syntax for find is:
find [path] [expression-1] [expression-2] ...
find will print all files by default, like ls — but unlike ls, it is recursive by default:
find zmays-snps
zmays-snps
zmays-snps/data
zmays-snps/data/seqs
zmays-snps/data/seqs/zmaysC_R1.fastq
zmays-snps/data/seqs/zmaysA_R1.fastq
zmays-snps/data/seqs/zmaysB_R1.fastq
zmays-snps/data/seqs/zmaysB_R2.fastq
zmays-snps/data/seqs/zmaysC_R2.fastq
zmays-snps/data/seqs/zmaysA_R2.fastq
zmays-snps/scripts
zmays-snps/analysis
Compare this with the corresponding ls output:
ls zmays-snps
analysis  data  scripts
Using the -name option, you can also glob like with ls:
cd zmays-snps
find data/seqs -name "zmaysB*fastq"
data/seqs/zmaysB_R1.fastq
data/seqs/zmaysB_R2.fastq


4.3 find functionality beyond that of ls
First, you can use -type as an expression to limit results by file type:
# "-type f" to only match regular files (not, e.g., dirs)
find data/seqs -name "zmaysB*fastq" -type f
data/seqs/zmaysB_R1.fastq
data/seqs/zmaysB_R2.fastq
In the previous command, the two expressions were implicitly connected with a logical and: the resulting matches had to be regular files and also had to have zmaysB*fastq in the name. You can connect expressions explicitly using the -and operator…
find data/seqs -name "zmaysB*fastq" -and -type f
data/seqs/zmaysB_R1.fastq
data/seqs/zmaysB_R2.fastq
…or the -or operator:
find data/seqs -name "zmaysA*fastq" -or -name "zmaysC*fastq"
data/seqs/zmaysA_R1.fastq
data/seqs/zmaysA_R2.fastq
data/seqs/zmaysC_R1.fastq
data/seqs/zmaysC_R2.fastq
You can negate expressions with ! — though you must quote the ! so it doesn’t get evaluated by the shell:
# Find regular files that do NOT match "zmaysC*fastq"
find data/seqs -type f "!" -name "zmaysC*fastq"
data/seqs/zmaysA_R1.fastq
data/seqs/zmaysA_R2.fastq
data/seqs/zmaysB_R1.fastq
data/seqs/zmaysB_R2.fastq
If the quoted "!" looks cryptic, you can use the equivalent -not instead, which doesn’t need quotes:
find data/seqs -type f -not -name "zmaysC*fastq"
As another negation example, say you have some files with temp in their names that you don’t want to include in the find output:
touch data/seqs/zmays{A,C}_R{1,2}-temp.fastq

find data/seqs -type f "!" -name "zmaysC*fastq" -and "!" -name "*-temp*"
data/seqs/zmaysA_R1.fastq
data/seqs/zmaysA_R2.fastq
data/seqs/zmaysB_R1.fastq
data/seqs/zmaysB_R2.fastq
The output is identical to that of the previous command, even though four new -temp files now exist: the zmaysC ones were excluded by the first negated expression, and the zmaysA ones by the second.






NoteIf ! gets evaluated by the shell, then what does it do?





So what does a ! mean to the shell? It accesses past commands — for example, to re-execute your most recent command, use the following:
!!





4.4 Selecting files by size and last-modified date
With -size, you can select files by their size, using + for “larger than” and - for “smaller than”, and a k, M, or G suffix for kilobytes, megabytes, or gigabytes. For example, to find unusually large FASTQ files in the practice dataset:
find /fs/ess/PAS3493/people/$USER/garrigos/fastq -size +24M
/fs/ess/PAS3493/people/jelmer/garrigos/fastq/S71_R1.fastq.gz
/fs/ess/PAS3493/people/jelmer/garrigos/fastq/S71_R2.fastq.gz
A related option is -empty, which is handy to spot output files that were created but never filled, e.g. because an analysis step failed:
# (All the dummy files you created with 'touch' are empty, so this lists them all)
find data/seqs -type f -empty
With -mmin (minutes) and -mtime (days), you can select files by when they were last modified:
# Files modified less than 60 minutes ago:
find data/seqs -mmin -60

# Files modified more than 30 days ago:
find /fs/ess/PAS3493/people/$USER -type f -mtime +30


4.5 Running commands on find’s results
Now, say that you instead want to remove the temporary files we saw above. We can do this using -exec followed by the rm command (in this case, using rm -i for interactive removal):
find data/seqs -name "*-temp.fastq" -exec rm -i {} \;
Here, {} is the placeholder for the file names we are passing on, and you have to indicate the end of our command with an escaped semicolon: \;.
-exec can be very useful to process file queries that are more complicated than what a simple globbing pattern allows for. With -exec, you can use any command to operate on the files that you found.
Finally, note that for the common operation of deleting files, a shortcut exists:
find data/seqs -name "*-temp.fastq" -delete

 Exercise 2: find

The practice dataset contains gzip-compressed (.gz) files of more than one type. Using a single find command, list all .gz files in garrigos that are not FASTQ files.


   Click to see the answer

find /fs/ess/PAS3493/people/$USER/garrigos -name "*.gz" "!" -name "*.fastq.gz"
/fs/ess/PAS3493/people/jelmer/garrigos/ref/annot.gtf.gz

Say that your working dir contains a file called notes.gz, and you forget the quotes around the pattern:
find /fs/ess/PAS3493/people/$USER/garrigos -name *.gz
What would happen, and why?


   Click to see the answer

Recall from w4b that the shell expands wildcards before the command runs. The shell therefore replaces *.gz with notes.gz, the only matching file in your working dir, and find receives -name notes.gz. It then looks only for files that are named exactly notes.gz, and finds nothing in garrigos.
Quoting the pattern prevents the shell from expanding it, so find receives the * and does the matching itself.

title: More Unix shell:wildcards, brace expansion, find & xargs
text:
5 xargs to repeat commands
xargs is to be read/pronounced as x-args, where “args” means “arguments”. This command passes arguments, supplied via standard in, on to another command. For example, first recreate the temporary files, then remove them with xargs:
touch data/seqs/zmays{A,C}_R{1,2}-temp.fastq

find data/seqs -name "*-temp.fastq" | xargs rm
The above command is equivalent to the following, where rm receives the very same list of files as its arguments:
rm data/seqs/*-temp.fastq
Unlike the glob, though, xargs won’t run into the argument list too long error: if the list of files is too long for a single command, xargs automatically splits it up and runs rm several times.
Two other useful xargs options are:

-I {} to put each item at a specific place in the command, e.g. when the file name should not be the last argument:
mkdir -p backup
find data/seqs -name "*_R1.fastq" | xargs -I {} cp {} backup/
-P to run several commands in parallel, combined here with -n 1 to process one file per command:
# Compress FASTQ files with gzip, up to 4 files at a time:
find fastq_dir -name "*.fastq" | xargs -n 1 -P 4 gzip


5.1 xargs versus find -exec
By using xargs instead of find -exec, you separate the process that finds the files you want to operate on, from the actual operations. This can be beneficial, such as when you want to carefully inspect a list of files before doing anything — for example:

Create some dummy files to practice on:
touch data/seqs/zmays{A,C}_R{1,2}-temp.fastq
Save the find results in a text file:
find data/seqs -name "*-temp.fastq" > files-to-delete.txt
cat files-to-delete.txt
data/seqs/zmaysC_R1-temp.fastq
data/seqs/zmaysA_R1-temp.fastq
data/seqs/zmaysA_R2-temp.fastq
data/seqs/zmaysC_R2-temp.fastq
Now pass that list of files to rm:
cat files-to-delete.txt | xargs rm



5.2 find | xargs and spaces in file names
As always, spaces in file names can trip you up — but you were promised a solution with find and xargs! However, out of the box, the below does in fact fail:
touch "samples A.txt"  "samples B.txt"

find . -name "samples [AB].txt" | xargs rm
rm: cannot remove './samples': No such file or directory
rm: cannot remove 'A.txt': No such file or directory
rm: cannot remove './samples': No such file or directory
rm: cannot remove 'B.txt': No such file or directory
The solution is to use -print0 with find, so it prints files with a “null byte” as the delimiter. Additionally, you need to tell xargs about the null-byte delimiter using -0:
find . -name "samples [AB].txt" -print0 | xargs -0 rm -v
removed './samples A.txt'
removed './samples B.txt'

 Exercise 3: xargs

Predict the output of each of these two commands, then run them to check:
find data/seqs -name "*_R1.fastq" | xargs echo
find data/seqs -name "*_R1.fastq" | xargs -n 1 echo


   Click to see the answer

data/seqs/zmaysA_R1.fastq data/seqs/zmaysB_R1.fastq data/seqs/zmaysC_R1.fastq
data/seqs/zmaysA_R1.fastq
data/seqs/zmaysB_R1.fastq
data/seqs/zmaysC_R1.fastq
In the first command, xargs runs echo once with all three file names as arguments, so they are printed on a single line. In the second command, -n 1 makes xargs run echo three times, with one file name each time.

Before running a command like find ... | xargs rm, how could you use echo to see exactly what would be run, without removing anything?


   Click to see the answer

Put echo in front of the actual command:
find data/seqs -name "*_R1.fastq" | xargs echo rm
rm data/seqs/zmaysA_R1.fastq data/seqs/zmaysB_R1.fastq data/seqs/zmaysC_R1.fastq
Now xargs runs echo, which prints the full rm command instead of running it. This kind of “dry run” is a good habit before running xargs with a destructive command.
