To apply for education benefits:

Go to https://github.com/settings/education/benefits.
Click “Start an application”:







Fill out the form as needed. (You will likely need a document that proves your current status at the university.)







Application approval is often quite fast (sometimes in minutes), but access is only granted 72 hours after approval. You can already sign in and use the free plan in the meantime.





2.3 Signing in to GitHub Copilot in VS Code
Start a VS Code Server session at OSC as usual, and open your personal dir in the course’s project dir (/fs/ess/PAS3493/people/<user>). Then:

Click “Sign In” next to the Copilot icon in the status bar at the bottom of the window:







Click “Continue with GitHub”:







VS Code will show you a one-time code. Click “Copy & Continue to Browser”, which copies the code:







Click “Open” to allow VS Code to open the GitHub website in a new browser tab:







In the new browser tab, check that you are signed in to the correct GitHub account and click “Continue”:







Paste the code that you copied in step 3 and click “Continue”:












TipLost the code? (Click to expand)





Back in VS Code, a notification in the bottom right also shows the code:









On the “Authorize Visual Studio Code” page, scroll down and click “Authorize Visual-Studio-Code”:

















The page shows that this request came from an OSC IP address (starting with 192.148) — that’s expected, because VS Code Server runs at OSC rather than on your computer.




GitHub may ask you to confirm access with your passkey, password, or two-factor authentication:






After this, you can close the browser tab and go back to VS Code.


2.4 Enabling inline suggestions
Click the Copilot icon in the status bar at the bottom again. This shows your plan and how much of your monthly allowance you have used. Inline suggestions may be disabled by default:





If so, enable them as follows:

Open the Command Palette via the bottom-left cog wheel or with the keyboard shortcut Ctrl+Shift+P (Windows) or Cmd+Shift+P (Mac)
Type “copilot inline” and select GitHub Copilot: Enable Inline Suggestions:







Click the Copilot icon in the status bar once more, and make sure that all boxes under “Inline Suggestions” are checked:








The second box refers to the type of file you have open (here, a plain-text file).

title: GitHub Copilot in VS Code
text:
3 GitHub Copilot inline suggestions
Let’s start by creating a dir for this week, navigating there, and creating and opening a Markdown file:
# You should be in /fs/ess/PAS3493/people/$USER
mkdir -p week08/copilot
cd week08/copilot
touch copilot.md
In the editor, paste the following into the copilot.md document:
```bash
# GTF file:
GTF=../../garrigos/ref/annot.gtf
```
When you go to a new line within the code block and wait a second, you should see a suggestion “in ghost text” (light gray text) appear. To accept the suggestion, press Tab.
But instead of letting GitHub Copilot go off on its own to randomly suggest ways to interrogate this file, let’s give it a prompt by typing a comment line first:
# Count the number of lines in the GTF file
Press Enter to go to a new line, and again wait for a second for the suggestion to appear. Accept it with Tab and run the code: does it seem to have given a correct suggestion?

3.1 Example prompts for the GTF file
# Count the number of lines in the GTF file, excluding the header

# Count the number of gene features in the GTF file

# Print a frequency table of all feature types in the GTF file

# Count the number of genes on the + versus the - strand

# How many genes have a description?






TipIterating questions and inline chat



When you are not happy with Copilot’s suggestion, you can delete the answer, modify your prompt line, and press Enter again. However, if you want to explicitly request a change to the current suggestion, you can also use the inline chat functionality by selecting the code and pressing ⌘+I (Mac) / Ctrl+I (Windows).
For example, I didn’t get a good answer to the last prompt above:





So I pressed the ⌘+I and reported the failure:





Copilot then came up with a fix, which I could accept:





Running the modified line did give the correct answer:













NoteMore complicated bonus prompts




# What is the average length of a gene in this GTF file?

# What is the average number of exons per gene in this GTF file?

# List all unique gene biotypes in the GTF file




3.2 Other example prompts
Here are a few other example prompts you can try in the same way — these are more general Unix shell tasks that are currently likely just beyond your abilities:
# List the top 5 largest files in the /fs/ess/PAS3493 directory and its subdirs

# Find all Markdown files in /fs/ess/PAS3493 and its subdirs

# Print a list of files that contain the word "cathemerium" in /fs/ess/PAS3493 and its subdirs






You can hover over suggestions to see alternative suggestions, if they are available – see the top-right of this screenshot:









 Exercise: Ask other questions
Be creative and ask GitHub Copilot to help you with some Unix shell tasks!

title: GitHub Copilot in VS Code
text:
4 GitHub Copilot Chat

4.1 The chat sidebar and chat options
Open the chat sidebar using the keyboard shortcut Ctrl+⌘+I (Mac) / Ctrl+Alt+I (Windows) or by clicking the icon in the top bar, shown on the far left in this screenshot:





The chat sidebar should open on the right side of your VS Code window, and look something like this:






File context
The chat automatically suggests to use the file you are currently viewing in the editor as its main context, which is why it says copilot.md at the top of the chat window above. If you click the + button next to that, it will actually use this file as context. Using the attachment icon next to that, you can also select other files to use as context.






TipFile/context tips



While you can select specific files as shown above, Copilot may look for context in any files in the folder you have open, especially the ones you have open in the editor. Therefore, when asking questions, consider opening relevant files and close irrelevant files.
Along similar lines, you can also select relevant code within a file.




Modes and models
The dropdown menu in the bottom-left corner of the chat window allows you to select different chat modes:

Agent – this is the most advanced mode, in which Copilot can create files and run commands on your behalf
Ask – this is closer to the in-browser chat that you’re used to, but with the added benefit of file context and easy code insertions
Edit – this mode focuses on editing existing code rather than creating new code from scratch. It’s especially useful when you have multiple interconnected files that need to be changed in concert.







NoteAbout models



One feature of GitHub Copilot is that it allows you to choose between completely different LLMs (GPT, Claude, Gemini, and others). On the free plan (which is what we’re using), however, Copilot picks a model for you automatically for each request – there’s no model dropdown to choose from. Paid Copilot plans do let you manually pick a specific model.





4.2 An example in “Ask” mode
Select “Ask” mode for now and type the following prompt:

Write a Bash script that runs FastQC for a single FASTQ file. The FASTQ file should be an argument to the script

You should get a response that includes a script block and some explanation. The explanation I got includes the following:





To create a new file with the suggested code, click the ... icon and then select “Insert into New File”:







Click to see the full script that I got

#!/bin/bash

# Script to run FastQC on a single FASTQ file
# Usage: ./run_fastqc.sh <fastq_file>

# Check if an argument was provided
if [ $# -eq 0 ]; then
    echo "Error: No FASTQ file provided"
    echo "Usage: $0 <fastq_file>"
    exit 1
fi

# Get the FASTQ file from the first argument
FASTQ_FILE="$1"

# Check if the file exists
if [ ! -f "$FASTQ_FILE" ]; then
    echo "Error: File '$FASTQ_FILE' not found"
    exit 1
fi

# Optional: Set output directory (default is current directory)
OUTPUT_DIR="fastqc_results"
mkdir -p "$OUTPUT_DIR"

# Run FastQC
echo "Running FastQC on $FASTQ_FILE..."
fastqc "$FASTQ_FILE" -o "$OUTPUT_DIR"

# Check if FastQC ran successfully
if [ $? -eq 0 ]; then
    echo "FastQC completed successfully"
    echo "Results saved in: $OUTPUT_DIR"
else
    echo "Error: FastQC failed"
    exit 1
fi

Let’s save that as fastqc.sh within the week08/copilot dir. If you got output similar to mine, the script was quite good, but did not include the strict Bash settings that we’ve been using.
So let’s follow up with the next prompt in the chat:

Include strict bash settings in the script

It should give an updated script, with an explanation of the key changes:





Now, we have a modified script and a very neat way to update our script is by clicking “Apply in Editor” (which was also visible in the above screenshot), which will show the “diffs” (remember this from Git?) and allow you to accept or reject them either wholly or bit-by-bit:







Click to see the full script that I got

#!/bin/bash

# Strict bash settings
set -euo pipefail

# Script to run FastQC on a single FASTQ file
# Usage: ./run_fastqc.sh <fastq_file>

# Check if an argument was provided
if [ $# -eq 0 ]; then
    echo "Error: No FASTQ file provided" >&2
    echo "Usage: $0 <fastq_file>" >&2
    exit 1
fi

# Get the FASTQ file from the first argument
FASTQ_FILE="$1"

# Check if the file exists
if [ ! -f "$FASTQ_FILE" ]; then
    echo "Error: File '$FASTQ_FILE' not found" >&2
    exit 1
fi

# Optional: Set output directory (default is current directory)
OUTPUT_DIR="fastqc_results"
mkdir -p "$OUTPUT_DIR"

# Run FastQC
echo "Running FastQC on $FASTQ_FILE..."
fastqc "$FASTQ_FILE" -o "$OUTPUT_DIR"

echo "FastQC completed successfully"
echo "Results saved in: $OUTPUT_DIR"

Let’s practice this procedure again with a final edit:

Now add an argument for the output directory



Click to see the full script that I got

#!/bin/bash

# Strict bash settings
set -euo pipefail

# Script to run FastQC on a single FASTQ file
# Usage: ./run_fastqc.sh <fastq_file> <output_dir>

# Check if arguments were provided
if [ $# -lt 2 ]; then
    echo "Error: Missing required arguments" >&2
    echo "Usage: $0 <fastq_file> <output_dir>" >&2
    exit 1
fi

# Get the arguments
FASTQ_FILE="$1"
OUTPUT_DIR="$2"

# Check if the file exists
if [ ! -f "$FASTQ_FILE" ]; then
    echo "Error: File '$FASTQ_FILE' not found" >&2
    exit 1
fi

# Create output directory if it doesn't exist
mkdir -p "$OUTPUT_DIR"

# Run FastQC
echo "Running FastQC on $FASTQ_FILE..."
fastqc "$FASTQ_FILE" -o "$OUTPUT_DIR"

echo "FastQC completed successfully"
echo "Results saved in: $OUTPUT_DIR"



4.3 An example in “Edit” mode
As we saw above, for iterative changes to code, the “Ask” mode works well. But if you have an existing script (or especially: multiple interconnected scripts), you may want to use the “Edit” mode instead. This will directly suggest to make changes in the editor (rather than only doing so when you click “Apply in Editor”).
Switch to “Edit” mode (confirm when it asks you about ending your current session). With the fastqc.sh script still open, this should be selected and shown as context in the chat window:





Ask:

Add code to print the current date before and after running FastQC

And it should immediately suggest the changes in the editor:







4.4 Some examples in “Agent” mode
Let’s start by asking the same question as we did in “Ask” mode:

Write a shell script to run the program FastQC on one FASTQ file






It found the fastqc.sh script that we created earlier! And look at the example usage, where it has found my dir with FASTQ files, but …


What mistake can you spot in the screenshot above?

There is no sample1_R1.fastq file in that dir – the Garrigos data files are named completely differently.

What about:

Write a similar script but to run the program trimgalore






It found TrimGalore scripts elsewhere in the project dir (i.e. the open folder, which is /fs/ess/PAS3493/people/$USER), and created a new script based on those! Note that you still need to “approve” the final creation of the file, e.g. by clicking “Keep” in the chat window on the right, or the checkmark icon in the top-right of the editor window (see the screenshot above).
Finally, let’s have the agent create a script to run a program for which we don’t have code yet – the program FeatureCounts, which can be used to count reads mapping to genes2:

Create a script to run the program FeatureCounts on BAM files in a given directory

5 Appendix

5.1 Copilot custom “background” instructions
It is possible to provide custom instructions to GitHub Copilot that will guide its behavior across all your questions. For example, let’s say you want to ask it to create a series of Bash scripts one-after-another, and all with some of the same settings and header comments that we’ve been using (or some others that you prefer!). You can specify such “global” instructions in a Markdown file (AIs like Markdown!), so that you don’t have to repeat them every time.
To do so:

Create a new folder called .github in your project root.
Inside the .github folder, create a file called copilot-instructions.md.
In that file, write your custom instructions in Markdown format.







For more info, see these VS Code docs





5.2 Copilot advanced chat usage with “slash commands” and more
As the chat window shows in ghost text, you can use keyboard shortcuts to activate certain options:

Context (files) with #:

#file to attach a relevant file

“Slash commands” with /:

/explain to get code explanations
/fix to receive a proposed fix for the problems in the selected code
/simplify to simplify the selected code

Extensions with @:

e.g. @workspace

Best practices for using GitHub Copilot (GitHub docs)
Some prompt writing tips from a GitHub blogpost
VS Code’s Github Copilot documentation

title: Claude Code: guardrails, memory, skills, and more
text:
1 Introduction
This page builds on the w8b lecture, where you set up Claude Code in VS Code Server and created a week08 project dir with a CLAUDE.md file. Here, you’ll learn about additional ways to make working with Claude safer and more effective: guardrails, memory, skills, and planning.

title: Claude Code: guardrails, memory, skills, and more
text:
2 Guardrails: Git and permissions
An agent that can edit files and run commands is powerful, but it can also make mistakes at a larger scale than a chatbot can. “Guardrails” are the practices and settings that limit the damage. Think of the guardrails on a mountain road: they don’t stop you from driving, but they keep you from accidentally going over the edge.

2.1 Git as your safety net
Version control (week 5) pairs very well with agentic AI:

Before asking Claude for a bigger change, commit your work, so that git status is clean.
After Claude is done, review all changes with git diff or the VS Code Source Control panel — including changes to files you didn’t have open.
Undo changes you don’t want with git restore <file>, or discard them in the Source Control panel.







Claude can write commit messages for you, too — but read them, and edit them where needed.





2.2 Built-in protections
By default, Claude Code:

Asks before editing files and before running commands (except a set of read-only commands, like ls).
Asks before accessing files outside your workspace.
Tries to detect “prompt injection”: instructions hidden in files or web pages that Claude reads, which try to make it do something you didn’t ask for. This protection is not foolproof.



2.3 Permission rules
You can add your own rules about what Claude may do, in a permissions section of a settings file. There are three types of rules:

allow: Claude may do this without asking.
ask: Claude must always ask first, even in permission modes that normally don’t ask.
deny: Claude may never do this.

For example:


.claude/settings.json

{
  "permissions": {
    "ask": [
      "Bash(rm *)",
      "Bash(git push *)"
    ],
    "deny": [
      "Read(~/.claude/settings.json)",
      "Edit(//fs/ess/PAS3493/people/*/garrigos/**)"
    ]
  }
}

This example:

Makes Claude always ask before removing files or pushing to GitHub.
Prevents Claude from reading your user settings file, which contains your API key.
Prevents Claude from editing anything in your raw data dir.

Where you put these rules determines where they apply:







File
Applies to




~/.claude/settings.json
All your projects (this is where your API key is)


.claude/settings.json in a project
That project; commit it to share the rules with collaborators


.claude/settings.local.json in a project
That project, just for you (don’t commit it)









When you choose “Yes, and don’t ask again” for a command, Claude saves an allow rule in .claude/settings.local.json. To see all rules that are currently active, and which file each comes from, type /permissions in the prompt box. The documentation on permissions describes the full rule syntax.




 Exercise: Add permission rules

Create a file .claude/settings.json in your week08 dir from the w8b lecture with the contents shown above.
Start a new conversation, and type /permissions to check that the rules are active.
Ask Claude:

Show me the contents of ~/.claude/settings.json

What happens?
Commit .claude/settings.json.








WarningGuardrails complement your own review, they don’t replace it



Permission rules can only block what you thought of in advance. Keep reading Claude’s proposed edits and commands, especially when you work with data that isn’t yours to share.

title: Claude Code: guardrails, memory, skills, and more
text:
3 Memory

3.1 How Claude’s memory works
In the lecture, you learned that Claude reads your CLAUDE.md at the start of every conversation. In addition, Claude keeps memory notes for itself (“auto memory”). As it works with you, it may save notes about:

Your preferences and corrections you’ve given it (e.g., “the user prefers lowercase variable names”)
Project context that it can’t work out from your files (e.g., a deadline, or why a decision was made)

It doesn’t save something in every conversation, only things it thinks will be useful later. When it does, you’ll see a message like “Saved 1 memory” in the Claude panel.
The memory is stored separately for each project (each Git repository), in a dir in your Home dir: ~/.claude/projects/<project>/memory/. That dir contains an index file, MEMORY.md, which is loaded into every conversation in that project, and one file for each memory, which Claude reads when it needs to.


3.2 Memory vs. CLAUDE.md









CLAUDE.md
Memory




Who writes it
You
Claude


Contains
Instructions and rules
Things Claude learned while working with you


Where
In your project (can be committed with Git)
In your Home dir (only for you)



Compared to browser-based chatbots, which may remember general things about you, this is a big advantage: both CLAUDE.md and Claude’s memory are specific to each project, so Claude can pick up where you left off in that project.
If you want Claude to remember something, you can tell it directly:

“Remember that …” makes Claude save a memory.
“Add this to CLAUDE.md: …” adds it to your CLAUDE.md instead. This is better for things that collaborators (or your future self) should also know, since CLAUDE.md is part of your project.



3.3 Viewing and editing memory
Type /memory in the prompt box to see your CLAUDE.md files and memory, and to open them for editing. Memory files are plain Markdown, so you can edit or delete them as you like — and it’s worth checking them now and then, since Claude may have saved something that’s wrong or no longer true.
You can also turn auto memory off with the toggle in /memory, or for a single project by adding "autoMemoryEnabled": false to the project’s .claude/settings.json. For more, see the documentation on CLAUDE.md and memory.

 Exercise: Make Claude remember something

In your week08 project, tell Claude:

Remember that when I ask you to explain code, I want a short explanation with an example

Type /memory and find the note Claude saved.
Start a new conversation, and ask Claude to explain a line from one of your scripts. Did it follow your preference?
If you don’t want to keep this memory, delete it (e.g., by asking Claude to forget it).

title: Claude Code: guardrails, memory, skills, and more
text:
4 Skills

4.1 What are skills?
CLAUDE.md is meant for information that Claude should always know about your project. But you may also have multi-step procedures or checklists that you only need for specific tasks — for example, reviewing a script, or checking the outputs of a workflow. For those, you can create a skill.
A skill is a Markdown file called SKILL.md, with instructions for one specific task. Each skill gets its own dir in .claude/skills in your project:
week08
├── .claude
│   └── skills
│       └── review-script
│           └── SKILL.md
├── CLAUDE.md
└── scripts






Skills in ~/.claude/skills instead are available in all your projects.





4.2 What’s in a SKILL.md file?
A SKILL.md file has two parts:

Front matter between two --- lines, like the YAML header of a Quarto document. Its most important field is the description, which Claude uses to decide when the skill is relevant.
The instructions: what Claude should do, and what it shouldn’t do.

For example:


.claude/skills/review-script/SKILL.md

---
description: Review a shell script for errors and for the conventions used in this project.
---

Review the shell script that the user points to:

1. Read the script and check for errors: syntax, unquoted variables,
   wrong paths, and commands or options that may not exist.
2. Check that it follows the shell script conventions in CLAUDE.md.
3. Report confirmed problems first, and optional improvements separately.
4. Don't edit the script, but ask whether the user wants you to apply the fixes.



4.3 Using a skill
You can use a skill in two ways:

Explicitly, by typing / followed by the name of its dir, e.g. /review-script.
Automatically: when your request matches a skill’s description, Claude will often use the skill without being told to.

For more options, see the documentation on skills.






TipSkills vs. CLAUDE.md












CLAUDE.md
Skill




Use for
Information Claude should always know
Procedures for specific tasks


Example
Project dirs, script conventions, rules
Reviewing a script, checking outputs


When loaded
At the start of every conversation
Only when used



Because a skill’s instructions are only loaded when needed, skills can be longer than CLAUDE.md without using tokens in every conversation.



 Exercise: Create and use a skill

In your week08 dir, create the file .claude/skills/review-script/SKILL.md, with the contents shown above.
Start a new conversation, type /review-script, and point Claude to scripts/fastqc.sh. Do you agree with its review?
Start another new conversation, open scripts/count_reads.sh, and ask:

Can you check this script for problems?

Did Claude use the skill? (You should see this in its response.)
Improve the skill based on what you saw, for example by adding a check that you think is missing. Then commit it.

title: Claude Code: guardrails, memory, skills, and more
section: 5 Plan mode, models, and effort levels
text:
5 Plan mode, models, and effort levels

5.1 Plan first, then act
For bigger tasks, it’s often better to have Claude write a plan first, before it changes anything. In Plan mode (select it with the permission mode button in the prompt box), Claude will look around your project, perhaps ask you some clarifying questions, and write a plan that opens as a Markdown document. You can then edit the plan, ask for changes, or approve it so that Claude carries it out.
Plans are also a good way to see how model choice and effort level affect Claude’s work, which is what you’ll explore in the exercise below.

 Exercise: Compare a “fast” and a “thorough” plan
You’ll ask Claude for the same plan twice: first quickly and cheaply, and then with the most capable model and more effort. Use the following prompt both times:
Write a plan for aligning the FASTQ files in ../garrigos/fastq to the reference genome
in ../garrigos/ref, and then counting the aligned reads to produce a gene count table.
We will run this at OSC with Apptainer containers.
Which alignment and counting programs would you recommend, and why?
Round 1 — fast:

Switch to Haiku with Low effort, and select Plan mode.
Send the prompt, and read the plan. For example: How many steps does it have? Does it name specific programs and versions? Does it ask you any clarifying questions, or mention uncertainties?

Round 2 — thorough:

Start a new conversation, so that the first plan doesn’t influence this one.
Switch to Opus with High effort, keeping Plan mode on.
Send the same prompt, and read the plan with the same questions in mind.

Discuss:

What differences do you notice between the two plans?
How would you check whether a plan is reasonable and complete?
How do the plans compare to what Garrigós et al. (2025) did?
Would the “fast” plan have been good enough?

Don’t let Claude carry out the plans: decline (or simply stop) when it asks to proceed.







The thorough round uses many more tokens, so don’t repeat it too often with your API key.

title: Claude Code: guardrails, memory, skills, and more
text:
6 Ideas for using agentic AI
So far, we’ve used Claude for fairly small tasks. Here are some ideas for what else it can be useful for in your research:

Troubleshooting complex errors. Agents can be surprisingly good at following the trail of an error through a complicated set of scripts or a workflow.
Things that are beyond your ability, but easy to verify. For example, a complicated software installation, or automating a tedious, repetitive task.
Proofreading code that works. In a large set of scripts, it’s easy to miss inconsistent variable names or similar small errors — agents can be quite meticulous at catching these.
Writing workflows, including in formal workflow languages like Nextflow (see week 11).
The “optional next steps” you never get to, such as:

Organizing a project dir, writing documentation, and putting it under version control (see week 10)
Turning a script into a Quarto document (see week 14)
Building a personal or lab website with Quarto

Keeping a log. For longer projects, ask Claude to keep a log file (e.g., LOG.md) of what it did and why, which helps both you and future conversations with Claude.

Looking for ideas beyond coding? This site by a political scientist is one starting point.

title: Graded Assignment 3: Software and shell scripts
text:
Overview and grading

What you’ll practice
In this graded assignment, you will practice with shell scripts, running software with containers, rendering Markdown with Pandoc, and version control with Git and GitHub.


Submission expectations

Deadline: Sunday Oct 11th at 11:59 pm.
Submission: You will submit your assignment by tagging the instructors in an Issue in your GitHub repository, as per the last step below.







NoteOral examination



For one of the three remaining graded assignments (this one, GA3, and GA4–GA5), each of you will be asked to explain your work in a short oral examination. You won’t know in advance which assignment this will be. We’ll ask you to walk us through how you approached a few of the questions and to explain your answers.
If you worked through the assignment yourself, there is nothing to worry about: we just want to hear you talk through your reasoning. It’s completely fine if you’ve forgotten details of a command or concept, even one you used correctly. You’ll only lose points for a question if it’s clear that you really don’t understand your own answer to it. If this is the case for several questions, you may be asked to redo the assignment in the form of a replacement assignment.
We’ll use 15-minute time slots for the oral examinations, and we’ll schedule them after the assignment deadline. We’d also like to use a few minutes of this time to hear about your overall experience with the course so far (this part is not graded).




Academic integrity












Use of generative AI tools is not permitted.



Open-book research for the assignment is permitted.



Getting help on the assignment is not permitted.



Collaborating, or completing the assignment with others, is not permitted.



Copying or reusing previous work is not permitted.



APA Citations and/or formatting for this assignment are not required.













ImportantGenAI check — like previously, but with more details on expectations



This is the last graded assignment for which you are not allowed to use generative AI tools. The guidelines are just like for the previous graded assignments, but we provide some additional details on proper citation:

You are allowed to search the internet, consult books, and so on, but you are not allowed to use generative AI tools. As such, using Google AI Mode output is not allowed either, but unfortunately, it may pop up even when you’re trying to use Google for regular web searches. In case that helps, please note that one way to prevent AI mode output from showing up at all is adding -ai to your Google search queries.
For any unprompted use of commands, options, or other code we didn’t cover in the course, you must provide, separately for each ‘novel’ use of code, the specific source, where you quote the relevant lines that explain it. A general reference to a website or book that may explain 100s of commands/options/etc. is not sufficient. Alternatively, you can argue you simply knew that command already, from previous self-study or experience. If you provide neither a source nor an explanation for commands not covered in the course, you will not earn any points for the relevant question(s).





Rubric
You can earn a maximum of 0.5 points for each of the 20 numbered questions/items below. There are two bonus questions (21 and 22) that can also earn you 0.5 points each, but only in case you dropped points elsewhere.

title: Graded Assignment 3: Software and shell scripts
text:
Detailed steps

General

We provide a template README.md (see “Setting up” below) with a section for each question, where you can add your answers:

Add the commands you ran only where the template has a bash code block for them.
Include a command’s output only where the template has an output block for it.

For each shell script you write, follow the practices from class: start with the shebang and safe-settings lines, and copy any placeholder variables like $1 to descriptively named variables. You don’t need to paste your scripts into your README, since we’ll look at them in your repo.
In any question where you’re asked to make predictions, and then to run commands to check your predictions, no points will be subtracted for any incorrect predictions.
Recommended: Keep a Markdown preview open to the side, so you can check that it renders as you intended.



Setting up

Start a VS Code (Code Server) session at OSC OnDemand as per usual, and open a terminal in that session.
Create a new dir for this assignment, /fs/ess/PAS3493/people/$USER/GA3, and navigate there. This will be your working dir for the entire assignment.
Copy the template file for this assignment, /fs/ess/PAS3493/share/GA3/GA3_template.md, into your working dir as README.md (keep this exact file name — so don’t include, e.g., your own name). You’ll use this file throughout the assignment to add your answers.



Part A: Your README, data, and Git repo

Inside dir GA3, create subdirs data, scripts, and results. Then, copy some files into your GA3 “project”1:
# Copy your FastQC results into your `results` dir:
cp -r ../week07/results/fastqc results/

# Copy the Garrigós metadata file into your `data` dir:
cp ../garrigos/meta/metadata.tsv data/


 Help! I don’t have those FastQC results.

You may not have those FastQC results (perhaps we didn’t get that far in class, or you didn’t manage to follow along). In that case, you can copy files from the share dir instead, as follows:
# Copy some FastQC results into your `results` dir:
cp -r /fs/ess/PAS3493/share/GA3/results/fastqc results/

Optional: Take a look at the structure of your GA3 dir after copying those files, for example using the tree command. Your results/fastqc dir should contain several dozen files.
Initialize a Git repository, and in a first commit, commit your README.md file (and nothing else). Then, create a .gitignore file that makes Git ignore the data and results dirs, and commit this file.
Throughout the assignment, commit your files to your Git repo as you go along, using informative commit messages. Besides the specific commits that questions ask for, commit at least once per Part.



Part B: Basic shell scripts

Save the code below in a script scripts/echo.sh. Then, look at the four commands below that will run the script, and for each, describe what you expect to be the output and why.

The script:


scripts/echo.sh

#!/bin/bash
set -euo pipefail

echo "$1"
echo "$2"
echo "$3"
echo "Finished"


The commands to run the script four times with different arguments:
bash scripts/echo.sh Oct07 Oct08
bash scripts/echo.sh Oct07 Oct08 Oct09 Oct10
bash scripts/echo.sh Oct07 Oct08 "Oct09 Oct10"
bash scripts/echo.sh results/fastqc/*.html

Run the commands, and if any output differed from your prediction, try to understand and explain why.
Write a shell script scripts/printline.sh that accepts two arguments, (1) an input file path and (2) a line number. The script should print (not store in a file) the requested line from the specified file and nothing else.


 Click here for a hint

Figure out a way to combine head and tail with a pipe to print one specific line from a file. If you don’t manage to, your script can instead print all lines up until the specified line, so you can still move on to the next question.

Test your printline.sh script twice. Each time, make it print one line from the data/metadata.tsv file you copied earlier. In one of these tests, redirect the script’s output to an appropriately named file in the results dir, and then check the contents of that file.



Part C: A script to run MultiQC
MultiQC is a very useful program that summarizes per-sample results of FastQC and other bioinformatics programs into a single multi-sample report. This allows you to easily compare results across multiple samples.
MultiQC takes a path to a directory as input, and it will recursively search that directory for files that it can summarize, such as FastQC results. It will then write its summary report to an output directory.

MultiQC isn’t available as an OSC module (optional: verify this). Get a link from the Seqera Containers website to a container with the most recent version of MultiQC (bioconda::multiqc is the correct hit).
Print MultiQC’s help info by running multiqc --help with your container link. Use the help info to figure out how to run MultiQC with results/fastqc as its input dir and results/multiqc as its output dir, and write down that command in your README.md (don’t run it yet).
Write a script, scripts/multiqc.sh, to run MultiQC using the command you wrote above. That is, the script will have the input and output paths “hard-coded” in it. Optional: add some logging statements to the script with echo, like we did in class for the fastqc.sh script.
Run your script to summarize the FastQC results with MultiQC. MultiQC will print logging information to the screen — how many FastQC reports does it say it found, and does that match what you expected? Commit your scripts/multiqc.sh script now that you know it works.
Change your scripts/multiqc.sh script so that it accepts two arguments, the input dir and the output dir, and uses these when running MultiQC. Then, rerun your script, passing the same input and output dirs as before (results/fastqc and results/multiqc) as arguments. Commit your updated script to Git, so your Git history will now contain both versions of the script.
Compare the second MultiQC run with the first one: do you notice any differences in what MultiQC printed to the screen, and in the names of the output files it created? What caused these differences?



Part D: Pandoc to render Markdown
So far, you’ve seen Markdown rendered in VS Code’s preview and on GitHub. But you haven’t yet converted (“rendered”) any of your Markdown files to another format, like HTML or PDF, yourself. The command-line program Pandoc can do this for you. That’s handy when, for example, you want to share your notes with someone who doesn’t use Markdown.

Here is a Pandoc command to render a Markdown file to PDF:
pandoc -o README.pdf README.md
Take a close look at the structure of this command: how would you describe it in terms of the option(s) and argument(s) it takes, and what does each do? Also, how do you think Pandoc knows which output format to produce?
Run the above command to render your README.md to PDF, and check that the PDF file was created. Then, based on your answer to the previous question, write and run a command to render your README.md to HTML instead.
Think about whether the rendered files you just produced should be committed to your Git repo or not, and explain your choice.
To view PDF files in VS Code, you’ll need to install the extension “PDF Viewer” by “Mathematic Inc”. Install it. Then, simply clicking on the PDF file in the VS Code file explorer will open it properly in a new editor tab. Make one observation about the rendered PDF file, like any formatting you hadn’t expected. Optional: If you see any formatting errors, update your Markdown file, rerender the PDF, and check again.








Part E: Publish your repo on GitHub
Finally, you’ll publish your Git repo on GitHub and “hand in” your assignment by creating an Issue.

Create a new, empty, public repository on GitHub. The repo’s name is up to you, but I’d suggest “GA3” or “PLNTPTH5006-GA3”2.
Make sure you have committed your final README.md. Then, connect the GitHub repo to your local repo, and push your local repo to GitHub.
Your README.md will appear in a nicely rendered form on your repo’s GitHub page, so this is another opportunity to review your document (and if needed, make final adjustments by editing the file in VS Code, committing the changes, and pushing to GitHub again).


 Click here for help if you don’t want to make the GitHub repo public


First, I’d reconsider, since you’re allowed to delete the repo as soon as your grade is in — and more broadly, there is little reason to make your repo private, since it contains no sensitive information.
If you still want to make it private, you can do so, but then you’ll need to add the instructors as collaborators to your repo, so we can see it and grade it.
To do this, go to your repo’s GitHub page, click on “Settings” > “Collaborators” > “Add people”, and add GitHub users kstarr791 and jelmerp. Also create an Issue in your repo, as instructed below.

Bonus

Because it has lots of interactive elements, the MultiQC report doesn’t render very well in the VS Code preview. Therefore, it’s better to download the file and open it in a web browser on your own computer. Find one of the MultiQC reports in the VS Code file explorer, right-click on it, and you should see a “Download…” item. Click on it to download the file, and open it3.
Then, explore the MultiQC report, and try to make sense of it. Note that there is lots of interactivity, and you can for example see sample IDs when you hover over lines and bars. Name one insight you gained from it, and one thing you’re confused about and would like to learn more about.

General

Part A: A Markdown document with class notes

Part B: A Markdown document with Unix shell exercises

Copy each of the numbered instructions below into your document, and insert your answers in between — with the code and its output each in its own code block:

title: Graded Assignment 1:Markdown and Unix shell basics
text:
Solutions
Part A doesn’t have a single correct answer, so below are solutions to Part B only. In the example output, paths and node names will differ from yours: <user> stands for your user name.

Part B


1. Print the location of your Home dir using a path shortcut.

The ~ path shortcut points to your Home dir:
# Print the path to my Home dir
echo ~
/users/PAS3493/<user>

The project ID in your path may differ (e.g. PAS0471).
Alternatively, you could have moved to your Home dir with cd ~ and then run pwd.
Note that echo $HOME prints the same path, but $HOME is an environment variable rather than a path shortcut.




2. Navigate to your Home dir using an environment variable.

# Move to my Home dir
cd $HOME
This command doesn’t print any output, though you could run pwd afterwards to confirm where you are. Note that cd ~ and cd without an argument would also take you to your Home dir, but neither uses an environment variable.



3. Relative or absolute path?

This was an absolute path: the shell replaces $HOME by the full path to your Home dir (/users/PAS3493/<user>), which starts with the root dir /. As a result, cd $HOME works regardless of what your working dir is.



4. Navigate from your Home dir to /fs/ess/PAS3493/people/$USER using a relative path.

# Move up three levels to the root dir, then down to my personal dir
cd ../../../fs/ess/PAS3493/people/$USER

Your Home dir /users/PAS3493/<user> is three levels below the root dir /, so you need three .. to get there.
Typing out your user name instead of using $USER is fine too.
Any path starting with / or ~ is not a relative path.




5. Absolute path with Tab completion.

# Go back to my Home dir
cd ~

# Move to my personal dir with an absolute path
cd /fs/ess/PAS3493/people/<user>
Tab can’t complete (all of) a name when multiple entries start with what you have typed so far:

After /fs/ess/P (or /fs/ess/PAS): there are many project dirs starting with PAS, so you need to type (most of) 3493 before Tab can finish it.
Within your user name: other users’ dirs in people may start with the same letter(s) as yours. How many characters you had to type therefore depends on your user name — just enough to distinguish it from all others in /fs/ess/PAS3493/people.




6. Typing “ and pressing Enter.


What: The prompt is replaced by a > on the next line, and nothing is executed.
Why: The command is incomplete: the shell is waiting for the closing ".
How to get out: Press Ctrl+C to get your regular prompt back. (Typing a closing " and pressing Enter also gets you out, but produces an error, since "" is not a valid command.)




7. Pasting together long-form options.

# Try to paste together two long-form options
cal --julian--three
cal: unrecognized option '--julian--three'
Try 'cal --help' for more information.
No, long-form options can’t be pasted together: the result is interpreted as a single (non-existing) long option. Each long option needs its own --, as in cal --julian --three.



8. Julian calendar for the month and year of your birth.

For example, for July 1990:
# Print a Julian calendar for July 1990
cal -j 7 1990
          July 1990
Sun Mon Tue Wed Thu Fri Sat
182 183 184 185 186 187 188
189 190 191 192 193 194 195
196 197 198 199 200 201 202
203 204 205 206 207 208 209
210 211 212

In this example, July 15th, 1990 is day 196.
cal -j july 1990 and cal --julian 7 1990 also work. You can even include the day, as in cal -j 15 7 1990, which will highlight that day in the output.
The order of the arguments matters: the month comes before the year, so cal -j 1990 7 gives an error.




9. Login node or compute node?


You are on a compute node: you started VS Code (Code Server) as an OnDemand Interactive App, and these always run on compute nodes. (Another clue: the node name in your prompt, e.g. p0133, is not a login node name.)
Print the node name:
# Print the name of the node I'm working on
echo $HOSTNAME
p0133.ten.osc.edu
Your node name will differ: Pitzer compute node names start with a p followed by digits, whereas login node names look like pitzer-login01.

title: Final Project: general information
text:
Picking a topic
The topic and scope of the project are completely up to you. We recommend that you take advantage of this flexibility, so your Final Project will be as useful as possible for your own research and/or personal development. For example:

You may want to work with your own data or a publicly available dataset that is similar to data you expect to work with later.
You are also allowed to start working on a larger research project in your Final Project, even if you may not get far enough during the course to draw biological conclusions.
If you’re not sure what kind of data you’ll be working with in your research, you can simply pick something that seems of interest to you, and/or we could help you find something (see below).
Alternatively, you may prefer to focus on practicing the process that you’ve learned during this course (project structure, reproducibility, Slurm batch jobs, etc.). In that case, a small and simple dataset that isn’t necessarily relevant to your research is a perfectly fine choice.







TipContact the instructors to discuss Final Project ideas



We are happy to help you find a suitable topic and/or dataset. More generally, we highly recommend that you discuss your Final Project ideas with us before you settle on a topic — ideally by early November, well before the proposal is due on Nov 15. You can do so during office hours or by email.



Example projects
To give you an idea of the scope we have in mind, here are a few examples of suitable Final Projects:

RNA-seq: check read quality and quantify gene expression with CLI tools, and test for differential expression in a Quarto document.
Bacterial genomes: assemble the genomes of a handful of isolates, assess the quality of the assemblies, and summarize and plot the results in R.
Amplicon sequencing (metabarcoding): process 16S or ITS reads with the nf-core/ampliseq pipeline and analyze community composition in R.
Automating a lab or field data workflow (not omics): take the many raw output files from, for example, a plate reader, qPCR machine, or field sensors, use shell scripts to organize, check, and combine them, and summarize and plot the results in a Quarto report.

As a rough guide, a project with a few shell scripts (some of which you run as Slurm batch jobs) and one or two Quarto documents that take raw data all the way to a few summary tables and figures is a good size.
Your grade will mostly depend on the process you follow, not on the conclusions you draw from your data or on whether you used the “best” tools for the job — see the next section for more details.

title: Final Project: general information
text:
Graded aspects
Graded aspects of your Final Project revolve around appropriate usage of the tools and principles we covered during the course. To receive a high grade, your project should:

Be well-organized: contained in a single parent directory with a clear and sensible structure of subdirectories, descriptive file and directory names, no files floating around with unclear purpose or source, and so on.
Be well-documented, with at least one README in Markdown format in the root directory of your project.
Be version-controlled with Git throughout: with regular, meaningful commits. Use a .gitignore file to keep large files like raw data and most results out of your repository. You will need to push to GitHub at least for the proposal, progress report, and final submission checkpoints.
Contain both shell scripts and R scripts or Quarto documents that do data processing and/or analysis (we will cover R and Quarto in weeks 12–14). Avoid editing data or results files by hand (for example, fixing column names in Excel), since such steps aren’t recorded and can’t be rerun.
Be performed entirely at OSC, and include the running of one or more scripts as Slurm batch jobs.
Run external software (such as bioinformatics tools) using containers (preferred) or OSC modules.
Be easily re-runnable using a “protocol” in one of your Markdown files (we will cover such protocols in week 10). After your final submission, we will try to rerun your project as part of the grading process!

text:
Detailed steps

General

Execute Unix shell and Git commands to answer all questions unless explicitly instructed otherwise.
When you issue a command in the terminal, include the command in a Markdown code block, and the command’s output in another code block — same as you did for GA1. However, this isn’t needed for some Git commands, because we can check what you did by looking at your repository, and because you’re also allowed to use VS Code functionality instead of commands.
To avoid confusion and make life easier for you, we provide you with a template Markdown file where you can add your answers (see question 1), which contains code blocks wherever needed.






TipA worked example of how to answer a question when you ran a command (Click to expand)





Assignment questions:

Print your current working directory to screen.

Your answers as part of your Markdown document:
### 1: Print your current working directory to screen

```bash
pwd
```

The output of the command was:

```
/fs/ess/PAS3493/people/jelmer
```




Keep a Markdown preview open to the side while you work, like you did for GA1, so you can check that your answers render as you intended — especially the code blocks.



Setting up

Start a VS Code (Code Server) session at OSC OnDemand as per usual, and open a terminal in that session.
Create a new dir for this assignment, /fs/ess/PAS3493/people/$USER/GA2, and navigate there. This will be your working dir for the entire assignment.



Part A: Starting a Git repository

Copy the template file for this assignment, /fs/ess/PAS3493/share/GA2/GA2_template.md, into your working dir as README.md. Open it in the VS Code editor and modify its title (level 1 header) to include your name.
You’ll use this file throughout the assignment to add your answers (remove the instructional comments inside the file as you go: these are Markdown comments, i.e. text between <!-- and -->, which is hidden in the Markdown preview).
Initialize a Git repository inside your new directory.
Add & stage and then commit the README file with an appropriate commit message.



Part B: Exploring the GTF file with Unix data tools

Create a dir data and a dir results inside your working dir. Then, copy the genome annotation GTF file annot.gtf.gz that is in your copy of the Garrigós et al. (2025) data into your data dir, keeping the same file name.
Check the file size of annot.gtf.gz.
Decompress the GTF file with the gunzip command below, and check the size of the resulting annot.gtf file. Roughly how many times larger is the uncompressed file than the compressed file?
gunzip data/annot.gtf.gz
A GTF file starts with a few “header lines” (metadata), followed by its main/table section, in which each line describes one “genomic feature” (a gene, exon, etc.). Use a command to count the total number of lines in annot.gtf.
Now, look at the GTF file contents to count the number of header lines by eye, like in last week’s exercises. How many lines does that leave for the table section?
Now, count the number of lines in the table section in a more automated way: based on what you know about what GTF header lines look like, combine grep -v with another option or command to count the number of lines that are not header lines. What count do you get?


 Click here for some hints.


The -v option inverts grep’s behavior, so that it prints all lines that do not match the pattern (see the “Additional useful grep options” box in the section on grep). Use this option with a search pattern that matches the header lines.
Then, to get a line count, add another grep option to your command, or pipe the output of the grep command into wc -l.
You should encounter a minor difference in the number of lines counted in this question vs. the previous one. If you want to, you can try to figure out why that is as part of the bonus question at the end.


How many distinct “sequences” (chromosomes/scaffolds/contigs) are represented in the annotation file? Store a list of these distinct sequences in a file results/scaffolds.txt.


 Click here for some context and a hint.


Context: The number of sequences gives a rough idea of the quality of the genome assembly, because a high-quality assembly will have only a few sequences, ideally one per chromosome. (Note, though, that any sequences in the genome assembly FASTA file that don’t have any annotated features would not be represented in the GTF file.)
Hint: In this and the following GTF questions, you’ll only want to consider the table part of the file, so start your commands with the same (or a similar) grep -v command as above.


Print a “frequency table” of feature types in the annotation: this should have a count of the number of times each feature type occurs.


 Click here for some context and a hint.


Context: A frequency table of feature types will for example show how many genes have been annotated in this genome — that’s quite useful!
Hint: Feature types are in the 3rd column of the table part of the GTF file.


A labmate wants to know how many genes have been annotated in this genome, and runs the command below:
grep -c "gene" data/annot.gtf
Before running it, predict which of the following statements is true:

This gives the correct number of genes.
This overcounts the number of genes, because the word “gene” also occurs in lines for other feature types.
This undercounts the number of genes, because grep only matches whole words.
This command gives an error, because the file is tab-delimited.

Then, run the command and compare its output with the number of genes in your frequency table from question 11. Was your prediction correct, and what does this comparison tell you? (No points will be subtracted if you didn’t predict correctly.)



Part C: Updating your Git repository

Check the status of your Git repository. You should see that your README.md has changed but also that Git has detected the files in the data and results dirs.
You don’t want to commit any files in the data and results dirs, so create a .gitignore file that makes Git ignore them. Check the status of your repository again — is your .gitignore file working as intended?
Stage and commit the .gitignore file. Then, in a separate commit, stage and commit the README.md file again.



Part D: Exploring the FASTQ files with Unix data tools

Copy the FASTQ file S63_R1.fastq.gz of the Garrigós et al. (2025) data into your data dir, keeping the original file name.
Check the status of your Git repository. Does the FASTQ file show up? Why/why not?
How many reads does the FASTQ file contain?


 Click here for hints.

Recall from the week 4 exercises that a direct line count of the compressed file will not give you the correct answer. Also, don’t forget to convert the number of lines to the number of reads.

How many reads in the FASTQ file contain at least 10 consecutive Ns (i.e., uncalled bases)? (You can assume that stretches of Ns do not occur in the quality score lines.)
Stage and commit the README.md file again.



Bonus
(You don’t need to commit your answer to these questions with Git, but you can if you want to.)

In questions 8 and 9, you counted the number of lines in the table section of the GTF file in two different ways, but got different results. Can you figure out what accounts for the difference?


 Click here for some hints.


The file contains a line that is not a header line, but that also does not describe any genomic feature.
So the question boils down to: which line(s) other than the header lines contain the pattern you used with grep in question 9?
Review the “Additional useful grep options” box in the section on grep to find an option that might help you make sense of that.


Name at least two concepts or commands that we have gone over in the course so far, but which you feel you do not (fully) understand. It helps to be specific about what you struggle with.

title: Graded Assignment 2:Unix shell data tools and version control
text:
Solutions
The commands below assume that your working dir is /fs/ess/PAS3493/people/<user>/GA2 and that your copy of the Garrigós et al. (2025) data is in /fs/ess/PAS3493/people/<user>/garrigos. In the example output, <user> stands for your user name, and file dates, commit IDs, etc. will differ from yours.

Part A: Starting a Git repository


1. Copy the template file and add your name.

cp /fs/ess/PAS3493/share/GA2/GA2_template.md README.md
Then, in the VS Code editor, change the level 1 header at the top of README.md to something like:
# GA2 answers - Jane Doe



2. Initialize a Git repository.

git init
Initialized empty Git repository in /fs/ess/PAS3493/people/<user>/GA2/.git/



3. Stage and commit the README file.

git add README.md
git commit -m "Add README"

Any commit message that describes the change is fine.
You could also have done this with the VS Code Source Control panel.




Part B: Exploring the GTF file with Unix data tools


4. Create data and results dirs and copy the GTF file.

mkdir data results
cp ../garrigos/ref/annot.gtf.gz data/
Neither command prints any output. Using the absolute path to the GTF file (/fs/ess/PAS3493/people/<user>/garrigos/ref/annot.gtf.gz) is fine too.



5. Check the file size of annot.gtf.gz.

ls -lh data/annot.gtf.gz
-rw-r--r-- 1 <user> PAS3493 5.1M Sep 25 14:02 data/annot.gtf.gz
The compressed file is 5.1 MB.



6. Decompress the GTF file and compare file sizes.

gunzip data/annot.gtf.gz
ls -lh data/annot.gtf
-rw-r--r-- 1 <user> PAS3493 123M Sep 25 14:02 data/annot.gtf
The uncompressed file is 123 MB, which is roughly 24 times larger than the compressed file (123 / 5.1 ≈ 24). That’s a big difference, and the reason that large genomic files are typically stored in compressed form.



7. Count the total number of lines in annot.gtf.

wc -l data/annot.gtf
408402 data/annot.gtf
The file has 408,402 lines in total.



8. Count the header lines by eye.

head -n 5 data/annot.gtf
#gtf-version 2.2
#!genome-build TS_CPP_V2
#!genome-build-accession NCBI_Assembly:GCF_016801865.2
#!annotation-source NCBI RefSeq GCF_016801865.2-RS_2022_12
NC_068937.1     Gnomon  gene    2046    110808  .       +       .       gene_id "LOC120427725"; transcript_id ""; db_xref "GeneID:120427725"; description "homeotic protein deformed"; gbkey "Gene"; gene "LOC120427725"; gene_biotype "protein_coding";

There are 4 header lines, all starting with a #.
That leaves 408,402 - 4 = 408,398 lines for the table section.
Other commands to view the file, like less -S data/annot.gtf, are fine too.




9. Count the number of lines in the table section with grep -v.

grep -v "#" data/annot.gtf | wc -l
408397

This gives 408,397 lines: one less than in the previous question — see bonus question 21 for the explanation.
Instead of piping to wc -l, you can use grep’s -c option: grep -vc "#" data/annot.gtf.
The quotes around # are needed: without them, the shell interprets everything from the # onwards as a comment, so grep wouldn’t get a search pattern at all.




10. Count the distinct sequences and save them to results/scaffolds.txt.


First, exclude the header lines with grep -v.
Then, select the first column, which contains the sequence names, with cut -f 1.
To only keep distinct sequences, use sort | uniq, and write the output to a file.
Finally, count the number of lines in the resulting file with wc -l.

grep -v "#" data/annot.gtf | cut -f 1 | sort | uniq > results/scaffolds.txt
wc -l results/scaffolds.txt
167 results/scaffolds.txt

There are 167 distinct sequences.
If you forgot grep -v "#", you got 172: the # lines don’t contain any tabs, so cut prints them in full, and each of these 5 lines is counted as an additional “sequence”.
The file results/scaffolds.txt should start like this:
head -n 4 results/scaffolds.txt
NC_015079.1
NC_068937.1
NC_068938.1
NC_068939.1




11. Print a frequency table of feature types.

The feature types are in the 3rd column:
grep -v "#" data/annot.gtf | cut -f 3 | sort | uniq -c
 141444 CDS
 166177 exon
  19673 gene
  25864 start_codon
  25892 stop_codon
  29347 transcript

So, for example, 19,673 genes have been annotated in this genome.
Adding | sort -nr to sort the table by count is a nice touch.




12. Predict, then run grep -c "gene".

grep -c "gene" data/annot.gtf
408397

The correct answer is b): this overcounts the number of genes. The command returns 408,397, which is far more than the 19,673 genes in the frequency table from question 11.
That’s because nearly every line in the GTF file contains “gene” in its 9th (attributes) column, in gene_id "..." and gene "LOC...". In fact, 408,397 is exactly the number of table lines from question 9: every line in the table section matches.
The lesson: grep matches a pattern anywhere in a line, so to count genes, you need to check the feature type column specifically, as you did in question 11.
Regarding the other answers: grep does not only match whole words (unless you use its -w option), and it doesn’t care whether a file is tab-delimited.




Part C: Updating your Git repository


13. Check the status of your Git repository.

git status
On branch main
Changes not staged for commit:
  (use "git add <file>..." to update what will be committed)
  (use "git restore <file>..." to discard changes in working directory)
        modified:   README.md

Untracked files:
  (use "git add <file>..." to include in what will be committed)
        data/
        results/

no changes added to commit (use "git add" and/or "git commit -a")
README.md has been modified since you committed it, and data/ and results/ are listed as untracked.



14. Create a .gitignore file and check the status again.

echo "data/" > .gitignore
echo "results/" >> .gitignore
git status
On branch main
Changes not staged for commit:
  (use "git add <file>..." to update what will be committed)
  (use "git restore <file>..." to discard changes in working directory)
        modified:   README.md

Untracked files:
  (use "git add <file>..." to include in what will be committed)
        .gitignore

no changes added to commit (use "git add" and/or "git commit -a")

Yes, the .gitignore file is working: data/ and results/ are no longer listed. Instead, the new .gitignore file itself shows up as untracked.
Creating the .gitignore file in the VS Code editor is fine too. Patterns like data and results, or data/* and results/*, also work.




15. Commit .gitignore and then README.md in separate commits.

git add .gitignore
git commit -m "Add .gitignore"

git add README.md
git commit -m "Add answers for Part B"
You can check that these are two separate commits with git log.



Part D: Exploring the FASTQ files with Unix data tools


16. Copy the FASTQ file.

cp ../garrigos/fastq/S63_R1.fastq.gz data/
This command doesn’t print any output.



17. Does the FASTQ file show up in git status?

git status
On branch main
Changes not staged for commit:
  (use "git add <file>..." to update what will be committed)
  (use "git restore <file>..." to discard changes in working directory)
        modified:   README.md

no changes added to commit (use "git add" and/or "git commit -a")

No, the FASTQ file doesn’t show up, because it is in the data dir, which is listed in .gitignore.
Whether README.md is listed as modified depends on whether you had already added answers to it after your last commit. If not, you’d see “nothing to commit, working tree clean”.




18. How many reads does the FASTQ file contain?

zcat data/S63_R1.fastq.gz | wc -l
2000000

Each read takes up 4 lines in a FASTQ file, so the file contains 2,000,000 / 4 = 500,000 reads.
Running wc -l data/S63_R1.fastq.gz directly on the compressed file returns 101,139, which is meaningless: you need to count the lines of the decompressed output.




19. How many reads contain at least 10 consecutive Ns?

zcat data/S63_R1.fastq.gz | grep -c "NNNNNNNNNN"
32612

32,612 reads contain at least 10 consecutive Ns.
A read with more than 10 consecutive Ns also matches, and is still counted only once, since grep -c counts matching lines.




20. Stage and commit the README file again.

git add README.md
git commit -m "Add answers for Parts C and D"



Bonus


21. Why do the counts from questions 8 and 9 differ?

Use grep’s -n option to print line numbers along with each matching line:
grep -n "#" data/annot.gtf
1:#gtf-version 2.2
2:#!genome-build TS_CPP_V2
3:#!genome-build-accession NCBI_Assembly:GCF_016801865.2
4:#!annotation-source NCBI RefSeq GCF_016801865.2-RS_2022_12
408402:###

Besides the 4 header lines, the last line of the file, ###, also contains a #. This line seems to function as an end-of-file marker.
It is not a header line, so you didn’t count it as one in question 8, but grep -v "#" did exclude it in question 9: 408,402 - 5 = 408,397.
You could also have found this line by looking at the end of the file with tail data/annot.gtf.




22. Concepts or commands you don’t (fully) understand.

There is no single correct answer here.

title: Ungraded Assignment: Set up Positron for R at OSC
text:
Introduction

Overview
By Sunday, November 8th (before our first R class), you should have Positron installed on your computer and be able to use it with R and its AI assistant at OSC.






If you run into problems with any of these steps, contact Jelmer — don’t wait until the weekend!





Why Positron?
For the R part of the course, we’ll use Positron, an IDE (Integrated Development Environment) for R and Python made by Posit, the company behind RStudio:

It has the panes you may know from RStudio, like a Console, Environment, and Plots, but it is built on VS Code, so much of it will look familiar.
Its AI assistant, Posit Assistant, can be used with your OSU API key from week 8. It can even see the objects in your R session, such as data frames. (RStudio Server at OSC has no AI assistant.)
Positron is the main focus of Posit’s development moving forward.

Unlike VS Code, Positron can’t be used through OnDemand at OSC. Instead, you’ll install it on your own computer and connect it to an OSC compute node, using the same setup as for a local VS Code installation.

title: Ungraded Assignment: Set up Positron for R at OSC
text:
Install Positron






WarningIf you have an OSU-managed computer (Click to expand)





If you have an OSU-managed computer, whether you can (easily) install Positron depends on your operating system and whether you have local administrative privileges:









Have administrative privileges
No administrative privileges




Windows
✅
❌ (contact the IT Service Desk)


Mac
✅

If you have an OSU-managed Windows computer without administrative privileges, contact Jelmer.




Go to the Positron download page and check the box to accept the license agreement.
Download the latest release for your operating system:

Mac: the .dmg file (Intel or Apple Silicon)
Windows: the .exe installer
Linux: the .deb or .rpm file, depending on your distribution

Install Positron:

Mac: Open the .dmg file and drag Positron to your Applications folder (on an OSU-managed Mac without administrative privileges, use the Applications folder in your Home folder).
Windows: Run the .exe installer and follow the prompts.
Linux: Use your package manager to install the downloaded file.

Open Positron.

title: Ungraded Assignment: Set up Positron for R at OSC
text:
Set up Posit Assistant
You’ll first set up Posit Assistant on your own computer. This configuration will carry over to OSC.

Install the extension



Open the Extensions view by clicking the Extensions icon in the Activity Bar (the narrow, leftmost sidebar).
In the search box, start typing “posit assistant”.
Click Install on the “Posit Assistant” extension by Posit.





The Extensions icon











Connect it to your OSU API key



Click on the newly added Posit Assistant icon in the Activity Bar.
Click “Help me set it up” and then “Configure LLM providers”:





The Posit Assistant icon




















At the top, select Custom Provider from the list of providers, and enter:

API Key: your OSU API key from week 8. (It’s the value of ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN in your ~/.claude/settings.json file at OSC.)
Base URL: https://litellm.cloud.osu.edu

Then, click Sign in.





If it worked, the assistant panel should now show:





In the bottom-right of the prompt box, click Select Model. The models available with your API key are under “OpenAI Compatible” — click “More models”:















In the (long!) list, select  claude-sonnet-.... The prompt box should then look something like this:












Not all models available with the OSU API key work with Posit Assistant. If you get an “internal error” when using it later, switch to a different model.

title: Ungraded Assignment: Set up Positron for R at OSC
text:
Connect Positron to OSC

The SSH connection
Because Positron is built on VS Code, it uses the same SSH configuration as VS Code.

If you already set up a local VS Code installation at OSC with the osc-pitzer-compute connection, you don’t need to repeat that: it will automatically work in Positron too. Just do step 1 under Connect below.
If you haven’t, follow the steps in Set up the OSC connections on that page, but do them in Positron instead of VS Code — they are identical. (You don’t need to install VS Code or the Remote Development extension: Positron has this functionality built in.)



Connect

In Positron’s Settings (cog wheel  > Settings), search for remote.SSH.connectTimeout and set it to 300 (seconds), if you haven’t already.
Open the Command Palette (Ctrl/⌘+Shift+P), start typing “SSH connect”, select Remote-SSH: Connect to Host..., and then select osc-pitzer-compute.
A new Positron window will open and connect to OSC. This may take 30 seconds or more while a compute job is starting. If you’re asked whether you “trust the authors”, click Trust and Continue.
Open your personal folder: in the Explorer, click Open Folder and enter /fs/ess/PAS3493/people/<user>, where <user> is your OSC username.












Like in VS Code, this folder will now appear in Positron’s “Recent” list on the Welcome page, so next time you can reconnect with a single click.





Make R available
R is installed at OSC, but has to be loaded as a module (as you learned in week 6). To make sure Positron finds R, you’ll load the module in your shell settings file ~/.bashrc:

Open a terminal in Positron (Terminal > New Terminal) and run:
echo 'module load gcc/12.3.0 R/4.5.2' >> ~/.bashrc
Reload Positron: in the Command Palette, start typing “Reload Window”, and select “Developer: Reload Window”.
Positron should now start R in the Console in the bottom panel.






WarningIf you’re seeing a Python console instead of R (Click to expand)






In the top-right corner of the Positron window, you’ll see something like this:





Click on the Python indicator, and then select New Console Session:





Select the R version:





The top-right corner should now show R, and your console should have switched to R as well:
















NoteWhy ~/.bashrc? (Click to expand)





Commands in ~/.bashrc are run every time you start a new shell at OSC (see the shell configuration self-study page). This is not a permanent solution: the R versions available at OSC change over time, so you may need to update this line in the future.





Install Posit Assistant at OSC
Extensions like Posit Assistant need to be installed separately on the remote: open the Extensions view, find Posit Assistant, and click “Install in SSH: osc-pitzer-compute”.





Your settings from earlier (API key and model) will carry over.

title: Ungraded Assignment: Set up Positron for R at OSC
text:
Test it

In the R Console, create a small data frame:
df <- data.frame(x = 1:10, y = rnorm(10))
In the Posit Assistant panel, ask:

Create a scatter plot of x vs y from df

Posit Assistant should write code for a plot and ask for permission to run it: click Allow.





It produces the plot, and shows it in its own panel along with suggestions for next steps. The plot should also appear in the Plots pane, since it was made by R code that ran in your R session at OSC.












Note that you didn’t have to tell Posit Assistant what df contains: it can see the objects in your R session.



All done! If everything worked, let Jelmer know — and if it didn’t, let him know too.
