title: Configuring your shell
text:
1 Introduction
This page covers how the shell finds the programs you run (the $PATH), and how you can make lasting changes to your shell’s settings using configuration files like ~/.bashrc. Understanding the $PATH helps you make sense of command not found errors, and of which version of a program runs when several are installed. And with a few lines in your ~/.bashrc, you can make your shell more convenient to work in, e.g. with shortcuts for commands you use often and a more informative prompt.

1.1 Setting up
To run the commands on this page yourself, start a VS Code session at https://ondemand.osc.edu in /fs/ess/PAS3493/people/$USER.

title: Configuring your shell
section: 2 $PATH: where the shell looks for programs
text:
2 $PATH: where the shell looks for programs

2.1 What is the $PATH?
$PATH is an environment variable like $HOME and $USER, which you learned about in week 3. It contains a list of directories, and whenever you type the name of a program, the shell searches these directories for an executable file with that name. This is why you can run programs without specifying the full path to their executable.
To see where the executable (binary) for a command is located, you can use the which command:
which git
/usr/bin/git
To check which directories are in your $PATH, you can simply echo it:

echo $PATH
/apps/xalt/xalt/bin:/opt/mvapich2/intel/19.0/2.3.3/bin:/apps/gnu/8.4.0/bin:/opt/intel/19.0.5/itac_latest/bin:/opt/intel/19.0.5/advisor/bin64:/opt/intel/19.0.5/vtune_amplifier/bin64:/opt/intel/19.0.5/inspector_2019/bin64:/opt/intel/19.0.5/compilers_and_libraries_2019/linux/bin/intel64:/apps/software_usage:/usr/lib64/qt-3.3/bin:/opt/osc/bin:/opt/moab/bin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/usr/local/sbin:/usr/sbin:/opt/ibutils/bin:/opt/ddn/ime/bin:/opt/puppetlabs/bin
That output is hard to read, because the directories are separated by colons :. Let’s make it a bit more readable by replacing the colons with newlines (tr ":" "\n"), and numbering the lines (nl):
echo $PATH | tr ":" "\n" | nl
     1  /apps/xalt/xalt/bin
     2  /opt/mvapich2/intel/19.0/2.3.3/bin
     3  /apps/gnu/8.4.0/bin
     4  /opt/intel/19.0.5/itac_latest/bin
     5  /opt/intel/19.0.5/advisor/bin64
     6  /opt/intel/19.0.5/vtune_amplifier/bin64
     7  /opt/intel/19.0.5/inspector_2019/bin64
     8  /opt/intel/19.0.5/compilers_and_libraries_2019/linux/bin/intel64
     9  /apps/software_usage
    10  /usr/lib64/qt-3.3/bin
    11  /opt/osc/bin
    12  /opt/moab/bin
    13  /usr/local/bin
    14  /usr/bin
    15  /usr/local/sbin
    16  /usr/sbin
    17  /opt/ibutils/bin
    18  /opt/ddn/ime/bin
    19  /opt/puppetlabs/bin
The order of the directories matters: the shell searches them from first to last, and runs the first matching executable that it finds.






NoteWhere do the directories in your $PATH come from?



You never set any of these directories yourself, so where do they come from? They were added by different sources when your shell started:

Standard Unix directories like /usr/bin and /usr/local/bin (lines 13–16) are part of the default $PATH on any Linux system, and contain basic commands like ls and git.
System-wide configuration files that OSC has set up (in /etc/, which run for every user when their shell starts) add OSC-specific directories like /opt/osc/bin (line 11).
Modules that OSC loads by default add the directories at the start (lines 1–8), like those for the Intel compilers. You can see which modules are currently loaded with module list.
Your own configuration files like ~/.bashrc can add directories as well (more on these below).





2.2 Modules (and Conda) change your $PATH
In week 6, you saw that the fastqc command is not available until you load its module. Now you can better understand what module load does: it adds the directory with FastQC’s executable to the start of your $PATH.
Before loading the module, which fastqc shows that the shell cannot find it:

which fastqc
/usr/bin/which: no fastqc in (/users/PAS0471/jelmer/micromamba/condabin:/apps/xalt/xalt/bin:/opt/mvapich2/intel/19.0/2.3.3/bin:/apps/gnu/8.4.0/bin:/opt/intel/19.0.5/itac_latest/bin:/opt/intel/19.0.5/advisor/bin64:/opt/intel/19.0.5/vtune_amplifier/bin64:/opt/intel/19.0.5/inspector_2019/bin64:/opt/intel/19.0.5/compilers_and_libraries_2019/linux/bin/intel64:/apps/software_usage:/usr/lib64/qt-3.3/bin:/opt/osc/bin:/opt/moab/bin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/usr/local/sbin:/usr/sbin:/opt/ibutils/bin:/opt/ddn/ime/bin:/opt/puppetlabs/bin:/users/PAS0471/jelmer/software/bin/:/users/PAS0471/jelmer/.local/bin:/users/PAS0471/jelmer/software/quarto/quarto-1.10.15/bin)
After loading the module, which fastqc shows the path to the executable:
module load fastqc/0.12.1
which fastqc
/apps/spack/0.21/cardinal/linux-rhel9-sapphirerapids/fastqc/gcc/11.3.1/0.12.1-ct5vuye/bin/fastqc
(Activating a Conda environment works the same way.)


Say you have your own, older fastqc in ~/software/bin, and your ~/.bashrc adds that dir to the start of your $PATH. If you then run module load fastqc/0.12.1, which fastqc will run?

The module’s version. Your ~/.bashrc added your dir to the start of the $PATH when the shell started, but module load runs later and adds its own dir in front of that. When in doubt, which fastqc tells you which one will run.



2.3 Changing your $PATH
You can add a directory to your $PATH by assigning a new value to the variable that consists of the old value ($PATH), a colon, and the new directory:
# Add a dir to the _end_ of the $PATH:
export PATH="$PATH:$HOME/software/bin"

# Or add a dir to the _start_ of the $PATH:
export PATH="$HOME/software/bin:$PATH"
Like any variable you set in the shell, this change only affects your current shell session. To make it permanent, you’ll need to add the line to a configuration file — see below.






NoteSome notes on the above commands




export makes a variable available to programs that you run from your shell. $PATH is already exported, so export is not strictly needed here, but it is customary to include it.
We use $HOME rather than ~ because the shell does not expand ~ inside double quotes.
Don’t forget the $PATH part! If you were to run PATH="$HOME/software/bin", the shell would no longer find basic commands like ls. If this happens, simply open a new terminal to start over.









TipRunning your own scripts like any other command (Click to expand)





In w7a, you saw that a script in your working dir needs to be run as ./script.sh when you don’t use bash script.sh. If you put scripts with execute permissions in a directory that is in your $PATH, you can run them from anywhere just by typing their name, e.g.:
mkdir -p ~/software/bin
cp scripts/fastqc.sh ~/software/bin
chmod +x ~/software/bin/fastqc.sh
export PATH="$PATH:$HOME/software/bin"

# You can now run the script without specifying its path:
fastqc.sh ../garrigos/fastq/S63_R1.fastq.gz results/fastqc
For scripts that belong to a specific research project, though, it is better to keep them within the project dir and run them from there, so that the project is self-contained and others can rerun your analysis.

title: Configuring your shell
text:
3 Shell configuration files

3.1 The ~/.bashrc file
Your Bash shell is configured by hidden text files in your Home dir, the most important of which is ~/.bashrc. The commands in this file are run every time you start a new shell, so it is the place to store settings that you want to keep.






NoteWhat about ~/.bash_profile? (Click to expand)





Strictly speaking, Bash reads different configuration files depending on the type of shell:








File
Read by
Example




~/.bash_profile
Login shells
The shell you get when you first log in.


~/.bashrc
Non-login interactive shells
Shells you start when you’re already logged in, e.g. by opening another terminal.



To avoid having to deal with this odd distinction, it is common to put all your settings in ~/.bashrc, and to have ~/.bash_profile run ~/.bashrc. At OSC, this is set up by default:
cat ~/.bash_profile
# Get the aliases and functions
if [ -f ~/.bashrc ]; then
        . ~/.bashrc
fi
This code checks whether ~/.bashrc exists (-f), and if so, runs it (. is a shorthand for the source command, which is explained below). So, you only need to edit your ~/.bashrc.





3.2 What to put in your ~/.bashrc
To see what’s currently in your ~/.bashrc, use cat or open the file in VS Code:

cat ~/.bashrc
# .bashrc

# Source global definitions
if [ -f /etc/bashrc ]; then
        . /etc/bashrc
fi

if [ -f ~/.bash_aliases ]; then
    . ~/.bash_aliases
fi

# Path
PATH=/apps/xalt/xalt/bin:/opt/mvapich2/intel/19.0/2.3.3/bin:/apps/gnu/8.4.0/bin:/opt/intel/19.0.5/itac_latest/bin:/opt/intel/19.0.5/advisor/bin64:/opt/intel/19.0.5/vtune_amplifier/bin64:/opt/intel/19.0.5/inspector_2019/bin64:/opt/intel/19.0.5/compilers_and_libraries_2019/linux/bin/intel64:/apps/software_usage:/usr/lib64/qt-3.3/bin:/opt/osc/bin:/opt/moab/bin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/usr/local/sbin:/usr/sbin:/opt/ibutils/bin:/opt/ddn/ime/bin:/opt/puppetlabs/bin
Some things that you can store in this file:

Changes to your $PATH, like the one in the previous section.
Other environment variables, like the $APPTAINER_CACHEDIR variable from week 6.
Aliases: your own shortcuts for commands — see below.
The look of your prompt.

To make a change, open the file in VS Code (e.g. with File > Open File... and typing ~/.bashrc), and add a line at the end. For example, to permanently add a directory to your $PATH:


~/.bashrc (excerpt)

# Add my own software dir to the $PATH:
export PATH="$PATH:$HOME/software/bin"

Changes to your ~/.bashrc take effect in new shells, because the file is read when the shell starts. To apply changes you just made to your current shell as well, run:
source ~/.bashrc






NoteWhy use the source command? (Click to expand)





~/.bashrc is really a shell script, so why not run it with bash ~/.bashrc instead of source ~/.bashrc?
bash ~/.bashrc would run the file in a new shell, and any variables or aliases that it sets would disappear as soon as that shell exits. In contrast, source runs the commands in your current shell, so that its changes stick.









NoteAdding a line to your ~/.bashrc with echo instead (Click to expand)





You can also add a line to your ~/.bashrc without opening the file, by appending it with echo and >>:
echo 'export PATH="$PATH:$HOME/software/bin"' >> ~/.bashrc
Two things to watch out for:

Use >> to append, and not >, which would overwrite the entire file!
Use single quotes: with double quotes, the shell would replace $PATH with its current value before the line is written to the file. Single quotes make sure that the line is written exactly as shown, so that $PATH is expanded each time the file is read instead.










WarningSome precautions when editing your ~/.bashrc (Click to expand)






Make a backup before making changes:
cp ~/.bashrc ~/.bashrc_backup
A mistake in your ~/.bashrc can cause errors every time you open a shell. If that happens, fix or remove the problematic line, or restore your backup. If your shell won’t even start anymore, you can still edit the file through the OnDemand Files menu (check Show Dotfiles to see hidden files).
Be careful with loading software in your ~/.bashrc, e.g. with module load or conda activate. This can be convenient for software that you use all the time, but that software will then be loaded in every shell, which can cause conflicts that are hard to track down. Also, make sure that your scripts don’t rely on this: they should still load the software they need themselves, so that they also work for others.
Don’t add commands that print output, like echo. This can break tools that transfer files over SSH, like scp, sftp, and rsync.

title: Configuring your shell
text:
4 Aliases
An alias is a custom shortcut for a command. Aliases save typing for commands you run often, especially ones with options you always use, and can help when you have trouble remembering long or complex commands.
You create one with the alias command, followed by the alias name, an equals sign, and the full command in quotes:
alias l='ls -lh'
l
total 32K
drwxrwx---+ 5 jelmer PAS0471 4.0K Oct  1 12:37 GA3
drwxrwx---+ 6 jelmer PAS0471 4.0K Sep 14 14:41 garrigos
drwxr-x---+ 3 jelmer PAS0471 4.0K Sep 11 15:04 week02
drwxr-x---+ 2 jelmer PAS0471 4.0K Sep 11 15:32 week03
drwxrwx---+ 6 jelmer PAS0471 4.0K Sep 25 15:20 week04
drwxrwx---+ 4 jelmer PAS0471 4.0K Sep 28 15:44 week05
drwxrwx---+ 2 jelmer PAS0471 4.0K Sep 30 14:14 week06
drwxrwx---+ 4 jelmer PAS0471 4.0K Oct  1 12:09 week07
From now on, typing l will run ls -lh.
You can also add further options and arguments when you use an alias:
# Add the alias
alias ae='apptainer exec'

# This will now do the same as `apptainer exec <image> <command>`:
container="oras://community.wave.seqera.io/library/fastqc:0.12.1--104d26ddd9519960"
ae "$container" fastqc --version
INFO:    Downloading oras image
384.0MiB / 384.0MiB [=========================================================================================] 100 % 37.5 MiB/s 0s
INFO:    gocryptfs not found, will not be able to use gocryptfs
FastQC v0.12.1
Or:
# Add the alias
alias gcm='git commit -m'

# This will now do the same as `git commit -m "Add new script"`:
gcm "Add new script"
To see all aliases that are currently defined, run alias without arguments. OSC has defined a bunch of aliases for you by default, mostly related to coloring the output of commands like ls and grep:
alias
alias egrep='egrep --color=auto'
alias fgrep='fgrep --color=auto'
alias grep='grep --color=auto'
alias l.='ls -d .* --color=auto'
alias ll='ls -l --color=auto'
alias ls='ls --color=auto'
alias mc='. /usr/libexec/mc/mc-wrapper.sh'
alias xzegrep='xzegrep --color=auto'
alias xzfgrep='xzfgrep --color=auto'
alias xzgrep='xzgrep --color=auto'
alias zegrep='zegrep --color=auto'
alias zfgrep='zfgrep --color=auto'
alias zgrep='zgrep --color=auto'
As with changes to your $PATH, aliases only last for the current shell session, unless you add them to your ~/.bashrc:


~/.bashrc (excerpt)

alias l='ls -lh'



You add alias l='ls -lh' to your ~/.bashrc and save the file. Then, in a terminal that was already open, you type l. What happens?

You’ll get bash: l: command not found (unless you had already typed the alias command in that shell). The ~/.bashrc file is only read when a shell starts, so your already-open shell doesn’t know about the new alias. Run source ~/.bashrc or open a new terminal.








WarningDon’t use aliases in scripts



Aliases are a convenience for working interactively. They are not available in scripts by default, and even if they were, a script that relies on your personal aliases would not work for anyone else. So, always write out the full commands in scripts.

title: Configuring your shell
text:
5 Customizing your prompt
The look of your prompt is controlled by the variable $PS1. Let’s see what it contains by default at OSC:
echo "$PS1"
[\u@\h \W]\$
The backslash codes in there are replaced by the shell each time the prompt is shown. Here are some useful ones:



Code
Meaning




\u
Your user name


\h
The name of the node you are on


\W
The name of the working dir (without the rest of its path)


\w
The full path to the working dir (with ~ for your Home dir)


\t
The current time


\n
A new line


\$
A $ sign




For example, a potentially useful change is to show the full path to your working dir, so you always know exactly where you are:

PS1='[\u@\h \w]\$ '
[jelmer@p0362 /fs/ess/PAS3493/people/jelmer]$
With a long path, there won’t be much room left for your command on the same line. You can fix that with \n, so you type your commands on the next line:
PS1='[\u@\h \w]\n\$ '
[jelmer@p0362 /fs/ess/PAS3493/people/jelmer]
$
You can also add color, which makes it easier to spot where the output of one command ends and the next command starts. For example, to make everything except the $ bold and blue:
PS1='\[\e[1;34m\][\u@\h \w]\[\e[0m\]\n\$ '
[jelmer@p0362 /fs/ess/PAS3493/people/jelmer]
$
Here, \[\e[1;34m\] switches to bold (1) blue (34) text, and \[\e[0m\] switches back to the default. Other color codes include 31 (red), 32 (green), 33 (yellow), and 35 (magenta). The \[ and \] around each color code tell the shell that these characters take up no space on screen. If you leave them out, the prompt still looks fine, but long commands will wrap onto the next line in strange ways.
Finally, you may not care much about seeing your user name and node name all the time. If so, you can leave those out and only show the full path to your working dir. In the example below, the path is bold and blue (1;34), the $ is bold and magenta (1;35), and the brackets are left in the default color:
PS1='[\[\e[1;34m\]\w\[\e[0m\]]\[\e[1;35m\]\$\[\e[0m\] '
[/fs/ess/PAS3493/people/jelmer]$
Like aliases, a change to $PS1 only lasts for the current shell session. This makes it easy to experiment: if you don’t like the result, just open a new shell. Once you’re happy, add the line to your ~/.bashrc:


~/.bashrc (excerpt)

PS1='\[\e[1;34m\][\u@\h \w]\[\e[0m\]\n\$ '








NoteWhy single quotes? (Click to expand)





Inside single quotes, nothing is interpreted by the shell, so $PS1 stores exactly what you typed, and the shell fills it in anew each time the prompt is shown. This matters for anything that should be updated every time. For example, the variable $PWD contains the path to your working dir:

With PS1='$PWD \$ ', the prompt always shows your current working dir.
With PS1="$PWD \$ ", $PWD is replaced by its value right away, so the prompt keeps showing the dir you were in when you set it, even after you cd elsewhere.

(This is also why you should use single quotes when adding a line to your ~/.bashrc with echo, as shown above.)
The quotes also preserve the space after \$, which separates the prompt from the command you type.

title: Advanced shell scripting
text:
1 Introduction
This page covers additional shell scripting topics that build on the w7a and w7b lectures: command substitution, extracting parts of file paths, renaming files with loops, conditionals, while loops, and more. If you’re short on time, prioritize the first two sections (command substitution and extracting parts of file paths), which will be useful for one of the upcoming graded assignments.

1.1 Setting up

At https://ondemand.osc.edu, start a VS Code session in /fs/ess/PAS3493/people/$USER.
In the terminal, navigate to your week07 dir.

Some of the examples and exercises use the scripts/printname.sh and scripts/fastqc.sh scripts that you wrote in w7a.

title: Advanced shell scripting
text:
2 Command substitution
Command substitution allows you to use the output of a command inside another command — most commonly, to store it in a variable. This is especially useful in scripts and loops. Let’s see an example. As you know, the date command will print the current date and time:
date
Mon Oct  5 14:52:22 EDT 2026
If you try to store the output of date like below, it doesn’t work — instead, the literal string “date” is stored:
today=date
echo "$today"
date
To run a command and store its output, you need command substitution, where the command is wrapped inside $():
today=$(date)
echo "$today"
Mon Oct  5 14:54:11 EDT 2026
A practical example of using command substitution is to automatically include the current date in a file name. “Automatically” means that the same command will work regardless of the date — for example, inside a script that you may run at any time.
Let’s first learn how to get the current date in a format that is suitable for file names. You can give date a format string that starts with a +, and date +%F will print the date in YYYY-MM-DD format and without the time:
date +%F
2026-10-05

Let’s use that in a command substitution:
# Store the current date in a variable:
today=$(date +%F)

# Use that variable in a file name:
touch README_"$today".md
Check if it worked:
ls README_*
README_2026-10-05.md

It is even possible to do this all in one go, by using the command substitution $(date +%F) directly in your touch command, rather than first assigning it to a variable:
touch README_"$(date +%F)".md






TipOlder syntax for command substitution



You may also come across an older syntax for command substitution that uses backticks, as in today=`date`. It does the same thing, but $() is easier to read, so we’ll stick to that.



 Exercise 1: Command substitution
Say that you want to count and report the number of FASTQ files in a directory in a generalized, programmatic way — like inside a script.

Count and report the number of FASTQ files in ../garrigos/fastq/:

Write a command that will count the number of FASTQ files in ../garrigos/fastq/.
Use command substitution to store the result in a variable.
Use echo to print the following using the variable you created:

The input dir has 44 files, now processing...


 Click for some hints


You can count the number of FASTQ files by piping the output of ls to wc -l.
Your final echo command should look something like this:
echo "The input dir has $n_files files, now processing..."
So, try to store the file count produced by the command in the variable $n_files.




 Click for the solution

n_files=$(ls ../garrigos/fastq/*fastq.gz | wc -l)

echo "The input dir has $n_files files, now processing..."
The input dir has 44 files, now processing...
Note: The variable is already inside a double-quoted string, so you don’t need to quote it separately. In fact, echo "The input dir has "$n_files" files" would end the quoted string right before the variable and start a new one after it, leaving the variable itself unquoted.

Adapt your commands to report the number of samples rather than files:
The input dir has 22 samples, now processing...


 Click for the solution

To count samples, only count the R1 files:
n_samples=$(ls ../garrigos/fastq/*_R1.fastq.gz | wc -l)

echo "The input dir has $n_samples samples, now processing..."
The input dir has 22 samples, now processing...










NoteDoing arithmetic with $(( )) (Click to expand)





A construct that looks similar to command substitution is $(( )), which does arithmetic rather than running a command. For example, an alternative way to count the number of samples in Exercise 1 is to divide the number of FASTQ files by 2:
n_files=$(ls ../garrigos/fastq/*fastq.gz | wc -l)
n_samples=$(( n_files / 2 ))
echo "$n_samples"
22
Inside $(( )), you can refer to variables without the $, and you can use +, -, *, and /. Note that Bash can only do integer arithmetic: any decimal part is simply discarded, so $(( 45 / 2 )) gives 22.

title: Advanced shell scripting
section: 3 Commands to extract parts of paths
text:
3 Commands to extract parts of paths
In loops and other contexts where you are working with file names programmatically, it is common to have a file path from which you want to extract just the “file name part” and/or the “directory part”:








Path
Directory part
File name part




data/fastq/sample1_R1.fastq
data/fastq
sample1_R1.fastq


../garrigos/fastq/S63_R1.fastq.gz
../garrigos/fastq
S63_R1.fastq.gz




Extracting these parts can be done with the dirname and basename commands. Running dirname on a path will return the directory part of that path:
dirname ../garrigos/fastq/S63_R1.fastq.gz
../garrigos/fastq
Similarly, basename will strip any directories and just return the file name:
basename ../garrigos/fastq/S63_R1.fastq.gz
S63_R1.fastq.gz
You can optionally provide a suffix to strip from the file name, simply as a second argument to basename. For example, to strip the .fastq.gz suffix:
basename ../garrigos/fastq/S63_R1.fastq.gz .fastq.gz
S63_R1
In practice, basename is often used in scripts to define output file paths that have the same file names as the input files, but are in a different dir. You’ll need this with programs that make you specify output file names rather than just an output dir.
For example, the fictional program trimmer2 requires the arguments --out1 and --out2 to specify the output file names. Create this script as scripts/trimmer2.sh:


scripts/trimmer2.sh

#!/bin/bash
set -euo pipefail

# Copy the placeholder variables
R1_in="$1"
R2_in="$2"
outdir="$3"

# Define the output file names: we want the input and output file names
# to be the same - they should just be in different dirs:
R1_out="$outdir"/$(basename "$R1_in")
R2_out="$outdir"/$(basename "$R2_in")

# Mock-run a fictional program that takes output file paths as arguments:
echo trimmer2 --in1 "$R1_in" --in2 "$R2_in" --out1 "$R1_out" --out2 "$R2_out"

Because the script “runs” trimmer2 with echo, running it will simply print the command with the output file paths filled in. Note that these have the same file names as the input files, but are in the output dir specified by the third argument:
bash scripts/trimmer2.sh ../garrigos/fastq/S63_R*.fastq.gz results/trim
trimmer2 --in1 ../garrigos/fastq/S63_R1.fastq.gz --in2 ../garrigos/fastq/S63_R2.fastq.gz --out1 results/trim/S63_R1.fastq.gz --out2 results/trim/S63_R2.fastq.gz







NoteGetting the full path with realpath (Click to expand)





A related command is realpath, which turns a relative path into an absolute (full) path:
realpath ../garrigos/fastq/S63_R1.fastq.gz
/fs/ess/PAS3493/people/jane/garrigos/fastq/S63_R1.fastq.gz
This can be useful when you want to record exactly which files were used — for example, by printing the full input file paths in a script’s log output, which will then be unambiguous regardless of where the script was run from.





 Exercise 2: basename and dirname
Predict the output of each of the following commands, and then run them to check your predictions:
basename ../garrigos/fastq/S63_R1.fastq.gz .fastq
dirname S63_R1.fastq.gz
basename ../garrigos/fastq/


 Click for the solution


basename removes the suffix only if the file name ends in it. .fastq occurs in the file name, but not at its end, so nothing is removed — and you don’t get an error or warning either:
S63_R1.fastq.gz
A file name without any dirs refers to a file in your working dir, so dirname returns ., the shorthand for the working dir:
.
basename doesn’t check whether a path points to a file or a dir: it simply returns the last part of the path (ignoring a trailing /):
fastq

title: Advanced shell scripting
text:
4 Renaming files with loops
Sometimes, you need to rename many files in a systematic/repetitive way. This is relatively common with omics data files, as you will often have separate files for each sample, and you may have many dozens of samples.
Manually renaming these one-by-one is tedious, error-prone, and not reproducible. There are many different ways to rename many files in a programmatic way in the shell — though admittedly, none as easy as one might have hoped. Here, we’ll use the basename command and a for loop.

4.1 Create a set of dummy files to work with
Start with creating some dummy files that represent alignments (the results of aligning reads in FASTQ files to a reference genome, stored in .sam or .bam files)1:
# Create the sandbox dir (if it doesn't already exist)
mkdir -p sandbox
# Use brace expansion to create 50 dummy SAM files:
touch sandbox/sample{01..50}.sam
Check the names of the files you created and how many there are:
ls sandbox/*.sam
sandbox/sample01.sam
sandbox/sample02.sam
sandbox/sample03.sam
sandbox/sample04.sam
# [...output truncated...]
ls sandbox/*.sam | wc -l
50
Now, say that you noticed these files somehow ended up with the wrong file extension: they are saved as .sam (SAM files) but are really .bam (BAM files). You’ll have to rename them before moving on to the next step in your analysis.


4.2 Rename a single file using variables
When renaming files in a loop, you will typically use variables to store the original and new file paths. Let’s practice that first with a single file, before we put it in a loop.

Your old file path is:
old_path=sandbox/sample01.sam
You extract the file ID from the old path using basename and store it in a variable:
# Save the filename without the extension using command substitution:
file_id=$(basename "$old_path" .sam)

# Check that it worked:
echo "$file_id"
sample01
Now, you can save the new file path in a variable, using that file ID:
new_path=sandbox/"$file_id".bam

# Check that it worked:
echo "$new_path"
sandbox/sample01.bam
And using these variables, the mv command to do the renaming would be:
# (We'll do this in a loop later, so for now, don't actually run it)
mv -v "$old_path" "$new_path"







TipAlternative ways to build the new path (Click to expand)






We used a two-step approach above for clarity, but you can also do it in one step with basename:
new_path=sandbox/$(basename "$old_path" .sam).bam
Alternatively, you could go a different route and use parameter expansion:
new_path=${old_path/.sam/.bam}






4.3 Loop over all files
Now, we’ll loop over all files and add the renaming code inside the loop. Before actually renaming, let’s do a “dry run” by putting echo in front of mv, which prints the commands instead of executing them. Because the commands contain variables, this is a good way to check that they look as intended:
for old_path in sandbox/*.sam; do
    # Build the new file path:
    file_id=$(basename "$old_path" .sam)
    new_path=sandbox/"$file_id".bam

    # Rename the file:
    echo mv -v "$old_path" "$new_path"
done
mv -v sandbox/sample01.sam sandbox/sample01.bam
mv -v sandbox/sample02.sam sandbox/sample02.bam
mv -v sandbox/sample03.sam sandbox/sample03.bam
mv -v sandbox/sample04.sam sandbox/sample04.bam
# [...output truncated...]
Finally, actually perform the renaming by removing echo:
for old_path in sandbox/*.sam; do
    # Build the new file path:
    file_id=$(basename "$old_path" .sam)
    new_path=sandbox/"$file_id".bam

    # Rename the file:
    mv -v "$old_path" "$new_path"
done
renamed 'sandbox/sample01.sam' -> 'sandbox/sample01.bam'
renamed 'sandbox/sample02.sam' -> 'sandbox/sample02.bam'
renamed 'sandbox/sample03.sam' -> 'sandbox/sample03.bam'
renamed 'sandbox/sample04.sam' -> 'sandbox/sample04.bam'
# [...output truncated...]






mv will silently overwrite an existing file with the same name as the new path. This is another reason to always check your renaming commands with echo first, especially when the new names are shorter or less unique than the old ones. You can also use mv -n (“no-clobber”), which will never overwrite an existing file.




 Exercise 3: Renaming files

What would happen if you ran the final renaming loop above a second time? Predict the output, and then run the loop again to check. Hint: recall the third loop in w7b Exercise 1.


 Click for the solution

There are no .sam files left, so the glob doesn’t match anything. Therefore, the loop runs once, with $old_path containing the literal string sandbox/*.sam.
mv then fails because no file with that name exists, so no harm is done:
mv: cannot stat 'sandbox/*.sam': No such file or directory


A labmate builds the new file path with parameter expansion instead: new_path="${old_path/sam/bam}". What would the new path be for sandbox/sample01.sam? Check your prediction with echo, and then fix the parameter expansion.


 Click for the solution

The first match of sam is in sample, not in the extension!
old_path=sandbox/sample01.sam
echo "${old_path/sam/bam}"
sandbox/bample01.sam
Including the period in the search pattern fixes this: new_path="${old_path/.sam/.bam}".

title: Advanced shell scripting
text:
5 Conditionals
With conditionals like if statements, you can run one or more commands only when a condition is met. You can additionally run a different set of commands when the condition is not met.

5.1 A first if statement
Let’s start with a simple example that you can run in the terminal. First, assign a value to a variable fruit:
fruit=apple
Next, use an if statement to print a message only if $fruit is “apple”:
if [[ "$fruit" == "apple" ]]; then
    echo "It's an apple!"
fi
It's an apple!
Now, assign a different value to fruit, and run the same if statement again:
fruit=banana

if [[ "$fruit" == "apple" ]]; then
    echo "It's an apple!"
fi
This time, nothing is printed, because the condition was not met, so the echo line was skipped. Here’s how that works:

After if comes the condition, where the double square brackets [[ ]] represent a test2, and == tests whether the text on either side is identical.
After then, you put one or more lines with commands that should run only if the condition is true.
The if statement ends with fi3.







WarningSpaces and double ==




The spaces bordering the brackets on the inside are necessary: [["$fruit" == "apple"]] would fail!
The same goes for the spaces around ==, and leaving those out is even more treacherous: [[ "$fruit"=="apple" ]] will not give an error, but will always be true, regardless of the value of $fruit.
A double == is common in programming to test for equality, as opposed to a single =, which is used for variable assignment.





5.2 Adding an else clause
To run alternative command(s) when the condition is not met, add an else clause:
fruit=banana

if [[ "$fruit" == "apple" ]]; then
    echo "It's an apple!"
else
    echo "It's not an apple, it's a $fruit."
fi
It's not an apple, it's a banana.
So, exactly one of the two echo lines is always run. In general, the syntax of an if statement is:
if <test>; then
    # Command(s) to run if the condition is true
else
    # Command(s) to run if the condition is false (optional)
fi


5.3 Conditionals in shell scripts
if statements are especially useful in shell scripts. You may, for instance, want to check that all inputs are correct, and exit with an informative error if that’s not the case. While doing this adds complexity to your shell script, it can be worth it because:

The sooner you stop a script from running when there are such problems, the better.
If you pass erroneous input to the program that your script runs, you may get confusing errors or, even worse, failure without any clear error message at all.

In the example below, an if statement checks whether the input file has a FASTQ file extension, and exits the script if it doesn’t:
if [[ "$fastq" == *.fastq.gz ]]; then
    echo "Processing FASTQ file $fastq..."
    # [Commands to process the FASTQ file...]
else
    echo "Error: input file $fastq does not have a .fastq.gz extension!"
    exit 1
fi
Note that *.fastq.gz is not quoted. When the right-hand side of == is unquoted, it is treated as a pattern with the same wildcards as globbing, so the test is true for any value of $fastq that ends in .fastq.gz. (With quotes, the test would only be true for a file literally named *.fastq.gz!)
When used inside a script, the exit command will stop the execution of the script. With exit 1, the exit status of our script is 1: an exit status of 0 means success — any other integer, including 1, means failure. (Don’t run exit directly in your terminal, though: that will exit your shell and close the terminal!)


5.4 String comparisons
The above test, "$fastq" == *.fastq.gz, was an example of a string comparison, where “string” is the programming term for text (as opposed to numbers). The two main string comparisons you can make are:







String comparison
Evaluates to true (condition is met) if




str1 == str2
Strings str1 and str2 are identical4


str1 != str2
Strings str1 and str2 are different





5.5 Integer (number) comparisons







Integer comparisons
Evaluates to true if




int1 -eq int2
Integers int1 and int2 are equal


int1 -ne int2
Integers int1 and int2 are not equal


int1 -lt int2
Integer int1 is less than int2 (-le for less than or equal to)


int1 -gt int2
Integer int1 is greater than int2 (-ge for greater than or equal to)









Why these odd-looking operators instead of < (smaller than) and > (greater than)? Inside [[ ]], < and > compare strings alphabetically, so for example, [[ 10 < 9 ]] is true, because “1” comes before “9”!









Bash can only compare integers: [[ 2.5 -gt 2 ]] will produce an error.



It can be a good idea to test at the beginning of a script whether the correct number of arguments were passed to it, and simply exit if that’s not the case. This can be done easily thanks to the $# variable, which, as you saw in w7a, contains the number of arguments that were passed to a script:
if [[ "$#" -ne 2 ]]; then
    echo "Error: wrong number of arguments"
    echo "You provided $# arguments, while 2 are required."
    echo "Usage: printname.sh <first-name> <last-name>"
    exit 1
fi






TipAnother integer comparison example (Click to expand)





Say you want to run a program but the specifics of running it (e.g., some settings) depend on how many samples you run the program with.
With the number of samples determined from the number of lines in a hypothetical file samples.txt and stored in a variable $n_samples, you can test if the number is greater than 9 as follows:
# Store the number of samples in variable $n_samples:
n_samples=$(cat samples.txt | wc -l)

# With '-gt 9', the if statement tests whether the number of samples is greater than 9:
if [[ "$n_samples" -gt 9 ]]; then
    # Commands to run if nr of samples >9:
    echo "Processing files with algorithm A"
else
    # Commands to run if nr of samples is <=9:
    echo "Processing files with algorithm B"
fi





5.6 File tests
Finally, you can test whether files or dirs exist (and more):



File/dir test
Evaluates to true if




-f file
file exists and is a regular file (not a dir)


-d dir
dir exists and is a directory


-s file
file exists and is not empty



For example, the code below tests whether an input file exists using the file test -f and if it does not (hence the !), it will stop the execution of the script:
# '-f' is true if the file exists, so '! -f' is true if the file doesn't exist
if [[ ! -f "$fastq_file" ]]; then
    echo "Error: Input file $fastq_file not found!"
    exit 1
fi







NoteTesting for multiple conditions at once with && and || (Click to expand)





To test for multiple conditions at once, use the && (“and”) and || (“or”) shell operators — for example:

If the number of samples is less than 100 and at least 50 (i.e. 50-99):
if [[ "$n_samples" -lt 100 && "$n_samples" -ge 50 ]]; then
    # Commands to run if the number of samples is 50-99
fi
If either one of two FASTQ files doesn’t exist:
if [[ ! -f "$fastq_R1" || ! -f "$fastq_R2" ]]; then
    # Commands to run if either file doesn't exist - probably report error & exit
fi






 Exercise 4: Number of arguments
You will add the if statement from above, which tests whether the correct number of arguments were passed, to your printname.sh script.


 Click to see the printname.sh script from w7a



scripts/printname.sh

#!/bin/bash
set -euo pipefail

first_name="$1"
last_name="$2"

echo "This script will print a first and a last name"
echo "First name: $first_name"
echo "Last name: $last_name"



First, think about where in the script the if statement should go. What would happen when you run the script with only 1 argument if you placed the if statement after the lines that copy $1 and $2?


 Click for the solution

The if statement should come before you copy the variables to first_name and last_name, otherwise you get the “unbound variable error” before your descriptive custom error, when you pass 0 or 1 arguments to the script.

Add the if statement to your script, and run the script consecutively with 1, 2, and 3 arguments. Recall what happened in the w7a exercise when you ran this script with the wrong number of arguments. For which of these runs does the if statement make the biggest difference?


 Click for the solution

The final script:


scripts/printname.sh

#!/bin/bash
set -euo pipefail

if [[ "$#" -ne 2 ]]; then
    echo "Error: wrong number of arguments"
    echo "You provided $# arguments, while 2 are required."
    echo "Usage: printname.sh <first-name> <last-name>"
    exit 1
fi

first_name="$1"
last_name="$2"

echo "This script will print a first and a last name"
echo "First name: $first_name"
echo "Last name: $last_name"

Run it with different numbers of arguments:
bash scripts/printname.sh Jelmer
Error: wrong number of arguments
You provided 1 arguments, while 2 are required.
Usage: printname.sh <first-name> <last-name>
bash scripts/printname.sh Jelmer Poelstra
This script will print a first and a last name
First name: Jelmer
Last name: Poelstra
bash scripts/printname.sh Jelmer Wijtze Poelstra
Error: wrong number of arguments
You provided 3 arguments, while 2 are required.
Usage: printname.sh <first-name> <last-name>
So, the check helps most when there are too many arguments. Without it, the script would silently print the wrong last name (Wijtze), whereas with too few arguments, set -u would already have stopped the script, albeit with a less informative $2: unbound variable error.




 Exercise 5: Check the input file
In w7b, you saw that if a glob doesn’t match any files, a loop will still run once, with the literal glob pattern as the “file name”. If such a loop calls one of your scripts, the script receives a “file” that doesn’t exist, such as ../garrigos/fastq/*_R3.fastq.gz. Input files can also simply be misspelled or have the wrong path.
Rather than letting the program inside your script fail with a confusing error, or fail silently, it’s better for the script itself to check that its input exists.
Here, you will add an if statement to your scripts/fastqc.sh script that checks whether the input FASTQ file exists.

First, think about where in the script this check should go.


 Click for the solution

The check should go right after copying the placeholder variables, and before the remaining code: the sooner you stop a script when there’s a problem, the better — here, for example, there’s no point in creating the output dir for a run that will fail.

Add the if statement to your script. If the input file doesn’t exist, it should print an informative error message and exit with exit status 1.


 Click for the solution



scripts/fastqc.sh (excerpt)

# Copy the placeholder variables
fastq="$1"
outdir="$2"

# Check that the input file exists
if [[ ! -f "$fastq" ]]; then
    echo "Error: Input file $fastq not found!"
    exit 1
fi


Test your script by passing an input file name with a typo, like ../garrigos/fastq/S63_R1.fastq.g.


 Click for the solution

bash scripts/fastqc.sh ../garrigos/fastq/S63_R1.fastq.g results/fastqc
Error: Input file ../garrigos/fastq/S63_R1.fastq.g not found!

Would your check also catch the following problems? Predict, and then test it:

The input is a dir instead of a file: bash scripts/fastqc.sh ../garrigos/fastq results/fastqc
The input file is empty: touch empty.fastq.gz and then bash scripts/fastqc.sh empty.fastq.gz results/fastqc

How could you modify your script to also catch (b)?


 Click for the solution


Yes: -f is only true for regular files, not for dirs.
No: empty.fastq.gz exists and is a regular file, so FastQC would be run and fail with a confusing error.

To also catch (b), add a second check with the -s test, which is only true for files that are not empty. Using a separate if statement makes for a more informative error message:


scripts/fastqc.sh (excerpt)

# Check that the input file exists and is not empty
if [[ ! -f "$fastq" ]]; then
    echo "Error: Input file $fastq not found!"
    exit 1
fi
if [[ ! -s "$fastq" ]]; then
    echo "Error: Input file $fastq is empty!"
    exit 1
fi

(Replacing -f with -s wouldn’t work well: a dir is not “empty” in this sense, so -s would no longer catch (a).)

title: Advanced shell scripting
text:
6 While loops

6.1 When are while loops useful?
A for loop iterates over a collection that you specify directly in the loop, such as a list of words or a glob pattern like *fastq.gz. A while loop instead runs as long as a condition is true.
In Bash, while loops are mostly used in combination with the read command, to loop over each line in a file. This is useful when:

The items you want to loop over are stored in a file, such as a list of sample IDs, file paths, or accession numbers for files to download.
Each line contains multiple pieces of information that belong together, like the rows of a metadata table with a sample ID, treatment, and time point.
The items contain spaces: read reads entire lines, whereas a for loop over $(cat file) would split items at spaces.



6.2 A first while loop
To see how a while loop works, let’s create a file with one fruit per line:
touch fruits.txt
Open that file in the editor, enter the following lines, and make sure to press Enter after the last line (see the box below for why):


fruits.txt

apple
banana
plum

Now, loop over the lines in that file, and print each fruit:
while read -r fruit; do
    echo "Fruit: $fruit"
done < fruits.txt
Fruit: apple
Fruit: banana
Fruit: plum
So, the output is the same as that of the for loop for fruit in apple banana plum in w7b, but now, the collection of items comes from a file.
Here’s how that works:

The < fruits.txt after done uses input redirection: just like > sends a command’s output to a file, < feeds a file’s contents into a command — here, the whole loop5.
The condition after while is read -r fruit6. Each time it is run, read reads one line from the input, and assigns it to the variable fruit.
The lines between do and done are run for that line, using $fruit — just like in a for loop.
Then, read is run again and reads the next line, and so on. Once there are no lines left, read “fails”, the condition is no longer true, and the loop stops.







WarningThe last line needs a line break



read only “succeeds” when it reaches the end of a line, which is marked by an invisible newline character. If the last line of a file isn’t followed by a newline, read fails on that line, and the loop silently skips it!
VS Code doesn’t add a final newline by default — so if plum was missing from your output, that’s why. You can make VS Code always add one by checking the setting “Files: Insert Final Newline”.




6.3 Looping over file names
Next, let’s loop over a list of FASTQ files. First, create a file with the paths to the two FASTQ files for one sample:
ls ../garrigos/fastq/S63_R*.fastq.gz > fastq_files.txt
cat fastq_files.txt
../garrigos/fastq/S63_R1.fastq.gz
../garrigos/fastq/S63_R2.fastq.gz
while read -r fastq_file; do
    echo "Processing file: $fastq_file"
    # More processing...
done < fastq_files.txt
Processing file: ../garrigos/fastq/S63_R1.fastq.gz
Processing file: ../garrigos/fastq/S63_R2.fastq.gz


6.4 Lines with multiple columns
We can also process each line of the file inside the while loop, like when we need to select a specific column. For this, we’ll use the Garrigós metadata file, which has one line per sample. First, create a copy of it without its header line (tail -n +2 prints all lines starting from line 2):
tail -n +2 ../garrigos/meta/metadata.tsv > samples.tsv
head -n 3 samples.tsv
S82 10dpi   cathemerium
S75 10dpi   cathemerium
S79 10dpi   cathemerium
Now, loop over the lines in this file, and extract the first column (the sample ID) with cut:
while read -r my_line; do
    echo "Have read line: $my_line"
    sample_id=$(echo "$my_line" | cut -f 1)
    echo "Processing sample: $sample_id"
    # More processing...
done < samples.tsv
Have read line: S82 10dpi   cathemerium
Processing sample: S82
Have read line: S75 10dpi   cathemerium
Processing sample: S75
# [...output truncated...]
Alternatively, you can process the file with another command before it goes into the loop. Below, cut extracts the first column, and the <(...) construct (called “process substitution”) makes the output of that command available as if it were a file, so it can be redirected into the loop with <:
while read -r sample_id; do
    echo "Processing sample: $sample_id"
    # More processing...
done < <(cut -f 1 samples.tsv)
Processing sample: S82
Processing sample: S75
Processing sample: S79
Processing sample: S83
# [...output truncated...]
(Note the space between the two <s, which is required: the first one is the redirection, and the second one is part of <(...).)
You can also extract columns directly by providing read with multiple variable names, as read will split each line at spaces and tabs:
while read -r sample_id time treatment; do
    echo "Processing sample: $sample_id (treatment: $treatment)"
    # More processing...
done < samples.tsv
Processing sample: S82 (treatment: cathemerium)
Processing sample: S75 (treatment: cathemerium)
# [...output truncated...]
Finally, we didn’t actually need to create the samples.tsv file at all: we can also remove the header line on the fly with process substitution, and read directly from the original metadata file:
while read -r sample_id time treatment; do
    echo "Processing sample: $sample_id (treatment: $treatment)"
    # More processing...
done < <(tail -n +2 ../garrigos/meta/metadata.tsv)
Processing sample: S82 (treatment: cathemerium)
Processing sample: S75 (treatment: cathemerium)
# [...output truncated...]


 Exercise 6: While loops

Below, read gets only two variable names for the three columns in samples.tsv. What do you think the loop will print for the first sample? Predict, then run it to check.
while read -r sample_id treatment; do
    echo "Sample: $sample_id / Treatment: $treatment"
done < samples.tsv


 Click for the solution

read assigns one column to each variable, but all remaining columns go into the last variable:
Sample: S82 / Treatment: 10dpi   cathemerium
# [...output truncated...]
This is why the examples above needed the time variable even though they never use it: it is a placeholder that “absorbs” the second column, so that the third column ends up in $treatment. A common convention for such a “throwaway” variable is to name it _, as in while read -r sample_id _ treatment; do.

Write a while loop that prints the sample IDs of the control samples only.


 Click for a hint

Use an if statement inside the while loop.



 Click for the solution

while read -r sample_id time treatment; do
    if [[ "$treatment" == "control" ]]; then
        echo "$sample_id"
    fi
done < samples.tsv

title: Advanced shell scripting
text:
7 Miscellaneous

7.1 More on the && and || operators
Above, you saw that multiple tests in if statements can be combined with && and ||. But these shell operators can be used to chain commands together in a more general way, as shown below. Here, a command “succeeds” if its exit status is 0, and “fails” otherwise. You can see the exit status of the last command you ran with the special variable $?:
ls nonexistent_dir
echo $?
ls: cannot access 'nonexistent_dir': No such file or directory
2

Only if the first command succeeds, also run the second command:
# Move into the data dir and if that succeeds, then list the files there:
cd data && ls
# Stage all changes => commit them => push the commit to remote:
git add --all && git commit -m "Add README" && git push
Only if the first command fails, also run the second command:
# Exit the script if you can't change into the output dir:
cd "$outdir" || exit 1
# Print a warning if the input file is empty (or doesn't exist):
[[ -s "$fastq" ]] || echo "Warning: input file $fastq is empty"

That last example works because a test like [[ -s "$fastq" ]] is simply a command with exit status 0 if the condition is true, and 1 if it is false. In fact, if works the same way: it runs the then block if the command after it has exit status 0.


7.2 Parameter expansion to provide default values
In scripts, it may be useful to have optional arguments that have a default value if they are not specified on the command line. You can use the following parameter expansion syntax for this — and unlike a plain $1, this won’t cause an “unbound variable” error with set -u when the argument is missing:

Assign the value of $1 to number_of_lines unless $1 is unset or empty: in that case, set it to a default value of 10:
number_of_lines="${1:-10}"
Assign the value of $3 to remove_unpaired, with a default value of true:
remove_unpaired="${3:-true}"

As a more worked-out example, say that your script takes an input dir and an output dir as arguments. But if the output dir is not specified, you want it to be the same as the input dir. You can do that like so:
input_dir="$1"
output_dir="${2:-$input_dir}"
Now you can call the script with or without the second argument, the output dir:
# Call the script with 2 args: input and output dir
bash scripts/sort_bam.sh results/bam results/bam_sorted
# Call the script with 1 arg: input dir (which will then also be the output dir)
bash scripts/sort_bam.sh results/bam


7.3 Standard output and standard error
As you briefly saw in week 4, when commands run into errors, they will print error messages. Error messages are not part of “standard out”, but represent a separate output stream: “standard error”.
We can see this when we try to list a non-existent directory and redirect the output of the ls command to a file:
ls solutions/ > solution_files.txt
ls: cannot access 'solutions/': No such file or directory
Evidently, the error was printed to screen rather than redirected to the output file. This is because > only redirects standard out, and not standard error. Was anything at all printed to the file?
cat solution_files.txt
# We just get our prompt back - the file is empty
No, because there were no files to list, only an error to report.
The figure below draws the in- and output streams without redirection (a) versus with > redirection (b):







Figure from Buffalo (2015).


To redirect the standard error, use 2>7:
ls solutions/ > solution_files.txt 2> errors.txt
To combine standard out and standard error, use &>:
# (&> out.txt is a Bash shortcut for: > out.txt 2>&1)
ls solutions/ &> out.txt
cat out.txt
ls: cannot access 'solutions/': No such file or directory
Finally, if you want to “manually” turn the output of an echo statement in a script into standard error instead of standard out, use >&2. This is good practice for your own error messages, like those in the if statements above:
echo "Error: Invalid line number" >&2
exit 1
That way, your error messages behave like those of other programs: for example, they will still be shown on screen when standard out is redirected to a file.

title: Advanced shell scripting
text:
8 Shell script options
It is also possible to make your shell script accept options (as opposed to positional arguments), just like most command-line programs do.
The example below uses both short and long options (e.g. -o and --outdir). It also uses a mix of “flag”-type options that turn functionality on/off (e.g. --no-gcbias) and options that take a value (e.g. --infile):


scripts/salmon.sh (excerpt)

# Default values (used when an option is not specified)
gcbias=true
outdir=results/salmon

# Process command-line options
while [[ "$#" -gt 0 ]]; do
    case "$1" in
        -i | --infile )     shift && infile="$1" ;;
        -o | --outdir )     shift && outdir="$1" ;;
        --no-gcbias )       gcbias=false ;;
        -v | --version )    echo "Version 2026-10-01" && exit 0 ;;
        * )                 echo "Invalid option $1" >&2 && exit 1 ;;
    esac
    shift
done

How this works:

The while loop keeps running as long as there are arguments left (i.e., as long as $# is greater than 0).
In each iteration, case compares the current first argument, $1, to each pattern (e.g. -o | --outdir, where | means “or”), and runs the command(s) after the matching pattern, up until ;;. The final * pattern matches anything, so it catches invalid options.
shift removes the first argument, so that the second one becomes $1, and so on. Options that take a value, like --outdir, have an extra shift inside the case statement, so that $1 then refers to the option’s value.

Such a script could for example be run like so:
bash scripts/salmon.sh -i my.bam -o results/salmon --no-gcbias
This is more readable and less error-prone than “anonymous” positional arguments, whose order you have to remember. It also makes it easy to have many settings with defaults that can be omitted, like --outdir and --no-gcbias above. In contrast, with positional arguments, only the last one(s) can be made optional.

title: Advanced shell scripting
text:
Footnotes


 The {01..50} construct is called brace expansion: the shell expands sample{01..50}.sam into the 50 file names sample01.sam, sample02.sam, …, sample50.sam before running touch.↩︎
 You can also use single square brackets [ ], but the double brackets have more functionality, and I recommend always using these.↩︎
 The fi ending (equivalent to done in loops) may seem peculiar, but it is simply “if” in reverse order (you’ll see the same trick with case … esac further down this page).↩︎
A single = also works but == is clearer.↩︎
 You may also see cat fruits.txt | while read -r ..., which works for simple cases. But because the loop then runs in a separate “subshell”, any variables you assign inside the loop are lost once the loop finishes.↩︎
 The -r option prevents read from treating backslashes (\) as special characters, and it’s good practice to always use it.↩︎
 Note that 1> is the full notation to redirect standard out, and the > we’ve been using is merely a shortcut for that.↩︎

title: Advanced Slurm batch jobs
text:
1 Introduction
This page covers some additional Slurm topics that build on the w9a and w9b lectures: Slurm environment variables, interactive shell jobs, additional commands to monitor jobs, and job arrays.

1.1 Setting up
To run the commands on this page yourself, start a VS Code session at https://ondemand.osc.edu in /fs/ess/PAS3493/people/$USER.

title: Advanced Slurm batch jobs
text:
2 Slurm environment variables
Inside a shell script that will be submitted as a batch job, you can use a number of Slurm environment variables that will automatically be available, such as:








Variable
Corresponding option
Description




$SLURM_JOB_ID
N/A
Job ID assigned by Slurm


$SLURM_JOB_NAME
--job-name
Job name


$SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK
-c / --cpus-per-task
Number of CPUs (~ cores/threads) available


$SLURM_MEM_PER_NODE
--mem
Amount of memory available (per node)


$TMPDIR
N/A
Path to the Compute storage available during the job


$SLURM_SUBMIT_DIR
N/A
Path to dir from which job was submitted.




As an example of how these environment variables can be useful, the command below uses $SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK in its call to the program STAR inside the script:
STAR --runThreadN "$SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK" --genomeDir ...
With this strategy, you will automatically use the correct (requested) number of cores, and don’t risk having a mismatch. Also, if you need to change the number of cores, you’ll only have to modify it in one place: in the resource request to Slurm.

title: Advanced Slurm batch jobs
text:
3 Interactive shell jobs
Interactive shell jobs will grant you interactive shell access on a compute node. We’ve been working in a shell in VS Code Server, which means that we already have interactive shell access on a compute node!
However, we only have access to 1 core and 4 GB of memory in this VS Code shell, and there is no way of changing this. If you want an interactive shell job with more resources, you’ll have to start one with Slurm commands.
A couple of different commands can be used to start an interactive shell job. I prefer the general srun command1, which we can use with --pty /bin/bash added to get an interactive Bash shell.
srun --account=PAS3493 --pty /bin/bash
srun: job 12431932 queued and waiting for resources
srun: job 12431932 has been allocated resources

[...regular login info, such as quota, not shown...]

[jelmer@a0133 PAS3493]$
There we go! First some Slurm scheduling info was printed to screen — initially, the job was queued, and then it was “allocated resources”: that is, computing resources such as a compute node were reserved for the job. After that:

The job starts and because we’ve reserved an interactive shell job, a new Bash shell is initiated: for that reason, we get to see our regular login info once again.
We have now moved to the compute node at which our interactive job is running, so you should have a different number in your prompt after @.

title: Advanced Slurm batch jobs
text:
4 Additional commands to monitor jobs






TipTBA Refer to scontrol etc for detailed stats







sstat for information about running jobs
To get information about things like memory usage, the sstat (for running jobs) and sacct (for finished jobs) commands are useful. The output of these commands is tabular and by default, too many columns are printed, so rather verbose calls are unfortunately necessary.
For example, you may want to use an sstat call like the following at the end of your script:
sstat -j $SLURM_JOB_ID --format=jobid,avecpu,averss,maxrss,ntasks
Which will give you output like the following printed in your Slurm log file:
       JobID     AveCPU     MaxRSS   NTasks
------------ ---------- ---------- --------
2979576.bat+  01:59.000    244368K        1
MaxRSS is the maximum amount of memory used by the job. It can be really good to know how much memory your job is using, so you can adjust future requests. Insufficient memory is also one of the most common causes of job failure.


4.1 sacct for info about finished jobs
Get information about all jobs – by default those run in the past day:
sacct -u $USER \
  --format=JobID,JobName,NodeList,Elapsed,State,ExitCode,MaxRSS,AllocTRES%32 |
  grep -v ".extern"
               JobID    JobName        NodeList    Elapsed      State ExitCode     MaxRSS                        AllocTRES
-------------------- ---------- --------------- ---------- ---------- -------- ---------- --------------------------------
             2978362 fastqc_si+           p0224   00:01:51  COMPLETED      0:0            billing=1,cpu=1,gres/gpfs:proje+
       2978362.batch      batch           p0224   00:01:51  COMPLETED      0:0    200004K           cpu=1,mem=4556M,node=1
             2978487  fqtest.sh           p0224   00:01:54  COMPLETED      0:0            billing=1,cpu=1,gres/gpfs:proje+
       2978487.batch      batch           p0224   00:01:54  COMPLETED      0:0    203332K           cpu=1,mem=4556M,node=1
             2978503  fqtest.sh           p0224   00:01:55  COMPLETED      0:0            billing=1,cpu=1,gres/gpfs:proje+
To get information about a specific job, by means of example job 2978487:
sacct -j 2978487 \
  --format=JobID,JobName,NodeList,Elapsed,State,ExitCode,MaxRSS,AllocTRES%32 |
  grep -v ".extern"
         JobID    JobName        NodeList    Elapsed      State ExitCode     MaxRSS                        AllocTRES
------------ ---------- --------------- ---------- ---------- -------- ---------- --------------------------------
2978487       fqtest.sh           p0224   00:01:54  COMPLETED      0:0            billing=1,cpu=1,gres/gpfs:proje+
2978487.bat+      batch           p0224   00:01:54  COMPLETED      0:0    203332K           cpu=1,mem=4556M,node=1






TipAliases for long job monitoring commands (Click to expand)





Because you won’t remember all of these formatting options, and even if you do, you don’t want to type them out, this is a case where aliases are really handy. For instance:
alias sact='sacct --format=JobID,JobName,NodeList,Elapsed,State,ExitCode,MaxRSS,AllocTRES%32'

alias stat='sstat --format=jobid,avecpu,averss,maxrss,ntasks'
You can then add other options when you use an alias, for example:
sact -j 123456
To make these aliases always available in interactive sessions, add lines such as these to your Bash configuration file ~/.bashrc. (Note that this file won’t be read by job scripts, so make sure to use the full specification in scripts.)





4.2 time
To get statistics on a single command, like a memory-intensive program you may be running, use the time utility. To use it, prepend /usr/bin/time to the beginning of a command:
/usr/bin/time fastqc "$fastq_file"
If you use this in a script, the result will be printed to the Slurm log file, e.g:
106.79user 4.10system 1:52.34elapsed 98%CPU (0avgtext+0avgdata 246444maxresident)k
0inputs+1760outputs (0major+35697minor)pagefaults 0swaps

User time (CPU time spent running your program)
System time (CPU time spent by your program in system calls)
Elapsed time (wallclock)
% CPU used
Memory, pagefault and swap statistics
I/O statistics

Note that you should use the full path /usr/bin/time rather than just time.

title: Advanced Slurm batch jobs
text:
5 Slurm Job arrays
As an alternative approach to looping over a script, you can also turn a script into a job “array”, i.e. a series of jobs.
Each job in the array gets an ID that you can then use in your script for each job to run with a different value of a certain parameter. Most commonly, you may have a file with sample names and then use the array IDs to subset lines from that file – for instance, for our FastQC script:
#SBATCH --array=1-25
#SBATCH --output=slurm-fastqc-%A-%a.out
fastq_file=$(sed -n "${SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID}p" fastq_files.txt)
fastqc "$fastq_file"

Above, the array was configured using the --array option, simply creating 25 jobs with array IDs from 1 to 25 (assuming 25 FASTQ files).
Then, the SLURM environment variable $SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID will contain the task ID for each job in the array, and we use that to pull out a line from a file with FASTQ file names with sed.
We also use %A (master job ID) and %a (ID that differs for each job in the array) for the log file name.

A full script example is below:
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --account=PAS0471
#SBATCH --time=60
#SBATCH --output=slurm-fastqc-%A-%a.out
#SBATCH --array=1-25
set -euo pipefail

module load fastqc/0.12.1

fastq_files_list="$1"
output_dir="$2"

fastq_file=$(sed -n "${SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID}p" $fastq_files_list)

echo "Running fastqc for file: $fastq_file"
echo "Output dir: $output_dir"

fastqc --outdir="$output_dir" "$fastq_file"

The array values can also be a comma separated list like SBATCH --array=8,10,15 and can even have a stride, with SBATCH --array=1-7:2 producing array tasks 1, 3, 5, and 7.
You can also throttle an array of jobs: only run a subset of jobs at a time. This can be done as follows:
sbatch --array [1-100]%10 fastq.sh
The above command would only submit 10 jobs at a time. (This can also be specified inside the script.)

title: Advanced Slurm batch jobs
text:
Footnotes


Other options: salloc works almost identically to srun, whereas sinteractive is an OSC convenience wrapper but with more limited options.↩︎

title: Using a local VS Code installation at OSC
text:
1 Introduction
So far, you’ve been connecting to OSC through the OnDemand web portal. However, there is another more basic and universal method to connect to remote computers: SSH, which is short for Secure Shell. An optional self-study page on SSH shows you how to directly use the ssh command in a terminal on your own computer to “move” to OSC within that terminal.
This page, on the other hand, shows you how to connect a VS Code installation on your computer to OSC using a process called “SSH tunneling”. This connects VS Code to OSC in such a way that not just the terminal but the entire program operates on OSC. Being able to use your own VS Code installation at OSC has several advantages over using VS Code Server through OnDemand, such as:

You won’t have to fill out an OnDemand form every time
You can easily have multiple VS Code windows open at the same time
You can use the latest version of VS Code “proper” rather than the Server version, which has slightly reduced functionality1
The same setup also works for Positron, an R (and Python) IDE that is built on VS Code

We will set up two connections: one to a compute node, which is the one you should normally use, and one to a login node, as a fallback. Connecting to a compute node takes more setup, but avoids running VS Code (and anything you do in its terminal) on a login node.
This page is entirely optional: everything in this course can be done with VS Code Server through OnDemand.

title: Using a local VS Code installation at OSC
section: 2 Install VS Code and the Remote Development extension
text:
2 Install VS Code and the Remote Development extension

Install VS Code on your own computer:

“Regular” installation instructions for Windows / Mac / Linux
If you are using an OSU computer, you may not have the required “administrative privileges” to install software on your computer the regular way. However, you should in that case have an OSU application on your computer that allows you to install a selection of approved software, and that selection should include VS Code. On Windows, this app seems to be simply called “Software Center”, whereas on Mac, it is called “Ohio State Application Self Service” (names likely vary).

Open VS Code and install the “Remote Development extension pack”: open the Extensions side bar and search for it there. Once you found it, click on its Install button like you’ve done previously with other extensions.
Open a terminal in VS Code (Terminal > New Terminal): you’ll need it in the steps below.

title: Using a local VS Code installation at OSC
text:
3 Set up the OSC connections

3.1 The SSH configuration file

Open the VS Code Command Palette (F1 or Ctrl/⌘+Shift+P) and start typing “remote open”:

Select “Remote-SSH: Open SSH Configuration File…”
Then, select the top option, a file that contains the username you have on your computer and ends in .ssh/config

Paste the following into the SSH configuration file that opens:

MacWindows


Host osc-pitzer-login
    User <osc-username>
    HostName pitzer.osc.edu

Host osc-pitzer-compute
    User <osc-username>
    ForwardAgent yes
    StrictHostKeyChecking no
    UserKnownHostsFile=/dev/null
    ConnectTimeout 120
    ProxyCommand ssh -o LogLevel=QUIET -o BatchMode=yes osc-pitzer-login ./osc-compute-proxy.sh








These instructions are for Windows, click “Mac” above to see the Mac instructions. (The only difference is the path to the ssh program in the last line.)



Host osc-pitzer-login
    User <osc-username>
    HostName pitzer.osc.edu

Host osc-pitzer-compute
    User <osc-username>
    ForwardAgent yes
    StrictHostKeyChecking no
    UserKnownHostsFile=/dev/null
    ConnectTimeout 120
    ProxyCommand C:/Windows/System32/OpenSSH/ssh.exe -o LogLevel=QUIET -o BatchMode=yes osc-pitzer-login ./osc-compute-proxy.sh



In both instances, change <osc-username> to your OSC username, e.g. to User jane. Then, save the file.







NoteWhat does this configuration do? (Click to expand)





It defines two remote “hosts” at OSC that you can connect to:

osc-pitzer-login connects to a login node of OSC’s Pitzer cluster.
osc-pitzer-compute connects to a compute node of OSC’s Pitzer cluster. You can’t connect directly to a compute node, so this connection first goes to a login node, and there runs a script (osc-compute-proxy.sh, see below) that requests a compute job and then passes on the connection to the compute node you’ve been assigned.






3.2 Avoid being prompted for your OSC password
Next, you’ll set up an “SSH key pair”, which lets OSC recognize your computer so you won’t be prompted for your password. This is required for the compute node connection, and convenient for the login node connection and any other SSH connection to OSC.

In the VS Code terminal (regardless of whether you’re using Windows or Mac), generate an SSH key pair:
ssh-keygen -t rsa
You’ll get some output and will then be asked several questions, but in each case, you can just press Enter to select the default answer.
Transfer the public key to OSC, replacing <user> with your OSC username. You’ll be prompted for your OSC password.

MacWindows


# Replace <user> by your username, e.g. "ssh-copy-id jelmer@pitzer.osc.edu"
ssh-copy-id <user>@pitzer.osc.edu


# Replace <user> by your username, e.g. "jelmer@pitzer.osc.edu"
cat ~/.ssh/id_rsa.pub | ssh <user>@pitzer.osc.edu 'mkdir -p .ssh && cat >> .ssh/authorized_keys'



Test it: the following should print the name of a Pitzer login node, without asking for your password:
ssh osc-pitzer-login hostname



3.3 The proxy script at OSC
The compute node connection runs a short “proxy script” in your Home dir at OSC. Copy it there by running the following command in your VS Code terminal:
ssh osc-pitzer-login 'cp /fs/ess/PAS3493/share/osc-compute-proxy.sh ~/ && chmod +x ~/osc-compute-proxy.sh'
This script contains the following:
#!/bin/bash
exec salloc --quiet -A PAS3493 -t 300 bash -c 'nc $SLURM_NODELIST 22'
That is, it requests a compute job (salloc) for 300 minutes (5 hours) with the course’s OSC Project PAS3493, and then connects to the compute node you were assigned (nc ... 22).






WarningAfter the course: change the OSC Project



Once the course is over, you should no longer use the course’s OSC Project. To change the Project, or the duration of your compute jobs, open ~/osc-compute-proxy.sh at OSC and edit PAS3493 and/or 300.




3.4 Increase the connection timeout
Because it can take a little while to get a compute job, you also need to increase the time VS Code will wait for a connection: open the VS Code Settings (cog wheel  > Settings), search for remote.SSH.connectTimeout, and change its value from 15 to 300 (seconds).






NoteAlternative: the proxy script on your own computer (Click to expand)





In our July 2026 workshop, we used a proxy script on participants’ own computers rather than at OSC. That setup was tested with VS Code and Positron on Mac and Windows, so use it if the above setup doesn’t work for you. In that case, skip the “proxy script at OSC” step above, and:

In the SSH configuration file, change the ProxyCommand line for osc-pitzer-compute to:

MacWindows


    ProxyCommand /Users/<computer-username>/.ssh/osc-compute-proxy.sh %h


    ProxyCommand C:/Users/<computer-username>/.ssh/osc-compute-proxy.cmd %h



where <computer-username> is your username on your computer (it’s also in the path to the SSH configuration file).
Create the proxy script by running the following in the VS Code terminal:

MacWindows


cat > ~/.ssh/osc-compute-proxy.sh << 'EOF'
#!/bin/bash
exec ssh -o LogLevel=QUIET -o BatchMode=yes osc-pitzer-login \
  "/usr/bin/salloc -A PAS3493 -t 300 /bin/bash -c 'nc \$SLURM_NODELIST 22'" 2>/dev/null
EOF

chmod +x ~/.ssh/osc-compute-proxy.sh








This assumes you are using PowerShell, the default Windows shell in VS Code (you should see “PowerShell” in the top right of the terminal). If you are using Git Bash or WSL, use the Mac instructions instead.



@'
@echo off
ssh -o LogLevel=QUIET -o BatchMode=yes osc-pitzer-login "/usr/bin/salloc -A PAS3493 -t 300 /bin/bash -lc 'nc $SLURM_NODELIST 22'"
'@ | Out-File -Encoding ascii "$env:USERPROFILE\.ssh\osc-compute-proxy.cmd"













TipConnecting to other OSC clusters



To also connect to Cardinal or Ascend, add additional entries to the SSH configuration file in which you replace pitzer by cardinal or ascend. (For the compute node connection, the ProxyCommand line should then refer to the matching login host, e.g. osc-cardinal-login.)

title: Using a local VS Code installation at OSC
text:
4 Connect to OSC

4.1 Connecting

Open the Command Palette (F1 or Ctrl/⌘+Shift+P), start typing “SSH connect”, and click on Remote-SSH: Connect to Host...
Select osc-pitzer-compute.
A new VS Code window will open. The connection may take a little while (typically 5–30 seconds, but longer when OSC is busy), because a compute job has to be requested and started.

If you’re asked about the operating system of the host, select Linux.
If you’re asked whether you “Trust the Authors” of the folder, click “Yes”.
If there is a pop-up in the bottom-right asking you to update Git, click “No” and check “Don’t show again”.

Like you’ve seen with VS Code Server, the program’s default location is your Home dir, and it is best to change this using File > Open Folder: go to your /fs/ess/PAS3493/people/$USER dir.







If the compute node connection fails or takes more than a few minutes, use the osc-pitzer-login connection instead — but see the warning below.









WarningWhen connected to osc-pitzer-login, you are on a login node!



With the login node connection, VS Code runs on a login node rather than on a compute node, so avoid running analyses directly in the terminal, and so on.




4.2 Connecting from now on to previously opened folders
Conveniently, VS Code will remember folders that you’ve opened this way, and show them on the “Welcome” tab that is always displayed when you open the program. Test this:

Completely quit VS Code
Open it again, and under “Recent” on the Welcome tab, look for your folder in /fs/ess/PAS3493/, and click on that to connect to OSC and open that folder!

Overview
Welcome to the autumn 2026 edition of the PLNTPTH 5006 course, Practical Computing Skills for Omics Data! In this first week of the course, you will get an overview of the course’s contents and an introduction to omics data.






NoteWhat is this website for?



This is the GitHub website for the course. It contains the course materials, including lecture slides, readings, and assignments. In other words, it contains most of the material you might normally find in CarmenCanvas. In this course, CarmenCanvas is only used for course announcements, grades, and a course calendar that includes assignment deadlines.

Multi-omics


In multi-omics studies, two or more omics data types are combined — ideally from the same set of samples.

title: An overview of omics data
text:
Sanger vs. high-throughput sequencing


Sanger sequencing

Since 1977 (technology) / 1986 (automated sequencer).
Sequencing of a single, short-ish DNA fragment at a time.
This fragment is typically PCR-amplified and therefore specifically targeted.






High-throughput sequencing (HTS)

Since 2005.x
Sequencing of hundreds of thousands to billions of DNA fragments at a time.
Fragments can be targeted in various ways or randomly generated from input DNA.










Reads and sequencing errors


The sequence determined from a DNA fragment is called a “read”. With current technologies, reads are never 100% accurate, and this has important consequences for downstream analyses.
