title: Working with files in the Unix shell I:The shell as a file browser
text:
1 Introduction

1.1 Overview & learning goals for this week’s shell lectures
We’ll pick up where we left off last week, continuing with basic Unix shell commands. We will focus on commands that operate on files and dirs. Specifically, you will learn to use the Unix shell to:

Create, copy, move, rename, and delete directories and files (this lecture)
Select multiple files with globbing (this lecture)
View the contents of text files in various ways (next lecture)
Use redirection and the pipe to flexibly process the output of commands (next lecture)
Search within, manipulate, and extract information from text files (next lecture)



1.2 Lecture context & overview
GUI-based file browsers (such as “Finder” on Mac, “File Explorer” on Windows, and the interface we saw in OSC OnDemand’s Files menu) can perform operations like listing, creating, moving, renaming, copying, and removing files and folders. Here, you will learn to use Unix shell commands that can perform these actions.
Why do I need to learn to do these relatively trivial tasks in the shell? 🤨

This will help you to get more comfortable with working in the shell.
The general benefits of using code — automation and reproducibility — apply here too.
With practice, using the shell is faster and more powerful than a GUI file browser (certainly at OSC).

(You may also run into situations where a GUI file browser is not available.)


1.3 Getting ready

Start a VS Code session
Open a VS Code session in exactly the same way as last week:

Log in to OSC’s OnDemand portal at https://ondemand.osc.edu.
In the blue top bar, select Interactive Apps and near the bottom, click Code Server.
Fill out the form as follows (these fields should be prefilled now — just check them):

Cluster: pitzer
Account: PAS3493
Number of hours: 2
Working Directory: /fs/ess/PAS3493/people/<user> (replace <user> with your user name)
App Code Server version: 4.129.0

Click Launch, and in the next page, click the Connect to VS Code button once it appears.
In VS Code, open a terminal by either:

Clicking  → Terminal → New Terminal
Using the keyboard shortcut Ctrl+`

Check that you are in /fs/ess/PAS3493/people/$USER by typing pwd in the terminal.






TipWorking dir check



First, recall that $USER is a variable that represents your username.
Second, if you’re not in /fs/ess/PAS3493/people/$USER, it may be listed under Recents in the Get Started document — if so, click on that entry. Otherwise, click File > Open Folder and type/select that path.

title: Working with files in the Unix shell I:The shell as a file browser
text:
2 Download the practice dataset
You will now download the practice/example dataset from Garrigós et al. (2025) that we’ve discussed. Use the git clone command (there is a space between git and clone1) to download a repository on GitHub that contains the practice dataset:
git clone https://github.com/cfaes-bioinfo/garrigos
Cloning into 'garrigos'...
remote: Enumerating objects: 52, done.
remote: Total 52 (delta 0), reused 0 (delta 0), pack-reused 52 (from 1)
Receiving objects: 100% (52/52), 945.76 MiB | 132.14 MiB/s, done.
Updating files: 100% (47/47), done.
This may take 10 or so seconds, since it will download almost 1 GB of data. Next, navigate into the dir that was just downloaded:
cd garrigos/






TipTrailing slash /



You don’t need the trailing slash after the directory name, but it is allowed. Since I will use Tab completion to complete the dir name, and encourage you to do the same, the trailing slash is included in these examples.

title: Working with files in the Unix shell I:The shell as a file browser
text:
3 ls and tree to list

3.1 ls
The ls command, short for list, will list files and directories — by default those in your current working dir:
ls
fastq  meta  README.md  ref
ls uses different colors to indicate different types of files:

Entries in blue are directories (fastq, meta and ref above).
Entries in black (or white in dark themes) are regular files (README.md above).
Entries in red are compressed files (we’ll see examples of this soon).

With ls, you can use:

One or more arguments to change the dir (or file) it operates on
One or more options to change how it shows the output

Let’s start with an option, -l (lowercase L):
ls -l
total 2
drwxr-x---+ 2 jelmer PAS0471 4096 Sep 14 11:14 fastq
drwxr-x---+ 2 jelmer PAS0471 4096 Sep 14 11:14 meta
-rw-rw----+ 1 jelmer PAS0471 2856 Sep 14 11:14 README.md
drwxr-x---+ 2 jelmer PAS0471 4096 Sep 14 11:14 ref
The same items as before were printed, but now in a different format: one item per line, with additional information such as the date and time that each file was last modified, and the file sizes in bytes directly to the left of the date. (The user name, project ID, and dates will differ in your output; my project ID is PAS0471 — see the box below for more info.)
Let’s add another option, -h:
ls -lh
total 2.0K
drwxr-x---+ 2 jelmer PAS0471 4.0K Sep 14 11:14 fastq
drwxr-x---+ 2 jelmer PAS0471 4.0K Sep 14 11:14 meta
-rw-rw----+ 1 jelmer PAS0471 2.8K Sep 14 11:14 README.md
drwxr-x---+ 2 jelmer PAS0471 4.0K Sep 14 11:14 ref


How does the output differ after adding -h, and what do you think that means? (Click to see the answer)

The only difference is in the format of the column reporting the sizes of the items listed.
We now have “Human-readable file sizes” (hence -h), where sizes on the scale of kilobytes will be shown with Ks, of megabytes with Ms, and of gigabytes with Gs. That can be useful especially for large files.







NoteOptional reading: More info about the columns in long-format ls output (Click to expand)





A lot of information is shown in long-format ls output, and it can be a bit overwhelming at first. You’ll learn to ignore the majority of columns, which are only relevant in specific contexts.
The following image shows what each column in long-format ls represents:





Some notes about the above:

We will talk about file “permissions” later in the course.
You can ignore the column with the “number of links”, as this is not informative for regular users.
Sizes shown for directories unfortunately do not correspond to the total size of the dir and its contents. Basically, you should only pay attention to sizes of files when looking at long-format ls output (to get the total size of a dir, use du -sh <dir>).
The default “group” for your account is the group shown for your Home dir. This is the group that will be assigned to any new files or directories you create. For me, it is PAS0471 — even when I create dirs and files in other locations, the default group will still be PAS0471. This has relevance for file permissions, which we will discuss later in the course.

Finally, the first line of long-format ls output (total 2 / total 2.0K in the examples above) gives an indication of the total size of files that are directly located in this folder, i.e. not including those in subdirs.



Moving on to argument(s) — to list the contents of one or more other dirs, specify these as arguments:
# [Your output should show file names in red]
ls fastq/
S63_R1.fastq.gz  S67_R1.fastq.gz  S71_R1.fastq.gz  S77_R1.fastq.gz  S81_R1.fastq.gz  S85_R1.fastq.gzS63_R2.fastq.gz  S67_R2.fastq.gz  S71_R2.fastq.gz  S77_R2.fastq.gz  S81_R2.fastq.gz  S85_R2.fastq.gzS64_R1.fastq.gz  S68_R1.fastq.gz  S74_R1.fastq.gz  S78_R1.fastq.gz  S82_R1.fastq.gz  S86_R1.fastq.gzS64_R2.fastq.gz  S68_R2.fastq.gz  S74_R2.fastq.gz  S78_R2.fastq.gz  S82_R2.fastq.gz  S86_R2.fastq.gzS65_R1.fastq.gz  S69_R1.fastq.gz  S75_R1.fastq.gz  S79_R1.fastq.gz  S83_R1.fastq.gzS65_R2.fastq.gz  S69_R2.fastq.gz  S75_R2.fastq.gz  S79_R2.fastq.gz  S83_R2.fastq.gzS66_R1.fastq.gz  S70_R1.fastq.gz  S76_R1.fastq.gz  S80_R1.fastq.gz  S84_R1.fastq.gzS66_R2.fastq.gz  S70_R2.fastq.gz  S76_R2.fastq.gz  S80_R2.fastq.gz  S84_R2.fastq.gz
And like you saw last week with cal, options and arguments can be combined:
ls -lh fastq/
total 941M
-rw-r-----+ 1 jelmer PAS0471 21M Nov 13  2024 S63_R1.fastq.gz
-rw-r-----+ 1 jelmer PAS0471 22M Nov 13  2024 S63_R2.fastq.gz
-rw-r-----+ 1 jelmer PAS0471 21M Nov 13  2024 S64_R1.fastq.gz
-rw-r-----+ 1 jelmer PAS0471 22M Nov 13  2024 S64_R2.fastq.gz
-rw-r-----+ 1 jelmer PAS0471 22M Nov 13  2024 S65_R1.fastq.gz
-rw-r-----+ 1 jelmer PAS0471 22M Nov 13  2024 S65_R2.fastq.gz
# [...output truncated...]
Some notes about these FASTQ files:

They are printed in red because they are compressed, as the added .gz extension also indicates.
There are two files per sample: _R1 (forward reads) and _R2 (reverse reads).
The files are ~21-22 MB in size — much smaller than the original file sizes (~1-2 GB) because they were subsampled.


 Exercise 1: Listing a single file
If you want to check the size of a single file, it may not be convenient to list all of a dir’s contents. Can you get ls to show you the file size only for the S65_R2.fastq.gz file?


 Click to see the solution.

The argument to ls can be a path of any kind, including to a file rather than to a dir:
ls -lh fastq/S65_R2.fastq.gz
-rw-r-----+ 1 jelmer PAS0471 22M Nov 13  2024 fastq/S65_R2.fastq.gz




3.2 tree to recursively list files in tree-like format
By default, ls is not “recursive”, which means that it only shows results for one directory level. Compare that with the output of the tree command, which gives a nice recursive overview in a simple tree-like format:
tree
.
├── fastq
│   ├── S63_R1.fastq.gz
│   ├── S63_R2.fastq.gz
│   ├── S64_R1.fastq.gz
│   ├── S64_R2.fastq.gz
│   ├── S65_R1.fastq.gz
│   ├── S65_R2.fastq.gz
│   └── [...other FASTQ files not shown...]
├── meta
│   └── metadata.tsv
├── README.md
└── ref
    └── annot.gtf.gz

3 directories, 47 files
Let’s take a step back and consider what’s in our dataset:

44 FASTQ files with RNA-Seq reads for 22 samples (in the fastq dir).
A metadata file with treatment group info for each sample (in the meta dir).
A README.md Markdown file.
A GTF annotation file for the reference genome (in the ref dir).

We will take a closer look at these files this week and in the weeks to come.

title: Working with files in the Unix shell I:The shell as a file browser
section: 4 mkdir and touch to create dirs and files
text:
4 mkdir and touch to create dirs and files

4.1 mkdir to create new directories
The mkdir command creates one or more new directories. Let’s create a dir for this week and navigate there:
mkdir ../week04
cd ../week04/
By default, mkdir is not recursive either: it won’t create a dir inside a dir that doesn’t exist yet. The -p option is needed to enable recursive behavior:
mkdir -p sandbox/jar
This command was recursive because both the sandbox dir and the jar dir within it had to be created at once. The name sandbox is common for dirs meant for experimentation and testing. Now, navigate into the sandbox dir you just created:
cd sandbox/
ls
jar
For the rest of this lecture and most of the next one, you’ll work inside this sandbox dir, so let’s take a moment to look at the layout:
/fs/ess/PAS3493/people/$USER
├── garrigos           <- The practice dataset: only read from it, don't change it
│   ├── fastq
│   ├── meta
│   └── ref
└── week04             <- Your dir for this week
    └── sandbox        <- Your working dir for the rest of this week's classes
        └── jar

 Exercise 2: mkdir and recursiveness
What do you think the following mkdir command does, and would you consider that recursive? Then, run the command and see what it did.
mkdir cup pot


   Click to see the answer.

This command created two dirs at once. It is not recursive, because it only operated on one “dir level”, i.e. it did not need to create two dir levels (or put another way, it did not create a dir within a dir).
ls
cup  jar  pot








NoteSelf-study: what else does the -p option to mkdir do? (Click to expand)





Run the below two commands one by one, and read any output the commands print to the screen. Why does the first command fail? What can you conclude about the -p option other than that it enables recursiveness?
mkdir jar/
mkdir -p jar/


   Click to see the answer.


mkdir jar/ produces an error, because you’re trying to create a dir that already exists:
mkdir jar/
mkdir: cannot create directory 'jar/': File exists
While mkdir -p jar/ doesn’t print anything:
mkdir -p jar/
The latter may either mean that mkdir -p recreated the dir, or that it did nothing but also didn’t complain. Here’s the answer: mkdir -p doesn’t do anything when the dir already exists, and won’t produce an error either. We’ll come back to why that is useful when we start writing shell scripts.








4.2 touch to create a new file
To create new, empty files, use the touch command, specifying the file name(s) as the argument(s):
# Create a single new file called apple.txt
touch apple.txt

# Create two additional files:
touch fig.txt kiwi.txt






TipOperating on multiple files



As you just saw, both mkdir and touch can take multiple arguments. Notably, almost all shell commands that operate on files and/or dirs can operate on multiple (many!) files at a time, which is one reason that using these commands can be highly efficient. That’s especially true once you know how to select/specify many files at once using globbing (later in this lecture).



 Exercise 3: Creating a file in a new dir
Create a new file mango.txt inside a new dir box. Don’t change your working dir while you’re doing this.


   Click to see the answer.

To make a new dir and create a file in there, you can’t just use the touch command, as it cannot create the directory for you (pay attention to the error, which may seem a bit confusing):
touch box/mango.txt
touch: cannot touch 'box/mango.txt': No such file or directory
Instead, you first have to create the new dir with mkdir, and then create the new file in there:
mkdir box
touch box/mango.txt

title: Working with files in the Unix shell I:The shell as a file browser
text:
5 cp to copy
The cp command copies files and/or dirs from one location to another. Just like when copying files in a GUI file browser, the new copy can have a different name than the original — or the same name, as long as it’s copied to a different dir.
cp has two required arguments in the following order:

What you want to copy (source path)
Where you want to copy it to (destination path)

That is, its basic syntax is cp <source path> <destination path>.






NoteRecap: The meaning of <...> notation



Recall that when I use < > around text in a line of code, that text is descriptive rather than literal, and has to be replaced. In this example, <source path> should be replaced in an actual line of code by whatever “source” you want to use, and likewise for the <destination path>.



Basic examples

Same directory, different file name:
cp kiwi.txt kiwi_copy.txt
Different directory, same file name:
cp kiwi.txt jar/
Different directory, different file name:
cp kiwi.txt jar/kiwi_backup.txt

In other words: if the destination is an existing dir, the copy is placed inside it with its original name — otherwise, the destination is the name of the copy.


Copying into your working dir without changing the name
It’s common to copy a file from elsewhere into your working dir while keeping its name. Instead of typing out the file name in the destination path, you can use the . shortcut to refer to your current working dir:
# Equivalent to: cp jar/kiwi_backup.txt kiwi_backup.txt
cp jar/kiwi_backup.txt .
Check the contents of the sandbox dir:
ls
apple.txt  box  cup  fig.txt  jar  kiwi_backup.txt  kiwi_copy.txt  kiwi.txt  pot


Copying dirs and their contents
Finally, cp will by default refuse to copy directories and their contents — that is, like ls and mkdir, it is not recursive2:
cp jar/ jar_copy
cp: -r not specified; omitting directory 'jar/'
As the error message above hints, the -r option is needed for recursive copying:
cp -r jar/ jar_copy
ls jar_copy/
kiwi_backup.txt  kiwi.txt







TipBoth the cp and mv (next up) commands will by default:




Be silent when they succeed (use the -v option for verbose to make them report what they do).
Overwrite existing files without reporting this (use the -i option for interactive to make them ask before overwriting).






 Self-study exercise: Copying a dir a second time
What do you think happens if you run the exact same command, cp -r jar/ jar_copy, a second time? Make a prediction, then run it and check the result with ls jar_copy/.


   Click to see the answer.

Recall that for files, if the destination is an existing dir, the copy is placed inside it — and the same is true for dirs. Because jar_copy now already exists, the second command creates a copy of jar inside jar_copy:
cp -r jar/ jar_copy
ls jar_copy/
jar  kiwi_backup.txt  kiwi.txt

title: Working with files in the Unix shell I:The shell as a file browser
text:
6 mv to move and rename
While copying a file creates a new copy of it, moving a file does not (think: copy-paste versus cut-paste).
Also, moving a file versus renaming it is fundamentally the same operation: in both cases, you are changing its path. After all, both a file’s name (e.g. mango.txt) and the dir that it’s inside (box/) are part of its path (box/mango.txt).
As such, the mv command can be used to move files, rename them, or do both at the same time — the same three scenarios you saw with cp:

Same directory, different file name (“renaming”):
mv -v kiwi_copy.txt plum.txt
renamed 'kiwi_copy.txt' -> 'plum.txt'
ls
apple.txt  box  cup  fig.txt  jar  jar_copy  kiwi_backup.txt  kiwi.txt  plum.txtpot
Different directory, same file name (“moving”):
# [Don't run this one: example only]
mv -v plum.txt cup/
renamed 'plum.txt' -> 'cup/plum.txt'
Different directory, different file name (“moving + renaming”):
# [Don't run this one: example only]
mv -v kiwi_backup.txt cup/kiwi_old.txt
renamed 'kiwi_backup.txt' -> 'cup/kiwi_old.txt'

Final notes:

While we used -v above to make mv report what it does, this is not required for the command to work.
Unlike cp, the mv command does not need an -r option to move or rename dirs!







WarningAvoid accidents due to typos by using Tab completion



Watch out for typos in a destination dir name: mv plum.txt cups would not give an error even though there is no cups dir: it would rename plum.txt to a file called cups. Including a trailing slash (cups/) protects against this, because mv will then give an error if that dir doesn’t exist (the same goes for cp).
Avoiding these mistakes is much easier if you consistently use Tab completion to type paths to existing dirs.








NoteOperating on multiple files with mv and cp (Click to expand)





You can move or copy multiple files at once with mv and cp. If you give these commands more than two arguments, the last argument is the destination, which must then be an existing dir — for example:
cp <source1> <source2> <destination>
mv <source1> <source2> <source3> <source4> <destination>

title: Working with files in the Unix shell I:The shell as a file browser
text:
7 rm to remove
The rm command removes files and optionally dirs. First, let’s remove one of the dummy files you created above:
rm apple.txt
As with cp, the -r option is needed to make the command work recursively:
# (box/ is the dir you created in Exercise 3)
rm box/
rm: cannot remove 'box/': Is a directory
# (This produces no output if it works)
rm -r box/






WarningThere is no trash bin when deleting files in the shell, so use rm with caution!



rm -r can be very dangerous. For example, rm -r / would try to remove the entire contents of the computer, including the operating system3. You’ll often see rm -rf online: the -f (force) option makes rm ignore nonexistent files and never ask for confirmation, so it’s even less forgiving. A couple of ways to take precautions:

You can add the -i option, which will make you confirm each individual removal (can be tedious).
When you intend to remove an empty dir, you can use the rmdir command. This command fails on non-empty dirs.




 Exercise 4: Spaces in file names — what could go wrong?
Consider the following hypothetical scenario:

You have a dir called data with important raw data, and a dir called extra data with additional data.
# [Hypothetical - don't run]
ls
data  'extra data'
You realize you won’t need the additional data at all, so you try to remove the extra data dir with the following command:
# [Hypothetical - don't run]
rm -r extra data

What do you expect would happen when that last command is run?

The extra data dir is removed, as intended.
Nothing is removed, and rm gives an error because there is no extra dir.
The data dir is removed, and rm gives an error because there is no extra dir.
Both the data and extra data dirs are removed.



   Click to see the answer.

The correct answer is C.
Because the space in the dir name was not “escaped” (for example, by quoting the name: rm -r "extra data"), rm will interpret extra and data as two separate arguments, i.e. as two separate files/dirs to remove.
Therefore, the rm command will not remove the extra data dir, but it will remove the data dir — now your project’s raw data has been erased! 😳
(Additionally, it will produce an error because it cannot find the extra dir. But this error does not stop rm from moving on to the next argument.)
Tab completion would have prevented this: it automatically “escapes” the space with a backslash, completing the name to extra\ data.

title: Working with files in the Unix shell I:The shell as a file browser
text:
8 Globbing
Globbing is a very useful shell technique to select multiple files at once, using wildcards — characters with a special meaning. To practice with this, start by creating some dummy FASTQ files in your sandbox dir:
# (Copy-and-paste this into the shell rather than typing it out)
touch sample1_R1.fastq sample1_R2.fastq
touch sample2_R1.fastq sample2_R2.fastq
touch sample3_R1.fastq sample3_R2.fastq






WarningNot able to paste?



Your browser may be blocking the paste action, but you can change that. Find a small clipboard icon in the address bar of your browser, click it, and allow pasting.


Let’s check the contents of the sandbox dir again:
ls
cup  fig.txt  jar  jar_copy  kiwi_backup.txt  kiwi.txt  plum.txt  potsample1_R1.fastq  sample1_R2.fastq  sample2_R1.fastq  sample2_R2.fastqsample3_R1.fastq  sample3_R2.fastq
We have a real mess now! Globbing will help us to select files to operate on without having to type out all of their names.
The most commonly used wildcard is *, which matches any number of any combination of characters (including “nothing”, the absence of any characters). For example, you can match only the FASTQ files with a * using:
# This matches files that end with "fastq"
ls *fastq
sample1_R1.fastq  sample2_R1.fastq  sample3_R1.fastq
sample1_R2.fastq  sample2_R2.fastq  sample3_R2.fastq
Or only the sample1 FASTQ files:
# This matches files that start with "sample1"
ls sample1*
sample1_R1.fastq  sample1_R2.fastq
When globbing, the pattern has to match the entire file name — therefore, the following doesn’t match anything:
# This matches files that *end* in R1, but there are no such files:
ls *R1
ls: cannot access '*R1': No such file or directory
So, if the text we use for matching is in the middle of the file name, like R1, we need a * on both sides of it:
# This matches files whose names contain "R1" anywhere:
ls *R1*
sample1_R1.fastq  sample2_R1.fastq  sample3_R1.fastq
In summary:







Pattern
Matches files whose names…




sample1*
start with “sample1”


*fastq
end with “fastq”


*R1*
contain “R1”


*
(matches all files and dirs in the working dir)4





 Exercise 5: File matching

Which files does ls *samp*le* match? Make a prediction before you try it.


   Click to see the answer.

It matches all the FASTQ files, because:

All the FASTQ file names start with sample.
Since * also matches “zero characters”, there is no requirement for the presence of characters at the locations of the “unnecessary” *s.


Create two new files called sample1.txt and sample2.txt in the current working dir. Then, only match the two FASTQ files for sample1 — that is, avoid matching these new .txt files.


   Click to see the answer.

First we create the files:
touch sample1.txt sample2.txt
Then we match only the two FASTQ files — the code below means any file that starts with “sample1” and ends with “fastq”:
ls sample1*fastq
sample1_R1.fastq  sample1_R2.fastq




Expansion is done by the shell itself
The “expansion” of a wildcard to matching file names is done by the shell itself, not by ls — or by any other command you might be using wildcards with. Therefore, a command like ls receives the list of files after the expansion has already happened. When you type…
ls sample2*fastq
…the shell will perform globbing before it runs the ls command. As such, the ls command will never see the * wildcard5. Instead, the command that is actually run is:
ls sample2_R1.fastq sample2_R2.fastq
You can see this expansion for yourself with echo, which simply prints whatever arguments it receives:
echo sample2*fastq
sample2_R1.fastq sample2_R2.fastq


Practical examples
So far, we’ve only used globbing with the ls command to list files. But because the expansion is done by the shell, globbing works with any command, and is especially useful with commands that accept multiple paths as arguments, such as copy (cp), move (mv), and remove (rm). As some initial examples of how useful globbing is, we can:

Remove all stray .txt files at once. Before removing files with a pattern, it’s a good habit to first check what the pattern matches with ls:
ls *.txt
fig.txt  kiwi_backup.txt  kiwi.txt  plum.txt  sample1.txt  sample2.txt
Then remove them (adding the -v option just to make rm report what it is removing):
rm -v *.txt
removed 'fig.txt'
removed 'kiwi_backup.txt'
removed 'kiwi.txt'
removed 'plum.txt'
removed 'sample1.txt'
removed 'sample2.txt'
Move all FASTQ files at once:
mkdir fastq_files
mv -v *fastq fastq_files/
renamed 'sample1_R1.fastq' -> 'fastq_files/sample1_R1.fastq'
renamed 'sample1_R2.fastq' -> 'fastq_files/sample1_R2.fastq'
renamed 'sample2_R1.fastq' -> 'fastq_files/sample2_R1.fastq'
renamed 'sample2_R2.fastq' -> 'fastq_files/sample2_R2.fastq'
renamed 'sample3_R1.fastq' -> 'fastq_files/sample3_R1.fastq'
renamed 'sample3_R2.fastq' -> 'fastq_files/sample3_R2.fastq'

Globbing is incredibly handy for working with large numbers of files, and is one of the reasons that shell commands are so powerful and efficient. Later on, you’ll use it, for example, to iterate over all FASTQ files in a dir to run a command on each of them.


 Self-study exercise: Globbing pitfalls

Say your dir contained only two R1 FASTQ files, sample1_R1.fastq and sample2_R1.fastq. You want to copy them into another dir, but forget to type the destination:
# [Hypothetical - don't run]
cp *_R1.fastq
Knowing that the shell expands the pattern before cp runs, what would happen?


   Click to see the answer.

After the shell has expanded the pattern, cp receives two arguments:
cp sample1_R1.fastq sample2_R1.fastq
So, cp treats the second file as the destination, and it will silently overwrite sample2_R1.fastq with a copy of sample1_R1.fastq! 😳
(With three or more matching files, you would instead get an error such as cp: target 'sample3_R1.fastq' is not a directory, because when cp gets more than two arguments, the last one has to be a dir.)

You want to remove all .txt files in your working dir, but accidentally type a space after the *:
# [Hypothetical - don't run]
rm * .txt
What would happen?


   Click to see the answer.

A single stray space makes a big difference: rm *.txt removes all .txt files, but rm * .txt removes all files in your working dir (dirs are only spared because you didn’t use -r, though rm prints an error for each of them), and it also complains that there is no file called .txt.
A good habit is to first run ls with the same pattern to check what it matches, and only then run rm.

What would have happened if you had used *fastq* instead of *fastq in the mv example above, i.e. mv -v *fastq* fastq_files/?


   Click to see the answer.

The pattern *fastq* also matches the fastq_files dir itself! So mv tries to move that dir into itself, which fails with an error. The FASTQ files are still moved:
mv: cannot move 'fastq_files' to a subdirectory of itself, 'fastq_files/fastq_files'
renamed 'sample1_R1.fastq' -> 'fastq_files/sample1_R1.fastq'
[...]

title: Working with files in the Unix shell I:The shell as a file browser
text:
Footnotes


 git is a type of command that has “subcommands”, such as clone and many others. You will learn much more about Git next week.↩︎
 Non-recursive defaults act as a kind of safety mechanism, since they make it harder to accidentally operate on very large amounts of data.↩︎
 Luckily, rm nowadays refuses this particular command — but it will not stop you from e.g. wiping your entire home dir with rm -r ~.↩︎
Except so-called hidden files, whose names start with a ..↩︎
 If nothing matches, the shell leaves the pattern as is — which is why the error message for ls *R1 above showed *R1 literally.↩︎

title: Week 5: Version control with Git & GitHub
text:
Overview
This week, you will learn about the why and how of storing different versions of files using Git, a formal Version Control System — and sharing the resulting repositories on the GitHub website.

title: Week 5: Version control with Git & GitHub
text:
Lectures & Learning goals
Some of the things you will learn this week are:

A) Introduction to Version control (Monday)

Understand why it’s a good idea to use a formal Version Control System for research projects, and learn key Git concepts and terminology.



B) Version control with Git (Monday)

Learn the basics of creating version control repositories with Git, the most widely used Version Control System.



C) Remote repositories on GitHub (Wednesday)

Learn how to put your local repositories online at GitHub.
Learn how to keep local and online (“remote”) repositories synced.

title: Week 5: Version control with Git & GitHub
text:
Assignments and exercises

Ungraded Assignment: Create a GitHub account (Do this before Wednesday’s class)
Graded Assignment 2: Unix shell and Git (Due 9/27)

title: Week 5: Version control with Git & GitHub
text:
Optional self-study material

Optional self-study material on this website: Advanced version control

Learn how to move and remove tracked files, and how to unstage files.
Learn how to collaborate with others using Git and GitHub.
Learn how to undo things and “travel back in time” for your project using Git.
Learn how to use Git branches to safely make experimental changes.

Allesina and Wilmes (2019) — Chapter 2: “Version Control” (OSU library link )
Buffalo (2015) — Chapter 5: “Git for Scientists” (OSU library link )
For more background on why to use version control, and another perspective on Git basics, I highly recommend Bryan (2017): “Excuse me, do you have a moment to talk about version control?” Note that some of the content assumes you are an R user.

title: Version control with Git
text:
1 Introduction
This is the hands-on continuation of today’s lecture on version control with Git.

1.1 Learning goals for this lecture

Learn the basic Git workflow and the most common Git commands.
Make Git ignore specific files and dirs.
Undo accidental changes to your files.
Show the changes you’ve made to files, also using VS Code’s Git interface.



1.2 Getting ready
Start a VS Code session just like you’ve done before.


 Click here to see the instructions


Log in to OSC’s OnDemand portal at https://ondemand.osc.edu.
In the blue top bar, select Interactive Apps and near the bottom, click Code Server.
Fill out the form as follows (as necessary — should be prefilled now!):

Cluster: pitzer
Account: PAS3493
Number of hours: 2
Working Directory: /fs/ess/PAS3493/people/<user> (replace <user> with your user name)
App Code Server version: 4.129.0

Click Launch, and in the next page, click the Connect to VS Code button once it appears.
In VS Code, open a terminal by either:

Clicking  → Terminal → New Terminal
Using the keyboard shortcut Ctrl+`

Check that you are in /fs/ess/PAS3493/people/$USER by typing pwd in the terminal.






Recall that $USER is a variable that represents your username.
If you’re not in /fs/ess/PAS3493/people/$USER, it may be listed under Recents in the Get Started document — if so, click on that entry. Otherwise, click File > Open Folder and type/select that path.

title: Version control with Git
text:
2 One-time Git configuration
We will start with one-time personal Git configuration. This will apply anywhere on OSC, and won’t ever have to be redone unless you want to make changes.
These steps are all done with git config --global:

Make your name known to Git, since it will be recorded in every commit you make — your actual first and last name (not your OSC or GitHub username!):
git config --global user.name "John Doe"
Make your email address known (should match the address associated with your GitHub account, if you already created one):
git config --global user.email "doe.391@osu.edu"
Set a default text editor for Git. (Git may occasionally open a text editor for you. Even though we’re using VS Code, here it is better to select a text editor that runs in the shell, like nano1.)
git config --global core.editor "nano -w"
Change the default “branch” name to main (Git’s default is still the older master, whereas GitHub uses main)2:
git config --global init.defaultBranch main
Finally, print your current settings to check whether you successfully changed them:
git config --global --list
user.name=John Doe
user.email=doe.391@osu.edu
core.editor=nano -w
init.defaultbranch=main

title: Version control with Git
text:
3 The basic Git workflow
You’ll create a Git repository for a mock book project: writing Charles Darwin’s “On the Origin of Species”. This example follows Chapter 2 of Allesina and Wilmes (2019). The topic may seem silly, but keeping the content trivial means you can focus entirely on the Git workflow.

3.1 Create and move to a new project dir
Create a new dir for a mock project that you will version-control with Git:
# (Your starting point should be /fs/ess/PAS3493/people/$USER)
mkdir -p week05/evo
cd week05/evo
Next, we’ll open this dir in VS Code with “Open Folder” to move all of VS Code, not just the terminal, to this dir. For example, after moving, the file explorer will only show this project’s files, and VS Code’s Git functionality will work with the repo you’ll create here. (This is also how you’ll want to work with your own projects: open each project’s dir as the folder in VS Code.)

Click  → File → Open Folder.
Type/select /fs/ess/PAS3493/people/<user>/week05/evo, replacing <user> with your user name. This will cause VS Code to reload.
Open a new terminal and check that you are in the evo dir:
pwd
/fs/ess/PAS3493/people/jelmer/week05/evo



3.2 Start a new Git repository
Now we’re ready to start your first Git repository! The command to initialize a new Git repository is git init — use that to start a repo for the evo dir:
git init
Initialized empty Git repository in /fs/ess/PAS3493/people/jelmer/week05/evo/.git/
Can you confirm that this hidden dir is there? The ls command will show hidden files and dirs with the -a option, and indeed, the .git dir is present:
# (ls -a will also show the current dir "." and the parent dir "..")
ls -a
.  ..  .git






WarningWhere (not) to run git init (Click to expand)





Above, we created a Git repo in an empty dir, but you can use git init just the same in a dir that already contains files. However, only run it in the top-level dir of a single project, and never:

In a dir like your home dir or /fs/ess/PAS3493/people/$USER, which contains many projects,
Inside a dir that is already part of a Git repo.

If you did run git init in the wrong place, you can undo it by removing the .git dir that it created using rm -rf .git3.



Next, check the status of your new repository with git status:
git status
On branch main

No commits yet

nothing to commit (create/copy files and use "git add" to track)
Git reports that you:

Are on a “branch” called main. We won’t cover Git branches in class, but this is discussed in the optional self-study material and in Allesina and Wilmes (2019) Chapter 2.6. Basically, branches are “parallel versions” of your repository that are useful for collaborative and experimental work.
Have not created any commits yet.
Have “nothing to commit” because there are no files in this dir.







NoteThe “not a git repository” error (Click to expand)





If you run a Git command, like git status, outside of an existing Git repository, you’ll get this error:
fatal: not a git repository (or any of the parent directories): .git
That usually just means that you’re in the wrong dir: check with pwd. The bigger point is that Git commands only work inside a Git repository, not in any other directory.





3.3 Your first Git commit
Start writing the book (😉) by echo-ing text into a new file called origin.txt:
echo "An essay on ..." > origin.txt
Now, check the status of the repository again:
git status
On branch main

No commits yet

Untracked files:
  (use "git add <file>..." to include in what will be committed)
        origin.txt

nothing added to commit but untracked files present (use "git add" to track)
Git has clearly detected the new file. But as mentioned in the intro slides, Git does not automatically start “tracking” files — that is, it won’t automatically include all files that are in your dir in the repository. Instead, it tells you the file is “Untracked” and gives a hint on how to add it to the repository.
Start tracking the file and stage it in one go with git add:
git add origin.txt






As always, Tab-complete file names, like origin.txt above!



Next, check the status of the repo again:
git status
On branch main

No commits yet

Changes to be committed:
  (use "git rm --cached <file>..." to unstage)
        new file:   origin.txt
Now, your file has been added to the staging area (also called the Index) and is listed as a “change to be committed”4. That phrase means that if you now run git commit, the file will be included in that commit.
So, with your file tracked & staged, let’s make your first commit. Add the option -m followed by a “commit message”: a short description of the changes you are including in the current commit5:
git commit -m "Started the book"
[main (root-commit) 3df4361] Started the book
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+)
 create mode 100644 origin.txt
You’ve made your first commit! Here is another way of visualizing how changes are staged and committed in Git — and of the three areas that files can be in:

The working tree (also called working dir) is where you make changes to files.
The staging area (also called Index) is where you stage changes to be included in the next commit.
The commit history is where committed changes are stored. It has many “layers” of commits, and you can go back to any of them at any time.







Note that git add has a dual function: it starts tracking files and stages them.



Why might the term “working tree” be used instead of “working directory”? (Click to see the answer)

The term “working tree” is used in Git to emphasize that we are referring to the entire hierarchy of dirs and files that makes up your project, and not the single dir that your terminal is currently in.
That said, both terms are often used interchangeably. As such, if you hear “working dir” in a Git context, it usually refers to the entire hierarchy.



3.4 Checking the status and history
First, let’s check the status of the repo again:
git status
On branch main
nothing to commit, working tree clean
It reported “nothing to commit, working tree clean”, which means no changes have been made anywhere in the project dir since the last commit.






Try to get in the habit of using git status a lot — as a sanity check before and after other git actions.



Next, look at the commit history of the repo with git log:
git log
commit 3df4361c1de9b71e08bf6e050105d53097acec21 (HEAD -> main)
Author: Jelmer Poelstra <jelmerpoelstra@gmail.com>
Date:   Mon Mar 11 10:55:35 2024 -0400

    Started the book
Notes on the first line of the above output:

The long “hexadecimal code” (which uses numbers and the letters a–f) is a unique identifier for that commit, usually called the commit hash (or SHA-1 checksum). You can reference and access each past commit by its hash, and the first 7 characters are usually enough (as you’ll see with git log --oneline below).
(HEAD -> main) means that you are (your “HEAD” is) currently located at the commit in question, and that the commit was made on the main branch.

Below that, git log reports the author, date and time of the commit, and the commit message you provided.

 Exercise 1: Put the commands in order
Say you want to start a brand-new project with a Git repository, and make a first commit containing a single file, notes.md. In which order should you run the commands below? (Only figure out the order — don’t run these commands.)
git commit -m "Start notes"
git init
cd myproject
git add notes.md
echo "# Project notes" > notes.md
mkdir myproject


 Click for the solution.

mkdir myproject
cd myproject
git init
echo "# Project notes" > notes.md
git add notes.md
git commit -m "Start notes"

Bonus: two of these commands could be swapped without any problems. Which ones?


 Click for the solution.

git init and echo can be swapped: Git doesn’t care whether files already existed when you initialized the repo! Swapping git add and git commit, on the other hand, would make Git report that there is nothing to commit.




3.5 Your second commit
Find the file origin.txt in the VS Code file explorer, open it, and replace its line of text with the book’s final title:


origin.txt

On the Origin of Species

Check the status of the repo:
git status
On branch main
Changes not staged for commit:
  (use "git add <file>..." to update what will be committed)
  (use "git restore <file>..." to discard changes in working directory)
        modified:   origin.txt

no changes added to commit (use "git add" and/or "git commit -a")
Git has noticed the changes, because the file is being tracked: origin.txt is listed as “modified”. But changes to tracked files are not automatically staged.
Use git add to stage the file as a first step to committing these changes:
git add origin.txt






TipGit never acts on files by itself



Git behaves similarly when it comes to new files and changes to tracked files: it does not automatically do anything with them. That is deliberate: managing which files are tracked and staged is up to you.


Now, make your second commit, again adding a commit message. Like always, it’s up to you to decide what to write in the commit message, but the idea is that you give a short description of the changes you made:
git commit -m "Changed the title as suggested by Murray"
[main f106353] Changed the title as suggested by Murray
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+), 1 deletion(-)
Git gives a brief summary of the changes that were made: you changed 1 file (origin.txt), and since you replaced the line of text in that file, it interprets that as 1 insertion (the new line) and 1 deletion (the replaced line).
Check the history of the repo again — you’ll see that there are now 2 commits:
git log
commit f1063537b6a1e0d87d2d52c9e96c38694959997a (HEAD -> main)
Author: Jelmer Poelstra <jelmerpoelstra@gmail.com>
Date:   Mon Mar 11 11:01:49 2024 -0400

    Changed the title as suggested by Murray

commit 3df4361c1de9b71e08bf6e050105d53097acec21
Author: Jelmer Poelstra <jelmerpoelstra@gmail.com>
Date:   Mon Mar 11 10:55:35 2024 -0400

    Started the book
As you start accumulating commits, you might prefer git log --oneline for a one-line-per-commit summary:
git log --oneline
f106353 (HEAD -> main) Changed the title as suggested by Murray
3df4361 Started the book






WarningWhen git log output is longer than your screen (Click to expand)





Once your history is longer than your screen, git log opens in the less pager that you used last week: scroll with the arrow keys and press q to get back to your prompt. The same goes for long output of git diff, a command you’ll see later today.









NoteStaging multiple files at once, and git commit -a (Click to expand)





When you would like to stage multiple files, you don’t need to add them one by one. Here are a few other options:

Stage all files in the project/repository:
# [Don't run any of this - these are hypothetical examples]
git add --all
Stage all files in the current dir and its subdirs (when run from the repo’s root dir, this is the same as git add --all):
git add .
Stage all files in a specific dir (here: scripts) in the project:
git add scripts/

Finally, you can stage and commit all changes with a single command using the -a option for git commit (but be aware that this will not add untracked files):
git commit -am "My commit message"





3.6 What to include in individual commits
As shown in the box above, there’s a way to stage and commit all changes to tracked files at once. That may seem more convenient than separately git adding files before committing. However, we focus here on the more deliberate workflow of staging and committing files separately to encourage you to think about what changes you are committing.
In turn, that’s useful because it’s good practice to make each commit a unit of progress worth saving, rather than committing lots of things at once (say, at the end of each day). That is, you ideally create separate commits for distinct changes, even if those are small.
For example, say you use git status and find that since your last commit you have:

Updated a README file to include more information about your samples.
Worked on a script to run quality control of sequence files.

These are unrelated changes, and it’s not recommended to include both in a single commit.

 Exercise 2: A third change and commit

Create a new file todo.txt containing the line: “June 18, 1858: Read essay from Wallace”.


 Click for the solution.

echo "June 18, 1858: Read essay from Wallace" > todo.txt
Or: create the file with touch todo.txt or in the VS Code file explorer, and then open it and type the line in the editor.

Stage the file to be committed.


 Click for the solution.

git add todo.txt

Create a Git commit with the commit message “Added to-do list”.


 Click for the solution.

git commit -m "Added to-do list"




 Exercise 3: Separate commits?
Say that since your last commit, you have changed three files:

README.md: you added information about your samples.
scripts/qc.sh: you changed the output dir of this QC script from qc to results/qc.
scripts/qc_summary.sh: you changed the dir that this script reads QC results from, also from qc to results/qc.

How many commits would you make, and which file(s) would go in each?


 Click for the solution.

Two commits: one with README.md, and one with both scripts.
The changes to the two scripts are in different files, but they form a single unit of progress: if you committed only the change to qc.sh, that commit would contain a qc_summary.sh script that looks for QC results in the wrong place. So, the rule is “one commit per change”, not “one commit per file”.








WarningWhat if you have lots of changes and no time to sort through them? (Click to expand)





Separate commits for distinct changes are the ideal, but don’t let that ideal stop you from committing at all. If you’ve made lots of changes since your last commit and don’t have time to split them up (say, at the end of a long day, or before a deadline), committing everything at once is much better than not committing: until you commit, your changes are not saved in your Git history, so you can’t go back to this version later.
In that case:

Stage everything at once (see the box above), but check git status first to make sure you’re not including files you don’t want in the repo, such as large data files:
# [Don't run this - this is a hypothetical example]
git status
git add --all
git commit -m "Updated README; QC scripts now use results/qc"
Still, try to write a commit message that briefly summarizes the main changes, rather than something like “Various updates”. This will help you find your way back to this version later.




You have now learned the basic Git workflow! 🥳 Below, we’ll go through a few related key aspects of using Git.

title: Version control with Git
text:
4 Ignoring files and directories
As discussed in the intro slides, it’s best not to track some files, such as (bulky) data files, temporary files, and results. At the same time, we’ve seen that Git reports any “untracked” files in your project whenever you run git status.
Having these files reported every time you run git status can get annoying and make it harder to spot changes and untracked files that you do want to add. More importantly, it makes it easy to commit such files by accident — and once a large data file has been committed, it stays in the repo’s history even if you later delete it (!).
To deal with this, you can tell Git not to pay attention to certain files by adding file names and wildcard selections to a special file called .gitignore.
As an example, let’s start by adding some types of content you would not want to commit to your repository: a dir data, and a file ending in a ~ (a type of backup file that some text editors create):
mkdir data
touch data/drawings.png todo.txt~
Before checking what Git reports, let’s take a look at the current contents of our project dir with tree:
tree
.
├── data
│   └── drawings.png
├── origin.txt
├── todo.txt
└── todo.txt~

1 directory, 4 files
When you check the status of the repo, you should see that Git has noticed the new files:
git status
On branch main
Untracked files:
  (use "git add <file>..." to include in what will be committed)
        data/
        todo.txt~






NoteHow untracked dirs are reported



When a dir is untracked, Git reports the dir name and does not list the files inside it (above, the drawings.png file inside data is not shown). That is helpful, because it avoids cluttering the output of git status, but it’s good to be aware of.


You can create a .gitignore file to prevent Git from reporting these files whenever you run git status:

This is a plain text file that contains dir and file names/patterns, all of which will be ignored by Git.
The file should be called .gitignore and be placed in the project’s root dir (use one .gitignore file per repo).

Some more things to know about .gitignore:

As soon as a .gitignore file exists, Git automatically checks and processes its contents.
Perhaps somewhat counterintuitively, you should add and commit the .gitignore file itself (that way, it’s shared along with the rest of the repo, such as with collaborators or on GitHub).

Create a .gitignore file and open it in the editor:
# After this command, click on the file name in the file explorer to open it:
touch .gitignore
Then, type the following two lines in the file (press Enter at the end of the last line too):


.gitignore

data/
*~


The first line makes Git ignore everything in the data dir, and the second makes it ignore everything that ends in a ~. That is:

.gitignore files accept the same wildcard patterns as the shell, so * matches any string of characters.
But unlike wildcards in the shell, which only match files in the current dir, these patterns apply across the entire repo: *~ will also match files ending in ~ in any subdir (and data/ will match a data dir at any level).







TipIt doesn’t matter how you change files (Click to expand)





You have now changed files both with echo and in the editor. Git doesn’t care how a file changed: it only looks at file contents. In your own projects, you’ll mostly edit files in the editor, and then use the terminal to stage and commit your changes.



When you check the status again, you should see that Git has automatically processed the .gitignore file, since the targeted files are no longer listed as untracked:
git status
On branch main
Untracked files:
  (use "git add <file>..." to include in what will be committed)
        .gitignore
However, you do now have an untracked .gitignore file, so track and commit this file as follows:
git add .gitignore
git commit -m "Added a gitignore file"
[main 9715ab5] Added a gitignore file
 1 file changed, 2 insertions(+)
 create mode 100644 .gitignore

 Exercise 4: .gitignore

Say that a repo’s .gitignore file contains these two lines:


.gitignore

results/
*.log

Which of these new files would Git now ignore?

results/counts.tsv
run.log
scripts/run.log
scripts/qc.sh



 Click for the solution.

It would ignore all except d.
results/counts.tsv is inside an ignored dir, and both .log files match *.log. c is ignored too: patterns like *.log (and results/) match in any dir of the repo, not just in the top-level dir.

Bonus: Say that you add “todo.txt” to the .gitignore file of your evo repo, and then append another line to todo.txt. What do you think, would git status still report that todo.txt was modified?


 Click for the solution.

Yes, it would report that todo.txt was modified, because .gitignore only affects currently untracked files.
Since todo.txt is already tracked (you committed it in Exercise 2), Git keeps tracking it and reports changes to it.
To stop tracking a file, you’d first have to remove it from the repo, as shown in the optional self-study material for Git.










TipGood project file organization makes ignoring files easier



If you keep your data and results in their own top-level dirs, as recommended in week 2, the two lines data/ and results/ in your .gitignore file are all you need to ignore them. If you instead mix, for example, scripts and results within dirs, you’ll need many more specific and error-prone .gitignore entries.

title: Version control with Git
section: 5 Undoing changes that have not been committed
text:
5 Undoing changes that have not been committed
Now, we’ll practice undoing changes to your working tree by recovering a version from the repo: in other words, using Git as an “undo button” after accidental file changes or removal. (In the optional self-study Git material, you can learn how to unstage files and how to undo changes that have been committed.)
Say you accidentally overwrote a file, and want to recover the previous version from the repo:

Let’s first check the contents of todo.txt:
cat todo.txt
June 18, 1858: Read essay from Wallace
You accidentally overwrite the file contents instead of appending to it 😳:
echo "Finish taxidermy of the finches" > todo.txt
Confirm the disaster by checking the file contents again:
cat todo.txt
Finish taxidermy of the finches
Always start by checking the status:
git status
On branch main
Changes not staged for commit:
  (use "git add <file>..." to update what will be committed)
  (use "git restore <file>..." to discard changes in working directory)
        modified:   todo.txt

no changes added to commit (use "git add" and/or "git commit -a")
You’ll want to “discard changes in working directory”, and Git told you how to do this — with git restore:
git restore todo.txt
Check if it worked by looking at the file contents:
cat todo.txt
June 18, 1858: Read essay from Wallace

Great! You have successfully recovered the previous version of the file from the repo. If you accidentally deleted a file, you can similarly retrieve it with git restore:

You accidentally remove todo.txt:
rm todo.txt
Use git restore to get the file back!
git restore todo.txt

cat todo.txt
June 18, 1858: Read essay from Wallace








Warninggit restore can only bring back what Git has stored



git restore replaces your file with the version stored by Git (the last commit, or the staged version if you staged the file). Had you not committed todo.txt in Exercise 2, its contents would now be gone for good.








Warninggit restore itself cannot be undone (Click to expand)





git restore overwrites your current version of the file without asking for confirmation. So be careful when using it: if the file contained changes that you had not committed, those changes are gone for good — Git cannot undo a git restore.





 Self-study exercise: What can Git restore?
In which of these situations can git restore get back what you lost?

You accidentally removed a new file that you had never added with git add.
You accidentally removed a whole dir of committed files with rm -r.
You had edited a committed file without staging or committing those edits, and then accidentally overwrote the file. You want those edits back.



 Click for the solution.

The only correct answer is b, because Git can only restore versions of files that it has stored (and it can bring back a whole dir of committed files).
It never stored anything for the file in a, nor for the uncommitted edits in c. (In a, git restore would just give an error, and in c, it would only give you the last committed version.)

title: Version control with Git
text:
6 VS Code’s Git functionality
VS Code has built-in Git functionality, which can be more user-friendly than the Git command-line interface, especially for showing changes in files. To have a change to look at, let’s first modify the to-do list you made in Exercise 2.
Open todo.txt in the editor by clicking on it in the file explorer, and add a line to it (again, press Enter at the end of the line):


todo.txt

June 18, 1858: Read essay from Wallace
June 20, 1858: Send draft to Huxley



6.1 Git decorations in the file explorer


First, in the file explorer, several “decorations” related to Git are shown, as can be seen in the screenshot on the right:

Files that have been modified since the last commit are shown in orange and marked with an M.
The .gitignore file has a Git icon next to it.
Files that are ignored via .gitignore are shown in a paler color (data and todo.txt~ on the right).
Untracked files that are not ignored would be shown in green and marked with a U — there are none here.








File decorations in the VS Code file explorer.





6.2 The Source Control option in the side bar


Click on the version control icon in the narrow side bar (bottom icon in the screenshot on the right) to open the source control option of the wide side bar. (The icon should have an encircled 1 inside it, because we made one change since the last commit!)
The side bar should now show two sections, CHANGES at the top and GRAPH at the bottom, which together replicate the Git functionality we have so far used on the command line. Starting with the bottom one:


“GRAPH” (bottom) — shows a visual representation of the commit history of the repo, similar to git log --oneline.












“CHANGES” (top) — shows the files that have been modified since the last commit. You can stage changes, make commits, and more. You can also click on a file name to see the specific changes made to that file, which we’ll do now.


6.3 Showing changes made to a file

Under Changes, click on todo.txt, which has an M (for “modified”) next to it, as shown in the screenshot on the right.
Then, your editor should show a nice overview of the changes made to the file, with the old version on the left, the new version on the right, and changes highlighted in color (green for additions, red for deletions) — as shown in the screenshot below:









The source control side bar option.









The “diff” (difference) view of a file in VS Code, showing the old version on the left and the new version on the right.








NoteShowing changes on the command line with git diff (Click to expand)





The git diff command also shows changes made to tracked files. By default, for each file, it shows changes between the working tree and either the last commit or the staging area, depending on whether you have staged the file.
So, after the change to the to-do list that you just made, git diff shows the following:
git diff
diff --git a/todo.txt b/todo.txt
index e3b5e55..9aca508 100644
--- a/todo.txt
+++ b/todo.txt
@@ -1 +1,2 @@
 June 18, 1858: Read essay from Wallace
+June 20, 1858: Send draft to Huxley
We won’t go into the details of the above “diff format”, but at the bottom of the output above, you can see the specific change: the line “Send draft to Huxley” was added (hence the + sign) in our latest version of the file.
Two more notes on git diff:

To show differences between the staging area and the last commit, use the --staged option to git diff. So, don’t be surprised if git diff shows nothing right after you ran git add!
If you have changed multiple files, git diff will show all of them. If you only want to see differences for one of them, you can specify the filename to git diff. In our example, doing so prints the same output as the plain git diff command above, since we only changed one file:
git diff todo.txt
# Output not shown, same as above






6.4 Staging and committing
Finally, let’s commit the change that you made to the to-do list, now using the Source Control side bar instead of Git commands:

Hover over todo.txt under Changes, and click the + icon that appears to stage the file. It should move to a new Staged Changes section.
Type a commit message in the box at the top of the side bar: “Added Huxley draft to to-do list”.
Click the Commit button below the message box.

After that, the side bar should no longer list any changes, and the number in the version control icon should be gone: your working tree is “clean” again.






NoteCommitting this change on the command line instead (Click to expand)





The command-line equivalent of what you just did would have been:
git add todo.txt
git commit -m "Added Huxley draft to to-do list"
Or, with the -a option to git commit, which stages and commits changes in tracked files in one step:
git commit -am "Added Huxley draft to to-do list"









NoteWhat about the “Publish Branch” button? (Click to expand)





At the top of the Source Control side bar, you may have noticed a blue Publish Branch button. That button creates an online copy of your repo on GitHub in a few clicks.
We will create such an online copy (a “remote” repository) in the next lecture, but in a different way: on the GitHub website and with Git commands, so that you can see each of the steps involved. The VS Code alternative is explained in a callout there.









TipWhat am I allowed to use in this course?



In class, we will mostly use the command line for our Git operations. But it’s up to you whether you want to use the command line or the VS Code interface in your at-home course work, including graded assignments and the final project.

title: Version control with Git
text:
7 Self-study: Recap and best practices

7.1 The commands you learned today







Command
What it does




git init
Start a new repo in the current dir


git status
Show which files changed and what is staged


git add <file>
Start tracking a file and stage its changes


git commit -m "..."
Save a snapshot of all staged changes


git log [--oneline]
Show the commit history


git diff
Show what changed in tracked files


git restore <file>
Get a file back as it was in the last commit



And remember the .gitignore file, which keeps files you don’t want to track out of git status output.


7.2 A few Git best practices
Several of these have already been mentioned above, but here is a summary of some key points:

Write informative commit messages. Imagine looking back at your project in a few months, after finding an error that you introduced a while ago.

Not-so-good commit message: “Updated file”
Good commit message: “In file x, updated function y to include z”









By XKCD - image source



Commit often, using small commits.
This will also help to keep commit messages informative!
Before committing, check what you’ve changed.
Use git diff [--staged] or VS Code functionality.
Avoid including unrelated changes in commits.
Separate commits if your working tree contains work from disparate edits: use git add + git commit separately for two sets of files.
Don’t commit unnecessary files.
These clutter your repo and its history (especially automatically generated, temporary files), and when collaborating, they can lead to so-called merge conflicts.



 Self-study exercise: File states
Say that in a different repo, git status prints the following:
git status
On branch main
Changes to be committed:
  (use "git restore --staged <file>..." to unstage)
        modified:   scripts/qc.sh

Changes not staged for commit:
  (use "git add <file>..." to update what will be committed)
  (use "git restore <file>..." to discard changes in working directory)
        modified:   README.md

Untracked files:
  (use "git add <file>..." to include in what will be committed)
        scripts/trim.sh

Which file(s) would be included in a commit if you now ran git commit -m "My message"?

Only scripts/qc.sh
scripts/qc.sh and README.md
All three files
None of them: you first need to run git add



 Click for the solution.

The correct answer is a. Only staged changes are included in a commit. README.md was modified but not staged, and scripts/trim.sh is not even tracked.

And which file(s) would be included if you instead ran git commit -am "My message" (see this box above for the -a option to git commit)?


 Click for the solution.

scripts/qc.sh and README.md: the -a option stages all changes to tracked files, but it does not add untracked files.

Say that, before committing, you edit scripts/qc.sh once more, without running git add on it again. How do you think git status would list this file, and which version of it would git commit -m "My message" include?


 Click for the solution.

scripts/qc.sh would be listed twice: under “Changes to be committed” and under “Changes not staged for commit”. git add stages the file as it was at that moment, so the commit would only include the earlier, staged changes. To also include your newest edits, run git add on the file again.

title: Version control with Git
text:
Footnotes


 Git will open an editor when you need to provide a “commit message” but didn’t enter one on the command line. Its default editor is vi/vim, which is harder to use and notoriously hard for beginners to exit.↩︎
 We’ll talk a bit about what branches are later on.↩︎
 -f is needed because some files inside .git are write-protected — and recall from last week that rm -rf is unforgiving, so double-check that you are removing the correct .git dir!↩︎
 You also get a hint on how to “unstage” the file: i.e., reverting what you just did with git add and leaving the file untracked once again↩︎
 If you leave out -m, Git will instead open the nano editor that you configured above, so you can type your commit message there. Type your message, then press Ctrl+X, Y (to save), and Enter (to confirm the file name) — Git will then make the commit.↩︎

title: Week 6 Exercises: GitHub, OSC, and software
text:
Exercise 1: GitHub

Go to the GitHub website, log in, and create a new GitHub repository. This will be the remote counterpart of the Git repo you made as part of last week’s assignment.

You can give the GitHub repo any name you want.
Like we did in class, keep the repo Public (the default), because that’s needed for the instructor tagging exercise later on1.
Also like we did in class, don’t let GitHub add a README or any other files when you create the repo.

Navigate to your dir for last week’s assignment in the VS Code terminal (you can also use the “Open Folder” option in VS Code to open that folder if you want).
Set up a connection between the Git repo and the GitHub counterpart using Git commands.
Push your local repo to the online counterpart.
Explore your repo on GitHub. Does your README.md render well? Can you see all your commits? Are your data and results dirs there? Why or why not?
You will hand in the remaining assignments for this course by “tagging” the instructors in a GitHub Issue. To make sure you know how this works, let’s do a test run. On GitHub, open a GitHub Issue for your repo: click the Issues tab and then “New Issue”.

Under “Add a title”, give the issue a title like “Testing whether tagging works”.
Under “Add a description”, tag both instructors using @<username> syntax:


[GitHub Issue body]

Hey @jelmerp and @kstarr791, can you please take a look at my repo?

Click the green “Create” button to post your Issue. If the tagging worked, the @jelmerp and @kstarr791 should have turned into links to the instructors’ GitHub profiles.



 Click here to see screenshots of the tagging.


When you type the tags, it will look like regular plain text:







But once you create the issue, the tags, if they are valid, will turn bold and underlined, and are links to the instructors’ GitHub profiles. (You shouldn’t see a yellow background, though: that is only because I tagged myself to get this screenshot.)







Back in VS Code, add a line to your README.md to describe that you created a GitHub repo on today’s date (include the repo’s URL in the note).
Commit the change to README.md to your Git repo.
Push to the remote and on GitHub, check that the changes were applied in the online repo.

title: Week 6 Exercises: GitHub, OSC, and software
text:
Exercise 2: Login versus compute nodes
In GA1, you found out that your VS Code session runs on a compute node. Let’s explore that a bit more, and compare with a login node.

In OnDemand, open a shell on a login node by clicking “Clusters” in the top bar and then “Cardinal Shell Access”. You should see many lines of text printed to the terminal, which is standard information that OSC prints on login (but not compute) nodes, including details about your Project’s usage of its storage quota2.
In the Cardinal shell, run the command hostname, which prints the name of the node that you’re on (like echo $HOSTNAME that you used in GA1). Then, run the same command in your VS Code terminal, and compare the outputs. What in each node name tells you whether it is a login node or a compute node? And which cluster is each node part of?
Why does the Cardinal shell put you on a login node, whereas your VS Code session is on a compute node? And what does this mean for what you should (not) do in the Cardinal shell? For example, would it be OK to run FastQC on all FASTQ files of the Garrigós data there?
In the Cardinal shell, navigate to /fs/ess/PAS3493/people/$USER and list its contents. Do you see the same files as in VS Code, even though your VS Code session is running on a different cluster?
In your VS Code terminal, load the FastQC module and check that fastqc -v works. Predict whether fastqc -v will also work in the following two scenarios, and then check your predictions and interpret the results:

In the Cardinal shell.
In a second VS Code terminal (click the + icon in the terminal panel or the downward arrow next to it — see the screenshots below).



 Click here for screenshots on the second VS Code terminal.

If you click the downward arrow next to the + icon in the terminal panel, you get several options:





I like the “Split Terminal” option best, which allows you to see both terminals at once:





If you just click the + icon, or select “New Terminal” from the dropdown menu, you get a new terminal that takes up the entire panel, and you can switch between terminals using the panel on the side:





Either way, having multiple terminals can be quite handy!

In the lecture’s self-study exercise on modules, module spider salmon in VS Code said there was no Salmon module. Run the same command in the Cardinal shell. What do you get, and why?

Exercise 3: A specific software version
Say that you want to compare your results with those of a published study that used FastQC version 0.11.9, so you want to use that exact version as well.

Is FastQC version 0.11.9 available as an OSC module?
Get the URI of a Seqera container that contains FastQC version 0.11.9.
Check the container’s FastQC version.
Load the fastqc/0.12.1 module. You now have access to two different versions of FastQC. Before running anything, predict which version fastqc -v will print when you run it with and without the container prefix. Then, run both commands to check.

text:
Solutions

Exercise 1


2. Navigate to your dir for last week’s assignment

cd GA2



3. Set up a connection to the online repo

# (replace <SSH-URL-to-repo> with your actual SSH (not HTTPS!) URL,
#  which looks like 'git@github.com:<github-username>/<repo-name>.git')
git remote add origin <SSH-URL-to-repo>



4. Push your local repo to the online one you just created

When you push to a remote repo for the first time, you need to add the -u origin main part:
git push -u origin main



5. Are data and results on GitHub?

No: you listed these dirs in your .gitignore file, so their files were never committed, and git push only uploads commits. (Your .gitignore file itself is on GitHub, since you did commit it.)



8. Commit the change you made to README.md

# Stage the change to README.md
git add README.md

# Make a commit with a message describing the change
git commit -m "Update README with GitHub repo information"



9. Push to the remote again

Since you’ve pushed to this remote before, a simple git push works:
git push



Exercise 2


2. Node names

In the Cardinal shell:
hostname
cardinal-login01.hpc.osc.edu
In VS Code:
hostname
p0231.ten.osc.edu
(Your exact node names will differ.)

The Cardinal shell is on a login node, as you can tell from the login in its name, and it is on the Cardinal cluster, as the name also says.
VS Code is on a compute node, whose name is a letter followed by digits: the p means it is part of the Pitzer cluster.




3. Why a login node versus a compute node


The “Clusters” shell connects you directly to the cluster, without requesting any resources, so you end up on a login node.
By contrast, when you start a Code Server session, you request a compute job, and the job scheduler assigns your session to a compute node. This is because Code Server itself needs resources to run, and if many users were to run Code Server on a login node, it could become overloaded.
In the Cardinal shell, you share a login node with many other users, so you should only run light tasks there, like navigating, listing files, or checking which modules are available. Running FastQC on dozens of FASTQ files is a real analysis that would take a while and use considerable resources: do that on a compute node instead.




4. Files across clusters

cd /fs/ess/PAS3493/people/$USER
ls
You see the same files, because all of OSC’s nodes and clusters share the same file systems.



5. Loaded modules in other shells

# In the first VS Code terminal:
module load fastqc/0.12.1
fastqc -v
FastQC v0.12.1
# In the Cardinal shell, and in a second VS Code terminal:
fastqc -v
bash: fastqc: command not found...
Failed to search for file: GDBus.Error:org.freedesktop.DBus.Error.NameHasNoOwner: Could not activate remote peer.
It doesn’t work in either of them: loading a module only affects the shell session you loaded it in. The second VS Code terminal is on the same compute node as the first one, but it’s a separate shell session, so you would need to load the module there as well.



6. Salmon on Cardinal

In the Cardinal shell, module spider salmon finds a Salmon module, whereas in VS Code (on Pitzer) it didn’t. The clusters have mostly, but not entirely, the same modules.
Therefore, if you want to use modules, you should check that the software you need is available on the cluster you’ll run your analysis on. If that seems like a pain, I agree, and it’s one reason I prefer containers. Also note that this is quite an old version of Salmon (1.4.0, from 2020), whereas a container gives you the latest version.
module spider salmon
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  salmon: salmon/1.4.0
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

    This module can be loaded directly: module load salmon/1.4.0

    Help:
      This module loads salmon
      Configured and installed with modules:
      No modules loaded



Exercise 3


1. Is FastQC 0.11.9 available as a module?

No, only version 0.12.1 is available:
module spider fastqc
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  fastqc: fastqc/0.12.1
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

    This module can be loaded directly: module load fastqc/0.12.1




2. Get a container with FastQC 0.11.9

At https://seqera.io/containers, search for fastqc, select version 0.11.9 in the dropdown menu next to the bioconda::fastqc hit, and then proceed as shown in the lecture (don’t forget to select Singularity).
Your URI will look like oras://community.wave.seqera.io/library/fastqc:0.11.9--<hash>.



3. Check the container’s FastQC version

apptainer exec oras://community.wave.seqera.io/library/fastqc:0.11.9--1cc469c72218f8fc \
    fastqc -v
INFO:    Downloading oras image
352.3MiB / 352.3MiB [====================================================================================================================================================================================================] 100 % 43.1 MiB/s 0s
INFO:    gocryptfs not found, will not be able to use gocryptfs
FastQC v0.11.9



4. Compare the module and container versions

module load fastqc/0.12.1

apptainer exec oras://community.wave.seqera.io/library/fastqc:0.11.9--1cc469c72218f8fc \
    fastqc -v
INFO:    gocryptfs not found, will not be able to use gocryptfs
FastQC v0.11.9
fastqc -v
FastQC v0.12.1
With the container, you always get version 0.11.9, regardless of which modules are loaded: the container uses the software installed inside it. Without the container, you get the version from the loaded module.
