title: OSC: Beyond the basics
text:
Where we’re heading
Step by step, in this and the next few weeks,
you’ll learn to run command-line bioinformatics programs at OSC:


A deeper dive into OSC (this class)
How to use software at OSC, including programs that aren’t installed (next class)
How to write shell scripts (next week)
How to submit shell scripts as “batch jobs” (in week 9)
How to build functional commands to run such programs (throughout)

title: OSC: Beyond the basics
text:
Using compute nodes via “jobs”


Compute jobs
You can use compute nodes after requesting resources, such as a number of nodes and cores, and for how long you need them.
These requests result in “compute jobs” (or simply “jobs”). Our VS Code sessions are an example!





The job scheduler
Many users send requests all the time, so a job scheduler (at OSC, Slurm) considers each request and assigns resources to jobs as they become available.







In week 9, you’ll learn to submit scripts as “batch jobs” with Slurm.

title: OSC: Beyond the basics
text:
Recap: nodes and clusters



Node
A single computer that is a part of a supercomputer.

Supercomputer / Cluster
A collection of connected computers/nodes.

Supercomputer Center
A facility like OSC with one or more supercomputers. OSC has three: “Ascend”, “Cardinal”, and “Pitzer”.

title: OSC: Beyond the basics
text:
Cores
There is one more “level” than what was shown on the previous slide from week 2 —
each node has multiple cores:

title: OSC: Beyond the basics
text:
Cores


What is a core?

A component of a node (computer) that can independently perform a computing task, like running a bioinformatics program.
Also, many programs can use multiple cores for a single run, which can speed them up considerably.






Core / Processor / CPU / Thread

These terms are not technically synonyms, but are often used interchangeably.
For working at OSC, treat them as meaning the same thing: components of nodes that can be reserved and used independently.

title: OSC: Beyond the basics
text:
One node, several jobs
Typical compute jobs only use a part of a single node, yet multiple cores. For example:


Job A


Job A


Job B


Job B


Job B


Job B


free


free




A node with 8 cores (real Pitzer nodes have 40–48): Job A has 2 cores, Job B has 4, and 2 cores are free.



A job’s resource usage is measured in core hours. For example, if job A and job B above both request 2 hours, then job A would use 2 x 2 = 4 core hours, and job B would use 4 x 2 = 8 core hours.









Size of requests and wait times


When you request resources, the Slurm scheduler looks for a node with enough free cores. As such, smaller requests (fewer cores, less time) may start more quickly than larger ones, especially when the cluster is heavily used.

title: OSC: Beyond the basics
text:
System status
In OnDemand’s “Clusters” dropdown menu, click on the item at the bottom, “System Status”:





This page shows the live usage of the three clusters, and gives a good idea of the scale of the supercomputer center (next slide).




On the next slide, what does “processors” refer to?

Here, OSC uses the word “processor” to mean “core” (or “CPU”). As mentioned, these terms are often used interchangeably in practice.

title: OSC: Beyond the basics
text:
Side note






Why does OSC have multiple clusters rather than a single big one?


OSC buys a new cluster every few years and retires the oldest one,
so the clusters differ in age and hardware:

Pitzer (2018, expanded in 2020)
Ascend (2022, with many GPU nodes)
Cardinal (2024)

Among other things, rolling out clusters this way keeps some hardware up to date at all times,
and avoids downtime for the entire center.

title: OSC: Beyond the basics
text:
Compute node types


“Standard” nodes

By far the most numerous (Pitzer has 564).
Vary in size, e.g., 40–48 cores per node on Pitzer.
Used by default, and will serve you well for most omics analyses.






Other node types

Nodes with extra memory:
largemem and hugemem.
Nodes with GPUs (Graphics Processing Units) in addition to CPUs.









When are these useful?


You may occasionally need these, for example for genome or transcriptome assembly (large-memory nodes) or Oxford Nanopore base-calling (GPU nodes).

title: OSC: Beyond the basics
text:
Memory versus storage
When we talk about a computer’s memory, this refers to RAM — don’t confuse this with file storage.




Memory (RAM)

The data a computer is actively using.
Accessed orders of magnitude faster than data stored on disk.
E.g., heavily used when you play a game or have many browser tabs open.






Storage (disk)

The data that is saved in files on disk.








When your computer freezes, memory is often full, and it starts using disk storage as “virtual memory”, which is much slower.













Bioinformatics programs may load input data into memory for fast access, and hold intermediate results there too. With large datasets, they may need 10s–100s of GBs of memory.











At OSC, available memory is proportional to the number of cores you request (often 4 GB per core).

title: OSC: Beyond the basics
text:
OSC bills Project-wise
OSC bills Projects (not individual users), and only for two things:


File storage

File storage in the Project dirs (/fs/ess).
Charged per TB per month for what you have reserved, not what you actually use.




Compute

Compute node usage.
Charged per core hour.




Who pays?

Every OSU PI gets a $1,000 yearly credit.
OSU colleges pay some or all of the costs — CFAES currently pays all of it.










Prices for academic usage are generally low, but a Project using dozens of TBs and tens of thousands of core hours would still be charged over a thousand dollars per year.

title: OSC: Beyond the basics
text:
Using and managing OSC Projects
In this course, we only use the course’s OSC Project PAS3493. For your own research, you would likely use a Project specific to a research project, or your lab’s general-use Project.



Using a Project
In practice, “using” a Project means:

Storage: Storing data in its /fs/ess and/or /fs/scratch dirs.
Compute: Selecting the Project when starting compute jobs, like VS Code and batch jobs.






Managing a Project
Generally only PIs can do this (more info ). Project admins can, among other things:

Manage the compute budget and /fs/ess storage allocation.
Add users to the Project.

title: OSC: Beyond the basics
text:
Storage areas: final notes


Hidden files in Home

Your Home dir will have hidden files (those starting with a .) that are generated and used automatically by software.
Don’t mess with them unless you know what you’re doing!




Accessing backups

Home and Project dirs are backed up daily.
You don’t have direct access to the backups, but can email OSC to restore your files from a specific date.




Files across clusters

OSC’s clusters share the entire file system.
So, you can access your files with the same paths across all clusters.

Omics analyses use many programs
A typical omics data analysis workflow consists of a sequence of specialized bioinformatics programs (a.k.a. software or tools). For example, the RNA-seq workflow we’ll go through:

title: OSC: Beyond the basics
text:
Installed software at OSC


Basic system-wide installations

Besides the shell and Git commands we’ve been using, other commonly used software like Python and Apptainer can be used without any extra steps.






Modules

OSC has also installed a number of more specialized programs, including bioinformatics tools.
You can use these programs after loading their “module” using the module command — we’ll do this in the next class.








But: The collection of installed software at OSC is not comprehensive, and program versions are not always the most recent.

text:
Module Browser

title: OSC: Beyond the basics
text:
Other options


Installing software yourself?
Installing software like you would on your own computer is often not possible at OSC:

You don’t have administrator privileges.
You will often run into issues with dependencies (other software that a program depends on).






Conda and containers

Conda: Allows you to install software into “environments” you can load.
Containers: Self-contained software packages that can be distributed.
Both:

Bypass the dependency and administrator privilege issues.
Make it easy to switch between versions or use mutually incompatible software.
Are good for reproducibility.

Direct Unix shell access
The Clusters dropdown menu also gives direct access to a Unix shell on any of the three clusters.

In the course, we use VS Code (Code Server) to access a shell,
but the Clusters dropdown can occasionally be useful as a quicker access point.

title: OSC: Beyond the basics
text:
Contacting OSC to get help
Open a support case in the OSC Service Center (log in with your OSC credentials),
or email oschelp@osc.edu, with questions like:

Problems with your account
Installing or using specific software
Why your jobs keep failing

They are usually quite quick to respond!








Citing OSC


When you use OSC, it’s good practice to acknowledge and cite OSC in your papers — see their citation page.

title: Week 7: Shell scripts
text:
1 Overview
This week, you will learn how to write shell scripts and use them to run programs with command-line interfaces (CLIs), like various bioinformatics tools.
Looking at the bigger picture, one key goal of this course is to enable you to submit shell scripts as “batch jobs” at OSC. This week, we will focus on shell scripts, and in two weeks, we will move on to submitting these scripts as batch jobs.
This is a pretty packed week and we may not reach the end of the in-class material on Wednesday. If not, we will finish the remainder at the start of next week. (The assignment will only cover material from the first class page.)

title: Shell scripting II – rerunning scripts with loops
text:
1 Introduction

1.1 Learning goals
In the previous session, you wrote a shell script to run FastQC for a single FASTQ file. Here, we will focus on running that script many times with loops. Specifically, you will learn:

How for loops work
How to use a for loop to loop over files and run a shell script many times
How to keep a record of your analysis steps in a Markdown file
Self-study: How to use parameter expansion to search-and-replace text in variables
Self-study: How to loop over samples (e.g., pairs of FASTQ files) rather than individual files



1.2 The big picture
The strategy you’ve learned so far, and that we will stick to, is writing scripts that run a single program a single time. We do this even though you commonly need to run a CLI tool many times, e.g. separately for each file or sample. But at OSC, you can save a lot of time by submitting a separate batch job for each file or sample, since these jobs can all run simultaneously1. To accommodate this, you will:

Make your scripts flexible by passing arguments to them (as seen in the previous session)
Loop over files/samples outside of the script, and run/submit the script many times (as you’ll see today)

As a result, you’ll also type important code outside of your scripts, and that code orchestrates your workflow. You will store that code in Markdown files, which then provide a record of what you did.


1.3 Getting ready

At https://ondemand.osc.edu, start a VS Code session in /fs/ess/PAS3493/people/$USER.
In the terminal, navigate to your week07 dir.

title: Shell scripting II – rerunning scripts with loops
text:
3 For loops
Loops are used to repeat operations. Here, we’ll cover the most common type of loop, the for loop3, which iterates over a pre-defined collection, such as a list of files. Each iteration (or “round”) of the loop uses one element of the collection, and allows you to perform one or more actions for that element.

3.1 A non-coding example
In a way, you’re likely to already think in for loops regularly in your daily life. Say you have a rack with three tubes, and your protocol says:

For each tube in the rack: add 10 µL of buffer to the tube, vortex it, and spin it down.

Here’s what that instruction consists of:

A collection of items to go through: the tubes in the rack.
A set of actions that are repeated for every item: add buffer, vortex, spin down.
A placeholder that stands in for “the item I’m currently working on”: “the tube” or “it”. In the first round, “the tube” means tube 1; in the second round, tube 2; and so on.

You’d go through the tubes one at a time, doing all three actions for a tube before moving on to the next one. And you’re done when you run out of tubes: with three tubes, you’d do this three times. If we wrote that protocol step in for loop syntax, it would look like this (this is not real code!):
for tube in tube1 tube2 tube3; do
    add 10 µL buffer to $tube
    vortex $tube
    spin down $tube
done
In shell code, a for loop has the same three components:

The collection comes after in: here, tube1 tube2 tube3.
The actions go between do and done, in indented lines so it’s clear what is being repeated.
The placeholder is a variable, whose name you choose and put after for: here, tube. Inside the loop, you refer to it with $tube, and in each round of the loop, it contains a different item from the collection.



3.2 A first shell loop
Let’s type out the example below in your loops-practice.md and then run it in the terminal. Here, the collection is a short list of three fruits, and the only action is to print the current fruit.
In your code block below the “A first shell loop” header, type the following:


loops-practice.md (excerpt)

for fruit in apple banana plum; do
    echo "Fruit: $fruit"
done

Then, send the code to the terminal: either press the Play button at the right end of the code block, or press Shift+Enter with your cursor in the code block.
You should see your code appear in the terminal along with the following output. This output shows that the echo line ran three times, and each time, the variable $fruit contained a different fruit:
for fruit in apple banana plum; do
    echo "Fruit: $fruit"
done
Fruit: apple
Fruit: banana
Fruit: plum
Under the hood, the following was actually run by the shell — three times, a value was assigned to $fruit, and then the echo command was run:


fruit=apple
echo "Fruit: $fruit"

fruit=banana
echo "Fruit: $fruit"

fruit=plum
echo "Fruit: $fruit"







© Kellogg’s





3.3 Multiple actions per iteration
Just like in the tube example, you can perform multiple actions in each round of the loop: every line between do and done is run for every item.
For the next example, we will count the number of characters in each fruit’s name. Here’s how to do that for a single word, where we add the -n option to echo to prevent it from adding a newline (which would otherwise be counted as a character too), and use the -c option of wc to count the number of characters rather than lines:
echo -n "apple" | wc -c
5
Below, for each fruit, we print its name and then count the number of characters in its name:


loops-practice.md (excerpt)

for fruit in apple banana plum; do
    echo "Fruit: $fruit"
    echo "Number of characters:"
    echo -n "$fruit" | wc -c
    echo
done

Fruit: apple
Number of characters:
5

Fruit: banana
Number of characters:
6

Fruit: plum
Number of characters:
4

Notice that all four lines ran for apple before any of them ran for banana: the loop completes all actions for one item before moving on to the next item.


3.4 Loop recap so far
To recap some key things you should understand about for loops:

In each iteration of the loop, one element in the collection is being assigned to the variable specified after for.
The loop will run exactly as many times as there are items in the collection.
The indented lines’ code is being repeated: all lines are run for one item before the loop moves on to the next4.
The variable name is up to you. Like with other variables, try to choose a name that is descriptive.
Like with other variables, use a $ when you reference (echo "$fruit") but not when you assign (for fruit).







NoteMore about the syntax of for loops (Click to expand)





On the first and last, unindented lines, for loops contain the following mandatory keywords:







Keyword
Purpose




for
After for, we set the variable name (an arbitrary name; above we used fruit)


in
After in, we specify the collection (list of items) we are looping over


do
After do, we have one or more lines specifying what to do with each item


done
Tells the shell we are done with the loop












TipWhy is there “; do” in a for loop? (Click to expand)





You may find the ; do at the end of the first line of the for loop to be odd. What is that all about?
First, let’s see what a semicolon does in the first place. It’s a way to enter multiple commands on a single line — for example, the line below would first run ls and then echo "Hello":
ls; echo "Hello"
(So, ; can be thought of as a counterpart to \, which allows you to spread a single command across multiple lines: with a ;, you can have multiple commands on a single line.)
Alternatively, you could write for loops like so:
for fruit in apple banana plum
do
    echo "Fruit: $fruit"
done
Some people prefer that variant. You can do it either way, but we will continue to demonstrate the ; do variant, which is more symmetric, and saves a line of code.





3.5 Combining loops and globbing
In an omics data analysis, you will often have many files that need to be processed in the same way. For example, we wrote a fastqc.sh script that runs FastQC for a single FASTQ file, and we want to run that script for all FASTQ files in a directory. We can loop over file names just like we looped over fruits above:


loops-practice.md (excerpt)

for fastq_file in ../garrigos/fastq/S63_R1.fastq.gz ../garrigos/fastq/S63_R2.fastq.gz; do
    echo "Now processing file: $fastq_file"
done

Now processing file: ../garrigos/fastq/S63_R1.fastq.gz
Now processing file: ../garrigos/fastq/S63_R2.fastq.gz
However, typing out all file names is tedious and error-prone. Instead, we can use globbing to automatically generate a list of file names, and then loop over that list, all in one line of code:


loops-practice.md (excerpt)

for fastq_file in ../garrigos/fastq/*fastq.gz; do
    echo "Running an analysis on $fastq_file"
    # [This is where you would put additional commands to process each FASTQ file]
done

Running an analysis on ../garrigos/fastq/S63_R1.fastq.gz
Running an analysis on ../garrigos/fastq/S63_R2.fastq.gz
Running an analysis on ../garrigos/fastq/S64_R1.fastq.gz
Running an analysis on ../garrigos/fastq/S64_R2.fastq.gz
# [...output truncated...]
The shell expands the glob into a list of matching file names before the loop starts (recall from week 4 that expansion is done by the shell itself), so to the loop, this is no different from the typed-out list of file names above.


 Exercise 1: What will these loops print?
Create these files:
mkdir -p sandbox
touch sandbox/file1.txt sandbox/S1_R1.fastq.gz sandbox/S1_R2.fastq.gz
Now, what do you expect the output of each of the following loops to be? Test your predictions by running the loops (either directly in the terminal or by putting them in your Markdown file loops-practice.md and sending them to the terminal):
for file in sandbox/*fastq.gz; do
    echo "I have found file $file"
done

for file in sandbox/f*; do
    echo "$f"
done

for file in sandbox/*.bam; do
    echo "I have found file $file"
done



 Exercise 2: Another loop
Modify the globbing loop above (the one printing “Running an analysis on …”) to print the following for each FASTQ file (output for 2 files shown):
Running an analysis on ../garrigos/fastq/S63_R1.fastq.gz
File size:
-rw-rw----+ 1 jelmer PAS0471 21M Sep  9 13:46 ../garrigos/fastq/S63_R1.fastq.gz
Number of lines:
2000000

Running an analysis on ../garrigos/fastq/S63_R2.fastq.gz
File size:
-rw-rw----+ 1 jelmer PAS0471 22M Sep  9 13:46 ../garrigos/fastq/S63_R2.fastq.gz
Number of lines:
2000000
Then, take a look at the line counts in your output:

How many reads does each file contain?
Why do the R1 and R2 files of a sample contain the same number of reads?



 Click for a hint

To count the lines in a gzip-compressed file, recall from the week 4 exercises that zcat prints the decompressed contents of a file, which you can then pipe into another command.

section: 4 Running a script many times with a loop
text:
4 Running a script many times with a loop

4.1 Your FastQC script
In the previous session, you wrote the following script to run FastQC, which should be saved at scripts/fastqc.sh.


Click to see the script’s contents



scripts/fastqc.sh

#!/bin/bash
set -euo pipefail

# FastQC container
CONTAINER=oras://community.wave.seqera.io/library/fastqc:0.12.1--104d26ddd9519960

# Copy the placeholder variables
fastq="$1"
outdir="$2"

# Initial logging
echo "Starting script fastqc.sh"
date
echo "Input FASTQ file:   $fastq"
echo "Output dir:         $outdir"
echo

# Create the output dir if needed
mkdir -p "$outdir"

# Run FastQC with its container
apptainer exec "$CONTAINER" fastqc --outdir "$outdir" "$fastq"

# Final logging
echo
echo "Used FastQC version:"
apptainer exec "$CONTAINER" fastqc --version
echo
echo "Successfully finished script fastqc.sh"
date


Recall that the script accepts one FASTQ file as an argument, so it can only be run for one file at a time. For example:
bash scripts/fastqc.sh ../garrigos/fastq/S63_R1.fastq.gz results/fastqc


4.2 A “protocol” Markdown file
To run the script for all FASTQ files, we’ll use a loop. This is still practice, but unlike the loops in your loops-practice.md file, it does resemble a real analysis step. So, let’s use it to see what a proper record of such a step would look like: we’ll store the loop in a “protocol” section of a new README.md file, which also describes the project as a whole. For small projects, such a simple protocol in the main README.md can suffice.

Create a README.md file in your week07 dir and open it in the editor:
touch README.md
Copy-paste the following into your README.md:


README.md

# RNA-seq data analysis

## General information

- **Author**: <your-name>
- **Date**: 2026-10-07
- **Environment**: Pitzer cluster at OSC via VS Code
- **Working dir**: `/fs/ess/PAS3493/people/<user>/week07`

## Project background

This project is ...

## Protocol








In a few weeks, we’ll discuss how you can organize this kind of information for larger projects.





4.3 Looping over FASTQ files
You will now loop over all FASTQ files in the ../garrigos/fastq dir, and run your fastqc.sh script for each file. Add the following under ## Protocol in your README.md, and then run the code inside the code block (this will take a few minutes to run for all 44 files):


README.md (excerpt)

### Step 1 - Run FastQC for each FASTQ file:

```{bash}
for fastq in ../garrigos/fastq/*fastq.gz; do
    bash scripts/fastqc.sh "$fastq" results/fastqc
done
```

Starting script fastqc.sh
Wed Oct  7 13:58:21 EDT 2026
Input FASTQ file:   ../garrigos/fastq/S63_R1.fastq.gz
Output dir:         results/fastqc

Started analysis of S63_R1.fastq.gz
Approx 5% complete for S63_R1.fastq.gz
# [...output truncated...]

Successfully finished script fastqc.sh
Wed Oct  7 13:58:26 EDT 2026

Starting script fastqc.sh
Wed Oct  7 13:58:26 EDT 2026
Input FASTQ file:   ../garrigos/fastq/S63_R2.fastq.gz
Output dir:         results/fastqc

Started analysis of S63_R2.fastq.gz
Approx 5% complete for S63_R2.fastq.gz
# [...output truncated...]
That produces a lot of output! You can hopefully see that this looping approach is quite powerful, allowing you to easily run a script many times.






NoteTwo different variables called fastq



The loop variable fastq and the variable fastq inside the fastqc.sh script share a name, but they are separate variables: a script runs in its own, new shell, which can’t see the variables you assigned in your terminal. The only way the file name gets into the script is as an argument: the loop passes "$fastq" as the first argument, which the script receives as $1 and then copies to its own fastq variable.








TipThis loop runs the script sequentially, not in parallel



The loop above runs the fastqc.sh script sequentially: only after it has finished for the first FASTQ file, it will run for the second file, and so on. If these had been full-size FASTQ files, it may have taken hours for this to finish.
So, while you have now learned an elegant way to run a script many times, you have not yet learned how to run it simultaneously in parallel. In week 9, you’ll learn about doing this by submitting scripts as batch jobs.

title: Shell scripting II – rerunning scripts with loops
text:
5 Self-study: Looping over samples
FastQC is run separately for each FASTQ file, but many tools that process paired-end data need the R1 and R2 files of a sample together. Such tools should be run once per sample, i.e. once per pair of FASTQ files.
How can you loop over pairs of FASTQ files? There are two main ways:

Create a list of sample IDs, loop over these IDs, and find the pair of FASTQ files with matching names.
Loop over the R1 files only and then deduce the name of the corresponding R2 file inside the loop. This works because R1 and R2 file names are identical except for the read-direction identifier (typically _R1/_R2).

We will use the second method. To deduce the R2 file name, you’ll first need to learn about parameter expansion.






Type and run the code in this self-study section from your loops-practice.md file.




5.1 Parameter expansion
“Parameter expansion” (“parameter” is another word for variable) is the shell’s term for retrieving a variable’s value, as in $fastq. Some special forms of parameter expansion modify the value as it is retrieved — for example, to search-and-replace text:

Start by assigning a short DNA sequence to a variable:
dna_seq="AAGTTCAT"
echo "$dna_seq"
AAGTTCAT
Now, use parameter expansion to replace all Ts with Us:
echo "${dna_seq//T/U}"
AAGUUCAU
You can also assign the result of the parameter expansion back to a variable:
rna_seq="${dna_seq//T/U}"
echo "$rna_seq"
AAGUUCAU

So, the syntax for this type of parameter expansion is ${var_name//<search>/<replace>} — let’s deconstruct that:

You reference the variable using the “full notation” with braces: here, ${dna_seq}.
You add two forward slashes after the variable name, and then the search pattern: here, //T.
After another forward slash, enter the replacement: here, /U.








NoteReplace all matches or just the first? (Click to expand)





If you only want to replace the first match, use a single forward slash after the variable name: ${var_name/<search>/<replace>}. Compare:
echo "${dna_seq/T/U}"
AAGUTCAT




 Self-study exercise 1: Get the R2 file name with parameter expansion
After assigning the file name ../garrigos/fastq/S63_R1.fastq.gz to a variable, as shown below, add the parameter expansion to obtain the name of the corresponding R2 file to the second line:
fastq_R1=../garrigos/fastq/S63_R1.fastq.gz
fastq_R2=


 Click for the solution

fastq_R1=../garrigos/fastq/S63_R1.fastq.gz
fastq_R2="${fastq_R1/_R1/_R2}"
Test that it worked:
echo "$fastq_R2"
../garrigos/fastq/S63_R2.fastq.gz

Next, a labmate suggests the shorter fastq_R2="${fastq_R1/1/2}". Does that give the correct result for this file? Would it still work if the sample were called S61 instead of S63?


 Click for the solution

It works for S63, since the first 1 in the path happens to be the one in R1. But for ../garrigos/fastq/S61_R1.fastq.gz, the 1 in the sample ID would be replaced instead, giving ../garrigos/fastq/S62_R1.fastq.gz — the R1 file of a different sample! So, make your search pattern as specific as possible, like _R1.




5.2 A per-sample loop
Using parameter expansion, you can create a loop that iterates over R1 FASTQ files only, and then deduces the corresponding R2 file name. Here is a loop that runs once per sample, and prints the two file names for each:
for R1 in ../garrigos/fastq/*_R1.fastq.gz; do
    R2="${R1/_R1/_R2}"
    echo "R1 file: $R1"
    echo "R2 file: $R2"
    echo
done
R1 file: ../garrigos/fastq/S63_R1.fastq.gz
R2 file: ../garrigos/fastq/S63_R2.fastq.gz

R1 file: ../garrigos/fastq/S64_R1.fastq.gz
R2 file: ../garrigos/fastq/S64_R2.fastq.gz

# [...output truncated...]






Search for _R1 and not just R1: in other datasets, the string “R1” may also occur in the sample ID (e.g. ERR1234)!



To run a script for each sample, you would replace the echo lines with a call to a script that accepts both files as arguments. You’ll practice that in the exercise below with a “mock” script, and in next week’s exercises, you’ll write such a script for the program TrimGalore.


 Self-study exercise 2: Run a script with a per-sample loop

Write a script scripts/trim_mock.sh that accepts three arguments: an R1 FASTQ file (assigned to $R1), an R2 FASTQ file (assigned to $R2), and an output dir (assigned to $outdir).
You can use your fastqc.sh script as a template, but instead of running FastQC, this script should “mock-run” the fictional trimmer program as follows:
# Mock-run the tool: by prefacing the command with 'echo',
# the command will merely be printed, not run.
echo trimmer --in1 "$R1" --in2 "$R2" --outdir "$outdir"


 Click for the solution



scripts/trim_mock.sh

#!/bin/bash
set -euo pipefail

# Copy the placeholder variables
R1="$1"
R2="$2"
outdir="$3"

# Initial logging
echo "Starting script trim_mock.sh"
date
echo "Input R1 file:       $R1"
echo "Input R2 file:       $R2"
echo "Output dir:          $outdir"
echo

# Create the output dir if needed
mkdir -p "$outdir"

# Mock-run the tool
echo trimmer --in1 "$R1" --in2 "$R2" --outdir "$outdir"

# Final logging
echo
echo "Successfully finished script trim_mock.sh"
date


In your loops-practice.md file, write a loop over all R1 FASTQ files that runs the trim_mock.sh script for each sample.


 Click for the solution



loops-practice.md (excerpt)

## Self-study exercise 2

We will loop over R1 files only, and deduce the R2 file name:

```bash
for R1 in ../garrigos/fastq/*_R1.fastq.gz; do
    R2="${R1/_R1/_R2}"
    bash scripts/trim_mock.sh "$R1" "$R2" results/trim_mock
done
```

title: Shell scripting II – rerunning scripts with loops
text:
6 Recap and next steps
In this lecture, you’ve learned how to write and use for loops, and how to use them to run a shell script many times: both for each FASTQ file and, using parameter expansion, for each sample. You’ve also started recording your analysis steps in a “protocol” Markdown file.
The optional shell scripting self-study page covers command substitution, basename and dirname, renaming files with loops, and more. Next week, we’ll look at using generative AI when coding. And in week 9, we’ll move on to submitting shell scripts as batch jobs at OSC.

title: Shell scripting II – rerunning scripts with loops
text:
Footnotes


 It is possible to use another strategy that parallelizes program runs within a script, but we will use this strategy instead.↩︎
 This makes the code blocks “executable” — you’ll learn much more about that when we talk about using Quarto with R code in week 14.↩︎
 You can learn about while loops in the optional shell scripting self-study page.↩︎
 The indentation itself is optional for the shell, but makes loops much easier to read.↩︎
